2016 Early Access Review I love this game so much. Even in it's current pre-release status there is a lot to explore and do.Here are some of the main features of the game:- It's a sandbox game; Apart from the literal sense where most of the map is desert, you are also given a character and let loose into the world to do as you please.- It's challenging; Especially at the start of the game it will difficult as it will feel as if everything is stacked against you. This feeling is actually pretty accurate. Just about everything IS against you. But as you play, you will become more powerful and given enough time, you will eventually be in a position where you will gain the upper hand. Don't expect this to happen overnight though.- You can recruit followers; Most of them are just random nobodies who aren't good at anything. Just like you when you start a fresh game. Certain followers will sometimes have unique dialogue as you travel with them, giving the world a but more colour and the factions some background lore as they tell you about the areas you visit. This is still a work in progress though.- You can build outposts; Buy a house in one of the cities or build a comletely new outpost from scratch. You can have your followers farm and mine for resources and food, so your outpost can become completely self sufficient.- You will get your ass kicked; Yes, you will. But that's okay. Usually after being beaten into a bloody pulp by some angry bandits, one of your unconscious characters will wake up and you can have him heal the others. Consider it a learning experience. You will have time to reflect on what happened as your squad limps back to town. Unless the slavers find you first that is... Or the cannibals... or the giant, blind carnivorous beak things eat you alive...- It's hilarious;The npc in the game will occasionally tell you the most ridiculous stories. The people in kenshi usually have very few sensible things to say. And they lie. And they swear. A lot. There is a lot of very dry humor in this game.** This game is not for everyone!!! **If the above mentioned features sound appealing, I really suggest you try the demo first.Kenshi is a very difficult game, especially at the start. Some people WILL get frustrated and quit and if that's you, then that would be a waste of your money. Defeat is a big part of this game.Also realise that this game is still very much in development. Not all features have been implemented yet and those that have been might be changed or removed. If you want to get an idea of where the game is headed and what features are likely to be added then head over to the official lo-fi forum and have a look at the road map. There are however, frequent updates and stuff gets added, fixed and broken and then fixed again (usually).

2020 This game is very...... interesting,At first I thought this game was going a crock of garbage, given how when the game first came out, it was quite fitting of that description. But now, after two years of development from Bethesda, which included adding a free DLC fro everyone, adding free battle passes, and quite a lot more, I would actually recommend playing this if you are wanting a fresh new style to the fallout franchise.Now, this game is NOT perfect right now, it still has a lot of bugs and problems that need to be fixed, including fixing a main mission, which is needed in order to finish the main story, and a bug revolving around few of the Achievements. But honestly, if you are worried that the game is a bug filled broken mess of a game, don't worry, a bunch of the most game breaking bugs were and are now patched, with the exclusions posted above.Alright, getting into the gameplay itself, and man, was I surprised! Originally I thought the game was was going to be a very grindy styled game, that expected a lot out of it's players, and while it has that need to grind some materials for making power armors and mods for both weapons and armors, it's very generous on some, if not most of the materials you need, and grinding caps is pretty much just completing a few daily quests, mainly wanting to do the Factions Dailies to get extra respect from them on top of it. As for Main Events, such as Scorched Earth, and Colossal Problem, etc. They are actually loads of fun to hop into them. And there quick nature of only being 30 minutes long make for some fun, intense, especially on Colossal Problem. Do be wary though, these events are mostly made for higher leveled players, so if you're new to the game, don't expect these to be all sunshine and rainbows. But of course, with every positive to this game and it's content, there's gotta be some negatives, so let's them out of the way.The first, and my biggest complaint (as of right now) is the very odd choice that came when rebalancing weapons, mainly bloodied ones. While I do completely understand that bloodied builds do need to be nerfed due to their absurd damage output when fighting tougher foes such as Earle and SB Queen, it makes me very confused on why the percentages on weapons for the nerf are so drastic, especially for the Gatling Plasma and the Gatling Laser, as both were hit with an insane ~80-90 damage percentage nerf, making both of these weapons completely useles, while other weapons got away with a 30% or a 50% damage nerf. It's super odd on all these random percentages coming with weapons being either hurt softly or being thrown in the dirt. Secondly, Daily Ops needs to be reworked just a bit, the overwhelming amount of enemies that come out and just overrun the last part of daily ops is just annoying, and you have to spam stimpacks like no ones business. Lastly, just fix Fallout Forever Achievement and An Ounce of Prevation PLEASE!But looking past those, this game has a huge amount of charm, and I would totally recommend buying this game if you want a fresh new fallout game. :)

2020 I had this gifted to me by a friend and have since proceeded to gift it to another three friends with my highest recommendations. It's quite simply the best game I've ever played, though not for the faint of heart - my main save is sitting at 140 hours of playtime and I haven't yet exhausted its content.If you don't make a point of exploring everything thoroughly you're likely to end up missing most of the game, and the bosses and platforming challenges both escalate along a smooth learning curve into such lofty heights of difficulty that you'll get vertigo looking back down the slope.In addition, all gameplay mechanics and features are second in importance to the world of Hallownest and its internal logic, which some have complained about in terms of the common need for retracing your steps through different areas coupled with regular deaths as you gradually git gud.However, if you stick with it through the early rough patches you'll find yourself dying far less, enjoying the exploration and discovery more and more, and becoming ever more engaged with the Knight as it continues in its quest to destinations unknown.I found this game very challenging for most of my playtime, with bosses taking hours to beat and platforming seeming unreasonably difficult. I'd just resigned myself to never being able to complete the game without selling my soul when I got a new computer and found everything becoming fabulously smooth. Turns out the prohibitive challenge had been due almost entirely to my laptop with its regular microfreezes and dropped inputs, causing the bosses' telegraphs and attacks to regularly be frozen out of existence until I took damage from them.With that shackle released from my leg I have continued on to beat the game with 111% completion (working on the last percent) and more recently do a deathless 100% completion run in only 12 hours.Looking forward to Silksong and anything else Team Cherry decides to turn their hand to.112% completion edit: The art style, soundtrack and story are all an easy 10/10, and meld so seamlessly into the whole experience that I somehow managed to forget to mention them in my original review. There are also four free DLCs which add a significant chunk to the base game and also grant bonus kudos to Team Cherry for spending an extra few years working on them for no extra money after the game's original release. This is about as good value for money as you can get from a game, although it does occasionally prove frustrating in how difficult it is to throw more than $10 at Team Cherry.

2017 Early Access Review TLDR - I only wish I'd downloaded this earlierI'm a huge RTS fan but have never bought a game in Early Access before, so Northgard had been on my watch list for ages, just waiting for the full release. But then yesterday I was bored and it was in the sale so curiosity overcame me and, honestly, I was blown away.Just to make this clear, aside from the lack of a single player campaign, pretty limited tutorial instructions, and some reported issues with multiplayer, Northgard is more of a finished game than many others are months after release. There's still that campaign, some more tribes, and no doubt some other extras to come, and my only (tiny) gripe is that I think some more work is needed on balancing everything, but at £15 it's an absolute steal.What you get is the spiritual successor to The Settlers that many of us have longed for for years. Older gamers and those using emulators will see elements of The Settlers 1 and 2, and I detected a bit of Genesia and some other long-forgotten classics. Younger gamers may pick up on The Settlers 7 (my favourite of the later games) and some of the better near-misses vying for the abandoned crown. And that's important when it comes to justifying an early access purchase, because The Settlers was always a game where the real fun was in the huge skirmish maps, not the more restricted campaigns. This is one of those games you'll go back to just for the fun of it.In true Settlers style, it's pretty and it's pretty slow for an RTS, with the pace changing through the seasons and in response to (pretty frequent) incursions into your territory from the wildlife and your opponents. The expansion mechanic, which requires scouting territories and buying them out, is similar to the Settlers 7 mechanic and it does the job. It's nothing groundbreaking, but then it doesn't need to be.Likewise, all the usual RTS / city builder mechanics are there, focused around generating food, money, resources, and 'fame', and building a warband to go raiding; and the Viking setting ties all this together very nicely. This means that even though the instructions are a little sparse it's still easy to pick up, and anyway part of the fun of a good RTS is working out how everything works. If this sounds a little less than enthusiastic, it's not meant to be. RTS is a hard genre to perfect because in the heat of a fight small ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ can quickly become deal breakers, but even in its unfinished state I haven't found any.As other reviewers have said, Northgard has all the signs of becoming an absolute classic. It may already be one.

2016 I'm going to give an introduction to people who have no idea what Garry's mod is and why it's one o the most popular games available on steam. Garry's Mod isn't necessarily a game, it's a tool, it's a tool that the steam community have been able to turnaround and make into a game with servers, game modes, weapons and armour. I personally don't think Face punch are the developers of this game, they gave the community a basis to form their own game. If you get Garry's mod and nothing else, you are probably going to be confused why people like it this much. However, if u get around 10 mods off of the steam workshop, you will see why.One of the main reasons people love Garry's Mod this much is due to the community mods, it's not the game necessarily but the mods made by the community. Garry's Mod was originally released in 2004 as a mod for Half-Life 2 and escalated in popularity when it was brought onto Steam. A game that was released in 2004 still has 1000s of players going on each day, I have tons of friends that just play Garry's Mod an nothing else on their steam profile, because of the variety this game has.There's a sandbox mode which is what it is. You can do whatever the hell you want. You can make a zombie apocalypse happen, you can make NPCs into a happy family or you can shoot an NPC in the face. There are online servers dedicated to each of the Garry's Mod game modes so you can play multiplayer in sandbox which furthers the possibilities of what you can do. You can role-play, you can have a death match with your friends there are endless possibilities.There's Trouble in Terrorist Town which is best to be played with at least 4 players and is not possible to be played with 1 player. There are a group of players in a server, all of them are innocent except for one (depending on how many people are in the server there can be two terrorists and there can also be one detective who can examine a corpse and determine information about him) the terrorists' goal is to kill all the innocent without being suspected and not to be killed by the innocent. The innocents' goal is to stay alive for 5 minutes and find the terrorist and kill them. I personally don't play much of TTT mainly due to neither me or my friends having a mic but if you have a group of friends with a mic, this game is perfect.My personal favourite game mode is Prop Hunt. There are two teams, Hunters and Props. The Props are given 30 seconds to disguise themselves as props and hide in the map. After 30 seconds, the Hunters are released and they are given 4 minutes and 30 seconds to find all of the props. There's something about Prop Hunt which I find addicting. I always find achieved and feel like I outsmarted someone when I'm on either of the team. If you feel like you aren't accomplishing anything in life, give Prop Hunt a try.Another game mode that I've spent a lot of time on is death run. There are two teams (again), the Deaths and the Runners.The runners are unleashed upon a map and their goal is to get to the end. However there are traps hidden around the map which the Deaths need to activate to prevent the Runners from reaching the end. I found this game to probably be the most frustrating out of all of the game modes as I kept on dying half the time because of my own stupidity and not because of the traps. I only recommend that you play death run if you're experienced at Garry's Mod as there are a few things in death run that inexperienced players won't understand how to do.There's also Hide and Seek which is self explanatory. There are two teams, the hiders and the seekers, the hiders need to hide in the environment and the seekers have a certain amount of time to find all of the hiders. This is a bit like prop hunt but it's harder, when in prop hunt the "Hiders" could disguise themselves as props and blend in with the environment and the "seekers" had a full arsenal of weapons, in Hide and Seek, the Hiders won't be able to blend in with the environment and the Seekers don't have any weapons to kill the hiders with, they need to chase them and catch up with them. I only recommend this if you're finding Prop Hunt either boring, tedious or you're sick of winning each time as if you are still enjoying Prop Hunt there isn't much else here, it's only for the players that want a bit more of a challenge.The next game mode is Murder. Murder is basically like TTT but harder. In Murder there are two teams, Bystanders and the Murderer. The Murderer is given a knife and they need to kill everyone with it and the bystanders are defenceless except for one of them that has a Magnum revolver. Their goal is to figure out who is the murderer and the person who has the gun needs to shoot and kill the murderer. Similar to Hide and Seek, I only recommend this to people who are getting sick of TTT or are finding it too easy as if you're enjoying TTT there won't be anything here for you.The last game mode that I'm going to talk about is Jailbreak. This is basically like the Minecraft mod Cops and Robbers, There are two teams, the Prisoners and the Officers and one of the officers is the Warden. The prisoners' goal is to escape the prison, which will take about 10 minutes or to kill all of the officers. The officers goal is to keep the prisoners in check and stop them from leaving the prison and they win if all of the prisoners are all either dead or if they're still in the prison after the time limit has expired. This one is a breath of fresh air as this one has cooperation involve with it, it isn't necessarily every man for himself, the prisoners have to work together in order to escape the prison and the officers have to work together to keep the prisoners in check. I recommend this game mode to anyone getting GMod or anyone who has gotten it.I've just scraped the tip of the iceberg as there are tons of other game modes in GMod I haven't talked about like, Base Wars (a game where you defend your own base) and Zombie Survival (a game where you need to survive a zombie apocalypse.) If I have not convinced you to pick up GMod then I fail at being a reviewer. Just get GMod and enjoy it for what it is along with 1000s of other players.Pros+ Good graphics+ Tons of fun to be had+ Replay value even 10 years after it's original release+ Addicitng+ Something for nearly everyoneConsFinal verdict: 9/10My steam curator group: http://steamcommunity.com/groups/MellowReviews

review: 2015 The short answer is, it's holding up very well. The core action pits two teams of players against each other in a battle to capture points, move a cart, or steal a briefcase. The objective is always very straightforward; it's the interplay between the nine playable classes that makes things so varied and interesting. The speedy scout, the militant heavy, the diligent engineer, the conniving medic, the pesky sniper, the sneaky spy, the feisty pyro, the explosive soldier, and the even-more-explosive demoman all have unique weapons, attributes, and abilities that complement each other and clash in myriad ways. Encounters can vary widely depending on the match type and the makeup of each team, and this unpredictability is crucial to TF2's long-standing appeal. When you come out of the gate as a heavy with a medic in tow, you're a formidable offensive force, but if a spy loops around to back-stab the medic and you round the corner on a pyro, it can all come undone in a matter of seconds. Snipers can cover expected enemy paths, but rocket-jumping soldiers have a knack for finding alternative routes and raining explosive death from above. You may think you have a comparatively weak scout dead to rights, only to be stunned by a baseball and beaten to death. As you watch your giblets splatter on the ground and see a freeze-frame of your gleeful killer, it's hard not to chuckle at the sheer variety of ways you can meet an untimely demise. And the humorous quips, ridiculous outfits, and histrionic announcer help cultivate this lighthearted tone.Of course, this core dynamic has persisted for most of TF2's life span, so if you stopped playing it a few years ago and come back for a few matches, you'll find things are very familiar. Learning the ropes and getting the hang of your chosen role is still a gratifying experience, and mastering advanced techniques doesn't just make you deadlier; it gives you more options for how to approach combat. Keeping your options open is still valuable too, because being flexible with your choice of character can help you avoid ending up on a catastrophically imbalanced squad. It is Team Fortress, after all.But though there is much that has remained constant about the core game, there have been some notable changes over the years, as well as regular infusions of new weapons and items. Of the hundreds of things available in the online store, some can be unlocked through play, while others must be purchased with actual money. From small doodads that cost less than a dollar to massive bundles that cost hundreds, there's a wide range of ways to customize your experience.Many of the items offer nothing more than a playful twist on the game's already cheeky cartoon aesthetic. You can buy hats, shirts, shoes, and other cosmetic gear to dress up like a character from Adult Swim or don spooky seasonal garb that you can wear only during Halloween or a full moon. Even if you don't fancy shelling out for any of this stuff, it's fun to see some visual variety as you try to light your opponents on fire.Other weapons have more of an impact, like the ones that give your character a new chargeable and expendable power. The scout can build hype, which turns his usual double jump into a triple, quadruple, or quintuple jump, and the soldier can build rage, which allows him to rally his nearby teammates to do extra damage. Skills like these have more of a meaningful impact on the action, bringing something new to the table that your enemies must contend with. And then there are the totally out-there loadouts, like the one that turns the grenade-launching demoman into an extra from the movie Braveheart.In addition to the cosmetic options, there are a lot of weapons and items that offer small buffs or subtle tweaks to your attributes. Depending on which healing gun the medic equips, for example, he can imbue himself and his targeted ally with extra damage resistance or enable himself to match the speed of his target. Differences like these don't do much to change the core action, but they do give experienced players substantial room for strategic variation.These options broaden the field of viable strategies, which helps keep combat lively and varied. And fortunately, none of the purchasable weapons or items tip the scales unfairly towards those willing to pay. Buffs and bonuses usually come with caveats, and the weapons that bestow new abilities are usually unlocked for free. For this review, I spent some money on goofy hats and some of the stranger weaponry on offer, like the pyro's flamethrower that actually shoots bubbles and rainbows. It was fun to play with the new gear, but I still found myself switching my loadout between free and paid weapons regularly to adapt to the match situation.Very very fun game, I highly suggest everyone come try it! After all, it's free!

2021 Early Access Review First off, I found this game to be thoroughly entertaining. It looks great, plays smoothly, and kept my attention through a full playthrough. It is by no means perfect, and there are a few changes I would love to see (really more additions than changes) but overall a lot of fun.Having played both Factorio and Satisfactory, I feel like Dyston Sphere Program's 3D design combines the best of both. Adding in the multiple planets and even multiple star systems from which to extract resources is a great addition. Being able to "build up" with certain structures (like storage) is a great feature that takes away the frustration I always felt with Factorio. No need to tear it all down and redesign when it comes time to ramp up production.My only real "complaint" is that the Dyson Sphere itself isn't really necessary. Many other reviews have mentioned this, so I won't go into detail...but it's a valid point. The final "goal" is to complete a research task that requires a number of Universe Matrices, but there is no requirement that the sphere be used to create them. The same can be said for the other stars in your star cluster. You can visit others, and it is to your advantage to do so if you want to find some of the more rare resources and therefore increase efficiency...but none is required. Adding an additional stage beyond the current endgame that "uses" the sphere to accomplish something else, even just to provide closure, would be nice.Again, overall I loved it. I put in over 150 hours in a relatively short time, so clearly I got my money's worth. I will certainly do additional playthroughs and look forward to seeing how the game evolves as the devs add more content down the road.

Early Access Review This game has a lot of potential. It's hard to say right now with it being in Early Access, but I predict you can probably get about 35-50 or so hours of content out of the game at present with how much you can do at the moment.Using Stardew Valley as a comparison, I want to highlight the sort of unique differences that make this game stand out to it's competitors in the Life Simulation RPG area. The Art Style Probably the foremost point of difference comes down to Aesthetics. It's very clear that Fields of Mistria draws heavily upon the 90's anime aesthetic in it's sprite design. This is reflected in both the character portraits and the actual in-game sprites which tend to have big, expressive eyes. The overall aesthetic of the game is a very bright and creamy color palette that lends itself well to the GBA-styled graphics that seek to express more with less.It's a genuine treat to see it all come together as it does. The Fantasy/Magical Element It's no secret that Stardew Valley has it's own unique spin on supernatural, fantastical elements but I think one of the core differences is that Stardew Valley has magic in it's setting that's inaccesible for use by the protagonist in terms of game play interaction. In Fields of Mistria, the player gets to command magical powers that tend to have a direct impact on gameplay. So far, i've unlocked the ability to restore my own HP/Energy to full and create a localized rainstorm on my farm, thus watering all my crops for the day and allowing me to redirect that energy elsewhere. The Gameplay In this respect, I do feel like the games share an alarmingly high similarity. If you enjoyed Stardew Valley, you'll feel right at home here. There's a lot of wonderful quality of life and anti-frustration features seen in this game that I wish Stardew would implement. The one notable core difference I feel like is how crafting, smithing, and cooking are handled as activities that take up allotments of time out of the day, which speaking of...One major of aspect of difference between the two is time management It's very clear that in Fields of Mistria, the player is expected to make smart useage of their time, as the in-game clock goes faster then one might initially expect it to. Time is a valuable resource, and days pass quickly. There's little time for loitering and as a result each day feels like it's a carefully curated and strategic use of time.A lot of players have expressed concern over this, and I am sort of ambivalent about it. Part of the reason why crafting/gathering/cooking taking up time allotments is such a big deal is specifically because of how little of it you have to manage. If you're gonna spend a day crafting/cooking/smithing a bunch of stuff, you have to commit to that day being a day on which you do such. I do think it should be an option personally to tune how fast time passes, as it can make it hard to be able to interact with NPC's if you're constantly on the clock. I've also had several days where I was unable to exhaust all my energy prior to the day ending because of how little I was able to utilize of it during the day.Overall, I think it's a worthwhile experience. A lot of these life sim games lack that "magic factor" that keeps the player invested, because it's either needlessly complicated, or a bit too simple. Mistria feels like it hits that sweet spot that keeps the player excited for the next day.

review: Edit for a couple of additional thoughts after playing another 18 hours since the original review. I still think the game is great and would still recommend it but it is a really scummy move by NetEase to sack the entire studio behind this game and on the day this released no less. The team behind this did a really great job and they deserved much better than being unemployed. Sadly, this means there also likely won't be any further updates which is a shame since there are a few minor issues that keep the game from being as good as it could be. My biggest gripe besides the lackluster side quests is that fast travel in the game is a bit crap. You can fast travel within the zone you are in but still have to manually walk to the next zone even if you fast travel to the exit between zones. This makes traversing the span of a few zones much more tedious than it should be and traveling across the world a big pain. This is something that could absolutely be fixed through a patch that will likely not happen. I also ran into a weird bug where I got the cut scene for a boss fight and then the boss never spawned. This put me in a soft lock but thankfully I was able to re-load my save and it worked the second time. Really hoping this is something that doesn't repeat, and again, something that would be patched in a perfect world.Despite those negatives though, I am having a blast with the game (the combat is a lot more fun than the demo once you start unlocking class abilities) and I am really enjoying the darker and more thought provoking turn the story has taken versus earlier mana games. Still recommended.------------ Original Review Below------------Highly recommended. This is the first game since the 16 bit era to really nail everything that made Secret of Mana (and to a slightly lesser extent Seiken Densetsu 3) such charming and fun experiences. And seriously, I would put emphasis on the word "charm", the world and characters all ooze charm and it is clear that the team putting this together wanted to make something that stands out. The colorful aesthetics, cell shaded graphics, and the music really has a lot of the charm that made Secret of Mana such a hit and that subsequent follow-ups have lacked to varying degrees (I still like Seiken Densetsu 3 and Legend of Mana but they are just different experiences). The game really is the mana format brought forward without feeling like a simple remake or something tied purely to nostalgia and "remember this", Visions of Mana is it's own game.The combat is solid action RPG fare with a job system, customizeable skills, and even different weapon types depending on your job so it scratches both the character building/customization itch as well as different play styles based on your current weapon. Jobs and weapons all change your appearance as well. The world also has unique named enemies scattered around, some of which are quite challenging, and there are also enemy wave type challenges scattered around the world to take on.The music is a nice mix of tunes that call back to the pipes, steel drums and various wind instruments that made Secret of Mana's soundtrack standout mixed in with some fairly typical RPG fare. Overall, I dig it.I think what I am most intrigued about is the story. It is not entirely the happy go lucky bare minimum of story telling that Secret of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3 had, there are some really interesting things going on with the plot and character interactions and I like what I have seen so far. I'm looking forward to seeing where the game goes with the story a whole lot more than any previous mana game which is a huge plus for me. With that said though, everything is presented as very positive and upbeat so please don't take that to mean that the story is dark or negative, it is just different and I hate to spoil anything so I'm going to leave it intentionally vague.Performance has also been great. I'm running a Zen 2 processor and a Radeon 6800XT and I am playing the game at 4k with visuals maxed and have not seen a single hiccup. No bugs or crashes so far and my controller worked just fine without having to mess with anything. Load times are also fairly minimal which is appreciated.If I absolutely have to list a negative, I would say that, so far between this and the demo, the side quests are pretty basic fetch quests and "go kill X of enemy Y" type fare and definitely the least interesting part of the experience.So on balance I'd easily recommend this to anyone with an interest in action RPGs, the mana series or just anyone interested in a fun upbeat RPG with a very cool world that seems to be very well built with a lot of attention to detail and lots of nooks and crannies to explore and unique enemies to fight.

2021 As a cyclist, I am always on the lookout for bike games. I was a huge fan of Downhill Domination back on PS2, but haven't found anything that scratches that same itch, until now.Lonely Mountains: Downhill is an interesting game. The simply looking graphics might lead you to believe it is an easy game, and while there are many simple challenges, it also gets quite difficult in the later part of the game, with twisting trails littered with trees and rocks.The game is easy to control, and gives you two main control schemes. The camera is semi-fixed in placed, only moving slightly or pulling back when you need to see further ahead. Some people may not like the camera, but it is a fundamental part of the game. Not knowing what is around the next bend is a core part of learning a trail in real life, and in the game. Once you have ridden a trail a few times, you start to see the possibilities for shortcuts and little time-savers. Once you master a trail, then you start to see the huge drops and massive cuts that will score you the best times.The game comes with 4 mountains, each having 4 trails, making for 16 distinct paths to ride. Each mountain is lovely to look at and each feel natural. There is also a DLC mountain which I purchased for 5 dollars on sale, and I think it was worth it. Once you unlock the final challenge for a trail, you unlock the ability to play at night. This is an intense experience, with only your bike mounted light illuminating the way forward.While there are many challenges, you do not need to complete them all to unlock the majority of the games content. I have finished unlocking all the bicycles, of which there are 6, and still have a bunch of challenges to complete if I wish. I feel that the progression is done very well.Lastly, there are Daily Rides for the player to tackle each day. These are a selection of a trail, bike, time of day, and requirement to complete. They mix up the familiar trails by adding more rocks and fallen trees in your way, forcing you to find new routes down the mountain. I really enjoy these, and find myself making sure to do the daily ride every day before I go to bed, or first thing in the morning while having my first coffee before heading out to work.Despite the trailer on Steam having a crazy guitar riff, the game doesn't really have any music other than on the menu. This works really well and creates a peaceful atmosphere where you can focus on the riding. The sounds from the bike and the sound of skidding on dirt are all done very well.I think this game is well-worth the price, and look forward to more from this developer.

2022 Sonic Frontiers didn't just live up to my hopes, but actually managed to exceed them in many areas.The graphics are beautiful. Placing Sonic against this realistic world is a way to show that he is somewhat out of his element and in a brand new situation. Juxtapose that with the classically Sonic-esque cartoonish style of the Cyberspace levels, and the contrast really allows both to shine beautifully. There's a good amount of pop-in just due to the sheer speed, but it's honestly not TOO too noticeably when you're just zooming around in the open field. Some of the particles are a bit wonky and the water effects in the fishing mini-game are a bit broken, but overall those are pretty minor nitpicks.The game play is natural and fluid. You're never really pausing to think of where to go next; You see something just on the edge of your field of view and you go there to investigate. These chain together and lead to very natural-feeling progression. Sometimes you want to head out in an entirely different direction, and the game rewards you with even more to explore and uncover. The "open zone" never feels empty. It feels like there's more to find over every hill. Sometimes the camera is a bit funny and jumps around when you're too close to cliff walls and the like. But otherwise, it's all good. Lots of options to tweak the camera too, if it's happening a bunch.Sonic's momentum is great. His starting speed is honestly just right, and paired with the Boost mechanic it's even better. I truly think this is where the Boost side of the Sonic franchise has been heading all this time. It just feels so natural and intuitive. Being able to upgrade Sonic's speed is a huge plus. I'm excited to level it all the way up to 99. I do wish some of the combat moves had more applications outside of fighting, but that's another minor nitpick. Some things like the light speed dash (I think it's called) through coins can stop momentum if you're not careful, but again you can just get right back up to speed.As far as other mechanics go, the collectibles are really enjoyable. Beating bosses is seriously intense and makes great use of the large levels and Sonic's top speed. You truly feel like you're taking on a formidable enemy each time. Replaying the Cyberspace levels is enjoyable and you have really solid goals to work towards. You'll definitely get better as time goes on, as long as you remember to use the Boost mechanic! I totally forgot about it until half an hour into the game and it helped so much.Just watch out for Level 1-2. S rank is practically impossible on it and I have a feeling that might get patched since even the media had trouble with it. The rest of the levels so far, I've had no problem after a bit of practice.The story so far is very mysterious and compelling. There are a few threads that get intertwined and I'm genuinely excited to see it through. However, you're not rushed in it. You're able to take your time and just explore as you see fit, after a certain point. I will say that I'm unsure at times why I'm interacting with Sage in the open field, but talking with her does give some unique characterization and bits of information about the world so I don't particularly mind it.The music, as always, is one of the best parts of the game. They really knocked it out of the park not only with the composition, but also with the cues for when music plays, fades in or out, and changes. It's a huge soundtrack and I don't think I've even scratched the surface so far. Really no complaints about it at all.Overall, Sonic Frontiers is a really fresh take on the franchise that I think many people will enjoy. It's not a perfect game, but I have enjoyed my time with it so far. I definitely recommend you give it a try! I'm just under 5 hours in and I'm not even halfway done with the first island. Hope that gives you an idea of the length.

2022 "This looks like a fun and relaxing game, guess I'll try it out." Yes, the game is very relaxing and extremely fun, but there is no "trying" Stardew Valley. Should you buy this game, then you best believe that you're going to spend at least 40-100+ hours playing it the first time around. It's not a waste of time, not at all. Call it an investment of your time. When it comes to this game, "like" is synonymous to "addicted". So telling others that you "like" the game is the same thing as hiding your addiction (so just accept it for what it is). Stardew Valley is also synonymous to "productiveness". No, it's actually the very definition of productivity, since you're going to wish you were as productive in real life as you are in-game.~~ It starts with making your own character, choosing the farm that you think looks the best or most fun and also picking your companion pet. I'm not going to spoil you on what "Favorite Thing" is about. During the first few days of Stardew, I pretty much spent my time cleaning up the front yard of the farm. I just couldn't stand the sight of all that clutter and foliage on the ground and repeatedly getting stuck between twigs and rocks was surprisingly infuriating. Lewis, the Mayor of the town, had given me 15 parsnip seeds on my first day to help me with starting my farm. But "cleaning" took a lot more energy out of my character than I expected. I found it to be quite enjoyable breaking all of those rocks, cutting down the trees and mowing the grass, since it felt like I was actually cleaning for once. It wasn't until later that I would regret not starting with the farm earlier, since that would have meant getting more income in the earlier stages of the game. That's the thing with these types of games though. You are always going to regret making some of your decisions, whether it's buying the wrong types of crops or planting too many crops and wasting all your energy watering those crops each and every morning. Or you can be like me and do both of those examples at once on top of planting your crops way too late into the season.Anyways, I obviously got the materials for cleaning the farm, but it's not like I knew what to do with it. I ended up just making a few chests, changed their individual colors and then I began organizing everything that I had gathered. Which was basically just plant fiber, twigs, stones and then the occasional clay that I accidentally got from using the wrong tools on the wrong things. After that, I finally decided I would head into town to try and interact with as many people as possible in one day. I kept getting handwritten mail from characters I had yet to actually meet each and every morning, so naturally I became more and more curious of the town and less interested in cleaning. It took me around 3-4 days before I began to explore, but my farm was basically clear of anything that I might get stuck on further down the line so I didn't really feel like I wasted any time. I began my exploration quest with going into random buildings and interacting with every person I saw. Gus, the owner of "The Stardrop Saloon". Alex, his sweet grandmother, Evelyn and his very friendly Grandpa, George that I gave a Dandelion to because I was curious as to what would happen if I gave someone a gift. “This is probably the worst gift I've ever seen. Thanks a lot.” No, thank you George for that lovely comment.I also talked to Pierre, the owner of the general store and his wife (Caroline) and daughter (Abigail). This was also when I used the starting money to buy more crop seeds, tulips and parsnips because "why not" I remember thinking to myself... I then decided to head down south to look for this "Willy" guy that said he was waiting near the beach or something. On the way there I noticed a trash can that I for some reason decided to try and interact with. I then learned something very interesting. Interacting with a trash can is the same as "searching" the trash can and that naturally grosses people out. This is how I met a girl by the name of Haley. She just kind of stood there staring at me while I was digging through the trash, and I was staring back at her. Since it worked so beautifully before, I decided to give her a gift as well because I didn't know if people would start to hate you for doing, well, what I did. I would like to say that I "learned from my mistakes", but that wasn't the case at all, I can't even say that as a joke. Yes, you probably guessed it right, I gave her a Dandelion, thinking that "She can't possibly hate them as much as George does right?"“Ugh...that's such a stupid gift.”Thinking "Haley must be related to George", I reluctantly went down to the beach wondering if I should give Willy, the fisherman guy a Dandelion. As it turns out, I was to be the one on the receiving end. He gave me his rod and man, I never thought that such a simple fishing Minigame could be so fun. I stood there for the rest of the day, wasting away on my character's energy till I had no more. "You feel sluggish from over-exertion." It was the first time I was staying up past 12 in-game and my character was walking slower than ever before. I already knew beforehand that your character faints after 2 am, but the only way to make it back to bed in time would be to eat one of the fishes I had caught to regain my stamina. But I wasn't going to break, bend the knee to a fish and eat it raw like Gollum. I was going to sell them all no matter what. So yeah, I just fainted and sold them all the next day at the cost of some extra energy. Probably wasn't worth it, but I did get a few extra pennies that I wasted on buying more seeds. I should've saved up for a better fishing rod...So anyways, good game.

Sekiro is a great souls-like, a great action, and I think it would be safe to say this at this point, a wonderful rhythm game with a deep lore and unexpectedly deep and satisfying combat system. As someone who had a prejudice towards souls-like genre due to its toxic fans, Sekiro managed to become one of my favorite games of all time and I’m actually craving for more souls-like now. However, I have no intention of becoming a sheep in the crowd. Thankfully, my self-esteem isn’t that low and I highly advise you to seek professional help if your only achievement in life is beating a game and bragging about it. Sorry, I had to point that out because they’ve been bugging me constantly while playing Sekiro and it was quite annoying. Anyway, with that out of my chest, let’s talk about the game itself a bit. Sekiro actually differs from the previous souls-like games because unlike dodging, it forces you to parry and deflect most of the enemy attacks to build up their posture bar to perform finishers on them. I’m quite good at parrying and deflecting, thus Sekiro felt right at home for me. Some people may find this change more difficult, but it’s a personal preference. Also, the reason why I pointed out that it’s a rhythm game is because you literally have to find a rhythm while your enemy is attacking you and keep it going until their posture bar is filled. You can also deplete their health bar of course, but it takes more time so, it’s just way better to learn how to properly parry and deflect their attacks. Since it’s an action game, Sekiro doesn’t have RPG elements, but a bunch of skills and combat arts for you to choose from. You also have a prosthetic arm and several prosthetic shinobi arm equipment such as shuriken and firecrackers. It’s possible to sneak past most of the enemy encounters without engaging in combat thanks to your prosthetic arm. There are also many consumables to use, but I ended up using only two or three of them. Most of the bosses are also humanoids except for Guardian Ape and Demon of Hatred, therefore; it is quite difficult to parry and deflect their attacks due to their size. In fact, I never parried Demon of Hatred and ended up running during the whole fight. So, the reward for beating them? Apart from personal satisfaction, you get to enhance your attack power using their memories. You also get to increase your vitality and posture bar using Prayer Beads dropped from mini-bosses or the ones you find scattered across Ashina. You also get to resurrect once. Later, you get two more resurrections, but they only work if you kill an enemy after you die. What happens if you die for good? You are taken to the last Sculptor’s Idol which serves as a checkpoint and lose half of your EXP and money. There’s a 30% chance of this not happening, but it gets lower and lower if you keep dying. There’s a way to prevent this, but I leave that to you to find.“How is it possible for our protagonist to resurrect?” I hear you ask and that is tied to the plot. I really don’t want to spoil anything by saying too much, but I’d like to mention the important bits to clarify. Our protagonist Wolf is tasked to serve a Divine Child called Kuro who has dragon’s blood which grants him immortality. He accepts our protagonist into his immortal oath which also grants him immortality. There’s also another guy called Genichiro who’s after the very same thing, but Kuro refuses to do so since he believes that the pursuit of immortality corrupts the lives of men, thus leads him to task his Shinobi, Wolf, to find a way to sever it. That’s Sekiro’s story in a nutshell, but the majority of its story is not explicitly stated because it’s a FromSoftware game. That’s… their charm, I guess? Apart from the rewarding gameplay, they also reward those who look hard enough into the plot of their games with knowledge and a false sense of accomplishment. I’m not gonna lie, the plot is engaging and the lores of certain characters are very, very interesting when you figure them out. There are also four endings and the requirements for two of them are so bizarre, but very rewarding since they unlock the best ones. I’m not going to mention anything about them, you’ll naturally realize the ones I’m talking about if you ever aim to get them. Apart from its gameplay and its lore, I’d like to mention additional challenges called “Gauntlet of Strength” that get unlocked after defeating certain bosses. They are not tied to any achievement or anything, but they unlock some cool outfits and a very useful combat art for you to use if you can conquer them. So, what’s so challenging about them? Facing certain bosses one after another without failing. Trust me, though. They are worth it. Once you conquer all of them, you unlock another one with ALL the bosses included, and the reward for beating it is nothing but your personal satisfaction and bragging rights for those with low-esteem issues. Speaking of achievements, they are very straightforward. However, the one that requires you to kill all bosses needs to be done on one save file and the minimum number of playthroughs you need to get all of them is three due to the amount of a very rare upgrade material. The enemy scaling is there with each NG+, so rest assured that you will never have an easier time with it. TL;DRSekiro is a wonderful action, a great souls-like, and a phenomenal rhythm game with an unexpectedly deep combat system and lore if you’re the one to connect the dots. Your main aim is to fill your enemies’ posture bars by parrying and deflecting. Since each area is carefully designed, you can choose how you want to approach them. You can even use your prosthetic tools to make things easier for yourself. The bosses are also very well designed for those who don’t hesitate.

One moment you're a whisker away from the throne, the next you're being chased by a guard who's got a grudge against rodents.The quests are as unpredictable as a raccoon in your garbage can. Just when you think you've got it all figured out, the game throws you a curveball. Or a spell card. Or a Bane. It's a wild ride from start to finish.The graphics are a feast for the eyes. Whether you're teaming up with friends or facing off against strangers, every game is a new adventure.In conclusion, Armello is a gem of a game. It's got charm, it's got challenge, and it's got a bear in a cloak. What more could you ask for? review: 2022 I have no doubt I will spend my afterlife by Odin's side in Valhalla after having played Northgard for 400 hours, winning 30+ conquests with 10+ different clans!! I love Northgard, but I have one big gripe with this game. I wish it had artificial intelligence that showed at least some signs of actual intelligence rather than relying on heavy cheating to increase difficulty.The current AI (I mostly play co-op conquests with my husband on Hard difficulty) results in most matches being either sort of boring or super frustrating, only occasionally something in between. It's really unnerving to see an enemy clan marching with 7 soldiers along the border of my territory in the summer of the very first year, because with the constraints human players have, it's absolutely unrealistic to have such an army that early in the game. Also, as the end-game stats reveal, it's not uncommon for the AI to easily sustain 9 military units with a total population of just 10. This is a joke. An infuriating one though. And this is on Hard difficulty, not even Extreme. At the same time, the enemy clans tend to just harass my outer territories, then withdraw and only come back when I recolonize them. If they were "intelligent" instead of just dumb cheaters, they could totally decimate me within minutes in the first or second year.Please, Shiro, shift your effort to improving the AI, rather than producing more and more clans. There are plenty of clans now, and a lot of wonderful content and unique game mechanics for each clan. It's time to dedicate considerable attention to the core feature of the game for all single-player and co-op players -- the AI. So many negative reviews on Steam complain about this very same thing. Everything else about Northgard is absolutely amazing, and the only reason I can foresee myself leaving this game behind in the near future (after my current almost 400 hours of playtime) is the laughable AI that makes me want to cry at the same time.I work in the AI field myself, so I understand that improving the AI is nothing trivial, and would be a major effort. However, I am sure there is a good proportion of players who would be more than happy to receive no content updates for the next year or two, but get a radical AI upgrade. I also understand that an AI update won't directly bring in more money like DLCs do, so the pay-off from Shiro's perspective might be rather low. But perhaps it will retain more players who will in turn be more likely to buy DLCs in the future and recommend the game to their friends rather than discouraging them from getting it.Thank you, Shiro, for making an otherwise fantastic and beautiful game, and actively maintaining and further developing it all these years after releasing it! It would be great to hear if you guys are even considering a major overhaul of the AI at any point in the future, or only new content and balancing updates.

Or rescueing a kerbal mark whatney from Mars (Duna) or doing a flyby of pluto (Eeloo). Or building a replica of the international space station one shuttle launch at a time. You will hit a science brick wall if you cant do moon flybys without manourvre nodes. But theres some cool scenarios and theres always sandbox mode. Mods! The only thing which needs to be improved is the part physics. Dont get me wrong, its gotten so much better since 1.1 and 1.2 but it could be better. Currently if you have more than about 250+ parts being rendered, the game slows down to about 15 fps on my GTX 980. Very large ships take a while to launch and docking a large shuttle with an even larger space station requires patience and precision. Just be careful to build ships without too many unnecessary parts and you will be fine.

So people quicktame Dodos to kill enough dodos to tame a T-Rex, if a creature of a tribe was killed and the taming limit is below the threshold for a minute, lol[X] If you decide to play PVP, bring friends or host the server yourself. The official servers are heavily unbalanced. Yes, there are servers with small tribes enforcement and servers for beginners. But even if you are experienced enough already, it's still a sea of sharks. Try to settle with level 20, while being attacked and chased by lvl 240 players and their tamed dinos. They know where you are and they will return to kill you again and again, robbing all your resources, so you're stuck naked punching palm trees again and again and again. It's basically like playing Anno on hard, and they sink your ship before you even reach an island to build a harbor on.So much for the multiplayer part.TL:DR: Bring your friends and play with them.Now for the technical part.- You'll face sudden unexpected death by tumbling and falling 1 meter or so. That's no joke, the colliders and physics are that bad. Don't believe me? Wear the metal armor and punch a Dilo. Did you nearly die for punching an absolute beginner threat dino in the face? Yep, that's what I mean.- Colliders also are a constant pain, because in ARK, there are the most rigid titanium-palmtrees. You may think that something like a 3 meter palmtree would be crushed by something other like a multiple ton Sarcosuchus in an instant. But due to special physics, big tamed dinos like a Sarco will get stuck between palmtrees all the time. And then a Pegomastax Lvl 10 can kill them, because they can't move and defend themselves. Only Giganotosaurus is an exception to that, since it's the largest dino. Even T-Rexes will get stuck between rocks, palmtrees, trees, in caves etc.- Dino-Waypoint-Navigation. Sometimes you'll look a tamed dino straight in the eye from 40 meters apart and want them to run through the big dino gate insde your base. They sometimes navigate the craziest routes, get stuck in spike walls, between rocks, because the won't follow or find the simple path through the gate. Bring a saddle for that case. - Dino-Behaviour: There a dozens of spawn points throughout the world and dinos spawn there and behave randomly. You won't see something like a pack of raptors out for a hunt, dilos guarding their nests with eggs, wild eggs and nests, etc... It's just a bunch of spawned dinos with a factor and their move randomly. T-Rexes walking in circles, attacking something...walking...attacking. There aren't even wild dino children.- Attacks and bounce back. When a big dino attacks you, it pushes you back several meters (Triceratops for example). It looks remarkably stupid and I think something like a ragdoll animaton or even tumbling and falling (like a car crash(after all the experience would be like getting hit by a truck)) would be better. For ARK 2, they announced a "soulslike" combat experience. We'll see ^^ During the beginning phase it's "poke something until it's dead", in the late stage it is just"shoot something until it is dead". The animations for the attacked dinos are all the same and unauthentic. A attacked dino will rotate towards you, cry in pain or for attack and then the bounces begin. - Flying Dinos/Birds/Whatever: Every flying animation is basically what modern doves do to lift themselves up from the ground. But the whole time. Take a look at birds and their flying techniques in reality. They take sharp turns, sail the wind, etc. It's not just flapping the wings the whole time. - Official Wiki for ARK has outdated content. You'll waste resources to craft recipes, that are no longer valid. Since it's their official wiki, it should be up to date after each patch.What I miss in ARK:- A diplomacy/trade system for both PVE and PVP. - Balancing mechanics for PVE-mode and resources (few on-man-partys rule the whole world now)- Good Physics (no collider-deaths, stuck-ups or bounce-backs)- Nocturnal fauna. With the exception of Megalosaurus in caves, no dino ever sleeps or hunts only during night or day- Dynamic flying/Wind (Use updrafts to sail with your tamed flyers)- Senses and hunt and prey behaviour (Rexes should pick up your scent, if the wind turns, then they will look for you (basically that's pretty RPG-Townsguard-Stuff, so nothing special). Dinos should protect their young and their nests. - Good Weather-System (besides rain, snow or sunny). Awesome thunderstorms with lightning, sandstorms, waves, dynamic ocean, floods, waves, rivers, tides- Better attacks (not just poking) and feedback in general. 2020 This review is based on my limited playtime (10 hours) and beating the final boss 1 time using a Silent armor DOT/debuff/combo deck. I'm usually very into card games and strategy games in general, but I just cannot find the motivation to keep playing and learning its strategies. I feel like the combination of rogue like and card game is just not the formula for me. Specifically, I feel that the progression of the game does not feel rewarding to me as a card game or a rogue like game. For a card game,I except to slowly accumulate cards/decks while expanding my knowledge through theory crafting. Building a deck that I like and can last is 50% of the fun, and the other 50% is from executing such deck. For Slay the Spire, the accumulation of the cards/deck only last for a single run, and the accumulation of the knowledge is limited by the game RNG which decides which cards will show up as rewards after every enemy encounter. There's no way in the game itself to see all the available cards but only about 3 new cards every battle for the player to increase the deck/knowledge. This is really frustration for me, because the only efficient way to learn the cards is to read the game wiki. By only playing the game, there's no way to know if picking card A is better for building a deck than picking card B, because there's no way to have any overview of the synergy between cards or have any knowledge of if a future card belongs to the same architect without seeing the cards already. The only way to see the cards, sadly, is to read the wiki, or to build a knowingly less optimal deck and hope it works. This learning process really feels like a waste of time for me. For a rogue like game, I except to have a really engaging game play mechanic/story etc to keep me engaged.The story/background of Slay the Spire is almost nonexistent. Different card mechanics while they are interesting, I can see a lot of similarities from other popular card games. The dry game play often makes me wonder what's the point of playing other than making myself more familiar with the game. Maybe I'll update my review if I spend more time playing the game, but this is my overall impression for now.P.S. my experience playing card games and rogue like games:Card games:Hearthstone legend rank season 36, Gwent close beta NA server rank #16, Thronebreaker: The Witcher Tale Hard Mode finished.Rogue like games:Hades steam 100% achievement, dead cell final boss beaten, Rogue Legacy final boss beaten

A Stunning Yet Slow-Burning Western EpicRed Dead Redemption 2 is an incredibly detailed and immersive open-world game that captures the essence of the Wild West. The game's stunning visuals and expansive world are truly impressive, but it can be difficult to get into at first.GameplayThe gameplay in Red Dead Redemption 2 is highly detailed, offering a wide range of activities from hunting and fishing to engaging in gunfights and heists. The controls are complex and realistic, adding to the immersion but also making the game feel sluggish at times. For newcomers, the slow pace and extensive tutorials can make the early stages of the game feel like a chore.GraphicsThe visuals in Red Dead Redemption 2 are breathtaking. The landscapes, character models, and weather effects are all meticulously crafted, creating a world that feels alive and authentic. The attention to detail is unmatched, making every scene a visual delight. However, the game's realism can sometimes come at the cost of convenience, such as the slow animations for mundane tasks.StoryThe narrative in Red Dead Redemption 2 is rich and engaging, with well-developed characters and a compelling plot. However, the missions can feel very long with little action, especially at the start. The slow build-up might be off-putting for players expecting more immediate excitement. The story unfolds gradually, requiring patience to appreciate the depth and nuance of the characters and their journeys.World and ExplorationExploring the world of Red Dead Redemption 2 is a rewarding experience. The game world is vast and filled with diverse environments, from snowy mountains to dense forests and bustling towns. There are countless side activities and random encounters that add to the richness of the world. Despite this, the open-world nature can sometimes feel overwhelming, and the slow pace of travel might test the patience of some players.Action and PacingFor a game with such a vast world, the action can feel sparse, particularly in the early missions. The pacing is deliberate, focusing on building the world and characters rather than constant action. While this approach creates a deeper, more immersive experience, it might not satisfy players looking for immediate thrills and fast-paced gameplay.OverallRed Dead Redemption 2 is a masterpiece in terms of world-building and storytelling, offering a deeply immersive and visually stunning experience. However, its slow pace and complex mechanics can make it hard to get into, especially for players seeking more immediate action. Despite its initial hurdles, those who stick with it will find a richly rewarding adventure filled with memorable moments and characters.Worth experiencing if you have the patience!

2020 One of the best RPGs I've ever played. I just have some gripes with the endings, pacing, the armor system and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ instant-kills, all of which are not totally unfun, but can be implemented in a better way. Some of the talents aren't even remotely useful, and crafting isn't all that remarkable, though most of these can be solved with mods. Some people may not like the writing, but I find it quite charming. These reasons may be enough to ruin the game for some people, but I think DOS2 has achieved so much that it deserves more praise than scorn. Everything else in the game has been a wondrous journey in a beautiful world, dialogue systems are well-designed which can even handle multiplayer in every possible outcome, full voice acting, and many exciting ways around problems with fun tactical combat that is not just about matching elements, but to look out for enemy weaknesses (or strengths for that matter), high ground, create cover, and using environmental hazards to your advantage. Being CC'ed and out-positioned in combat created many opportunities to re-examine what skills and items I have to solve the situation without losing a party member, heck, even a water balloon could come in handy at the right time, which is fantastic. You can even pick up chests and barrels, create a barricade and start fights to your advantage this way, very cheesy but all in the spirit of DOS2. If you can't win, you can always flee and come back another time, there's even a talent specifically for this, so it encourages much experimentation and failure. There are some inevitable fights, but it's possible to just sneak or talk your way past many of the encounters. You can respec your character at any time during Act 2, so don't worry if you screwed up. It's a good design choice in my opinion, and most of the game is filled with intuitive mechanics and UI that feels good. As a game, DOS2 has really solid mechanics which creates many opportunities for roleplay and planning. It's definitely worth experiencing.

2017 Probably the best Total War Game Since Shogun 2.Now haters are probably going to hate the game for not being Historical or for the DLC.. Take away those two negatives and you have one of my favorite Total War games and probably one of the best RTS Warhammer games since Black Omen on the PS1 and Dawn of War series. DLC is optional, and if you enjoy the game, you can either not buy the DLC or buy the DLC to support the game. It's great either way. I enjoyed the game from the get go, so i didn't Hesitate buying the DLC.So let me get this straight.. The Base Game is rather complete and fun by itself. You have 5 diverse factions with all unuqie playstyles and heroes and abilties. Humans, Orcs, Undead and Dwarfs. Sub-factions aren't playable by themselves but are interactable within the world and the DLC does unlock a few extra factions. Unit Roster is rather complete too, with the DLC fleshing out some gaps.Graphics are great, unit animations are probably the highlight by far with eagles, Dragons, Orcs everything is amazing to look at. Eagles swoop down. Dragon Ogres crush and destroy and instil fear. Trolls kick and barf acid.. It's all wonderful to look at. While individual combat animations found in previous total war games aren't present. Units still engage one another with attacks, and react to feedback accordingly to the damage they take.Multiplayer is what you expect. Nothing on the lines of Shogun 2. But more refined from Rome II. The balance is better though, each race has their own units so the Meta game is far evolved.Gameplay wise the game plays differently from the other Total war games. So don't go into this game expectin to play like you can in Rome II. Each unit has a specific role and purpose. There's a kinda rock, paper Sissors going off. Using none Armor piercing units on Dwarfs for example isn't gonna net you any kills.Anyway it's a great game. I bought the limited edition and bought the DLC over the course of a few weeks, and I don't feel ripped off at all. I recently bought the wood Elves DLC and its one of my favorite races in the game now, well worth the money.Great game. But remember to wait and buy the DLC on Sale if you can. And in my honest opinion if you can buy the game, then you sure as hell can buy the DLC.

2016 Early Access Review Taking into account this is an early release product...1. When playing in fullscreen mode, in either dx9 or dx11, the game repeatedly failed to pass the loading screen and subsequently locked my laptop such that a battery pull was necessary to restart.2. When playing in windowed mode in dx11 the results were the similar to the above, however, the initial tutorial was at least started--with a consistent crash and computer lock occuring when the inventory was pulled up.3. When playing in windowed mode in dx9, the game will run fine.Solution:In game options set the program to run in windowed mode.In steam, select subnautica, go to properties and "set launch options".In the "set launch options" enter: -force-d3d9Save/close.My system meets or exceeds the minimum specs for this product and my drivers are current/stable. Many other titles run fine under dx11. To say the above has been greatly frustrating is an understatement--with over a dozen battery pull restarts required through the day on an otherwise very stable and reliable system.So is Subnautica worth a buy? Yes.This is an early access title with vast potential. The gameplay is marginally frustrating, as some resources visually very indistinct--can we say limestone? However, there is enough depth to make the game very seaworthy. The environment is fairly unique, in the survival paradigm, and I have not found it overly grindy in my limited playtime to date.As resources seem to be universally finite, I remain uncertain as to just how open-sandbox this title is. Equally, I hope that more back story gets flushed out over time and/or a proper end game, if resources remain finite, is coded to afford either proper colonisation or escape. Again, this is early access and the potenial makes this worth a purchase whilst on sale.

In light of the fact that this game is currently sitting at mixed reviews as of 2024/03/31, I thought that I should actually attempt a serious review of this game. It will hopefully not be too long.Common Negative Review ReasoningI will address the most common issues touted in negative reviews in order from most valid to least valid. Optimization Bugs MicrotransactionsOptimizationOptimisation is easily the most valid criticism of this game.My Specs:Win 11 Home13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-13700KF - 3.40 GHzNvidia Geforce RTX 407032 GB DDR5 RAMRunning game off of SSDPlaying normally I can achieve 60 FPS with all the settings jacked up to max except shadows playing at 1920x1080. I STILL commonly dip below 60, especially in Vermund. This is completely unacceptable, never mind my specs when I'm playing at 1920x1080; 1440p is now considered the norm. I'm running a near top of the line rig, and I can't exceed 60 without massive jumps in my frame rate at 1080p. Unacceptable and perfectly valid complaint. 75% of people don't have the hardware to play this game above medium settings.BugsThis complaint is valid, and obviously extremely hard to tackle when everybody has a different experience. One person might not be able to launch the game, others might play through fine with very few bugs. I myself fit into the latter category, and I only had minimal issues through the 120 or so hours I used up enjoying the game. The real issue is that when there WERE bugs, they commonly did break things; I was completely unable to acquire the Spearhand Maister's quest because his quest just refused to fire no matter what I did.MicrotransactionsNot valid at all, in this case. ALL of the criticisms involving MTX are completely and utterly invalid. Capcom since around 2010 has had timesaving DLC included in the DLC sections of PSN/Xbox Live and now Steam forever. It will never change, and anyone who thought that'd be different here is an idiot. These same types of DLC were present at the original release of Dragon's Dogma. The nature of the DLC is completely benign and harmless, with NONE OF IT being inaccessible in the game. Nothing forces you to pay, and the microtransactions don't affect the game at all. There's one button on the main menu that redirects you to the Steam page; That's the limit of how invasive it is in game. Anybody making an issue of the microtransactions is purposefully and willingly being malicious in order to harm the game. Or stupid.The Actual ReviewI will break the review down into two parts: Gameplay, Exploration. This is a review from someone who has played the previous game extensively on multiple platforms, and will thus be catered towards such people. I will not be covering the game from the viewpoint of somebody with no experience with the franchise. I'd add a section for pawns, but Steam has given me a character limit.GameplayI classify gameplay as the base mechanics surrounding combat, and the outfitting of your characters for such, and in that sense the game is much like the first one with some differences, both good and bad. The base combat loop is much better, with melee combat being the best part of the experience. Melee combat is far more impactful, especially against larger enemies, who are now much more fun to climb now that you can walk around on top of a large enemy as opposed to just clinging to them. There are some issues though.First, the number of slots for skills has been lowered for everybody, and raised by one for Warrior; The lack of slots is not that bad on any of the melee or ranged classes, but magic suffers for it, partly because Sorcerer/Mage have had their skillsets and movesets cut down quite a bit, with much of the functionality of the previous game being ripped out for seemingly no reason. A good example is that you can no longer free aim spells like Maelstrom, you are FORCED to cast it on an enemy, or directly in front of you. Sorcerer/Mage are missing many of the other spells and tools that made them(particularly Sorcerer) great and fun to play in the last game, again, for seemingly little reason.Spells missing:Dark BoonHoly BoonMiasmaIngleLassitudeNecromancyBlearingExequyPetrifactionBrontideGicelFulminationSeriously? Why...? Why cut down over HALF of the original spell list? There's little to no actual choice in the number of spells, now. You are constricted to a small handful of total spells, few of which are actually useful as a Sorcerer/Mage, and it makes the classes feel like garbage a lot of the time, especially considering the utility of the existing spells that are still good have been cut-down as well. This is a martial or a hybrid's game. Do not play Sorcerer or Mage.There are a few new vocations that are Arisen only, and I will say that they are fun with one exception.Mystic Spearhand is supposed to be a replacement for Mystic Knight, but fails in terms of flavor. Gameplay wise, it's a more mediocre martial class with some of the best weapons in the game attached to it, and one stand out ability that can make your party completely invincible for as long as you deign to keep the ability active.Trickster is... different. I will say that it's kind of fun, but it's more a novelty than anything. Play Trickster if you like to watch your pawns play the game for you, cause that is about all that will happen. The class is all about controlling the battlefield, but the caveat to having total control over enemy aggro with the ability to buff your allies is that you literally do no damage. None.Warfarer allows you to take the skills of all vocations excluding maister-skills and use them all in one load-out with a limit of 3 slots(as you need the 4th to change weapons with Warfarer's maister-skill). You can essentially play as a DD:DA Assassin with this kit.One last mention, is that leveling has changed for the better in my opinion: NO MORE MEANINGFUL STAT-GROWTH. NO MORE MIN-MAXING. All vocations buff stats suited to the vocation, and base stats increase based on the vocation you had wihle leveling up, but now all stats cap out at a specific value around level 200. It no longer matters if you min-maxed or didn't; At level 200, everybody is the same besides gear and vocation.ExplorationThere's nothing really new here. You're looking at a world that's quite a bit larger than DD:DA's world, but you essentially do the same thing: Run around, find caves, open chests, kill bandits/goblins/lizards, kill bosses. The one big difference is that unlike DD:DA there are static AND dynamic spawns, seemingly.
