2016 I could write a review for Stellaris and go into a great deal of depth about its gameplay and aesthetics, but I'm not going to. Instead, I'm going to tell you the story of Admiral Cax.The Tale of Admiral Cax, Hero of the Blessed Light of TorobaLong before he was born, Cax's people, an atomic-age civilisation of reptilians called the Netraxi, had noticed something odd about their leaders. Sure, they seemed fine from afar but on closer inspection they were just a little bit too...mushroom-y. Still, they shrugged and kept on doing whatever nuclear-powered reptiles do. And then the day came when the disguises fell and the Netraxi were taken over by the fanatically religious empire of slave-taking mushrooms that had quietly infiltrated their society using some questionable shapeshifting magic. The Netraxi were aghast. They were enraged. And then they were enslaved.These conniving chantarelles, known to their friends (not many) as the Blessed Light of Toroba and their enemies (quite a bit more) as the Doom Shrooms, were to be masters of the Netraxi for a hundred years. For this darkest of centuries, the Netraxi slaved away to supply their overlords with ambiguously-defined but evidently useful minerals, their labour rewarded only with contempt, and a reminder to worship the God-Emperor of Toroba at all times. The unhappiest Netraxi were sent down the mines. The happiest were released, allowed to be outraged about their situation for a bit, and then enslaved again just for fun. And when the Torobin went to war, the Netraxi were chained together and dropped as a welcome-mat for the Toroban armed forces to march over.Those hundred years passed, and the Torobin began to see the Netraxi in a more enlightened way. It was decided that some - though not all - should be emancipated to test their loyalty to their God-Emperor. Surprisingly, they were indeed loyal. Within ten years, the remaining Netraxi had been freed, but this was only the beginning of the struggle for freedom, All across Torobin space, a dozen other races remained enslaved, and the blatantly racist policies of the Torobin meant that there was only room for Shroom in positions of power.And then the great, glorious and eternally enlightened God-Emperor Zifin I (may his spores find warm soils!) decided that one - but only one - filthy xeno would be given the opportunity to lead Toroban forces. His case would decide whether or not aliens were worthy of being equals to those they had once called master. They chose a lowly Netraxi called Cax.Cax was a badass.Hired at the age of 41, he was immediately thrust into the Toroban war of conquest against an alliance led by the Bavi, a technologically superior race. Four fleets were deployed: three led by Torobin and the fourth led by Cax. Almost immediately the fleets were heavily engaged, taking severe casualties. Cax was sent to support a Toroban admiral, but when he warped in he found the Admiral's fleet destroyed, the gallant mushroom shredded and scattered across the system. Undaunted, Cax sent his fleet into the attack and smashed the Admiral's killers, securing the system. As the Torobin lost a second fleet to the Bavi, it was only Cax holding the line that gave the Torobin enough leverage to force a white peace and retreat with their dignity intact.This was only the beginning.Cax was sent back to Torobos to rebuild his fleet and upgrade it, in the expectation that the Torobin would soon be having a second go at the Bavi. Five years into the refit, however, he received the chilling news that a portal had opened up only a few systems away, spewing forth energy demons that wished only to feast upon the mortals' planets. The unlucky star-system was consumed. And then another system fell. And another. And another. And then it was Netraxis' turn. Cax could only look on via his monitor as his beloved homeworld, his people that looked to him for salvation, everyone, were all annihilated in a heartbeat. As the Torobin military crumbled he took his fleet to the furthest sector, the Malthin Bulwark, and gathered his forces for a desperate counterattack.And then the Fox nation attacked.Either through cold malice or a hilarious inability to perceive the danger of FRICKIN' WORLD-EATING ENERGY DEMONS, the race known only as the Sly Foxes decided to attack the Toroban Glorious Alliance with overwhelming force, right along the line of the Malthin Bulwark. Cax found his reinforcements cut off, his spaceports attacked and his empire still dined upon by the dreaded Unbidden. It was then, in this darkest of hours, that Cax made his move.With the Bulwark crumbling behind him, Cax launched a desperate attack against the Unbidden Portal with every warship the Torobin could muster. It was do or die. If he won, the Unbidden would no longer be able to spam doomstacks to conquer the ungrateful galaxy. But if he lost...the galaxy would be lost with him. At the age of 54, with a hundred warships in tow, this would be his finest hour.He did it.He frickin' did it.Surrounded by no fewer than three Unbidden doomstacks, Admiral Cax somehow fought his way to the portal and shattered the demons' grip on the galaxy, destroying two of the doomstacks as he did so. With his mission accomplished, he warped away to safety. Fewer than a third of his captains made it out. But the galaxy was saved. For any ordinary admiral, this would have been a time to celebrate. But Cax was no ordinary admiral.Cax was a badass.Badly damaged from the Battle for the Portal, Cax immediately returned his fleet to the Bulwark and smashed the Sly Foxes in a series of fleet-to-fleet battles, taking the war deep into the enemy's heartland. A little too deep, some might say, because there was the slight issue of his fleet being surrounded and utterly destroyed, but Cax made it out and his heroic counter-attack had once again turned a losing situation into a White Peace. By now Cax was pushing 70. Time to retire, the Torobin said.But badassery doesn't retire.Cax immediately took command of a new fleet being built to purge the galaxy of the Unbidden for once and for all. Armed with the latest weapons and cutting-edge technology taken from the Sly Foxes, Cax's Crusaders came together from all corners of Torobin space to follow their inspiring commander. The liberation was long and bittersweet, as although Cax was proud to be the Admiral chosen to drive the Unbidden from his homeworld, he knew that only the dead would greet him on Netraxis. But liberate he did, and at the age of 100 he destroyed the last Unbidden installation and restored the lost worlds to the Torobin. In gratitude, the God-Emperor transformed Toroba into a Mega-Corporation and emancipated every last slave, all thanks to Cax's heroism. And they all lived happily ever after, right?Wrong.Happily ever after is for people who haven't tried hard enough.Cax had a score to settle with the Bavi. They had destroyed his companions in the Bavi War. They had stood back and watched as the Unbidden destroyed his homeworld. Worst of all, they were just kinda there, y'know?. And so, at the age of 108, Cax set out for one final war. The names and legends of that war still echo down the ages. At Zabeem it was Cax who ambushed the 12th Bavi Fleet and smashed it to scrap. At Gandaros it was Cax who rescued the allied fleets from certain doom. At Kovin it was Cax who held the line as fleet after fleet warped in and were suddenly, but unsurprisingly, vanquished. And it was behind Admiral Cax that the entire allied fleet mustered for the final assault on Hydrobius that ended the war. Best of all, the surviving Netraxi were given permission to colonise the new worlds opened up by the Second Bavi War. Cax hadn't just saved his people, he'd given them a future too.When he died at 113, the mourning was brief and efficient. He would've liked it that way. RIP Cax.

2019 Whatever floats your boat.Raft is an Early Access survival game developed by Redbeet Interactive. You begin with a tiny raft and over the course of the game you’ll collect flotsam for resources to help you expand your raft and make surviving just a little easier. Along the way, you’ll run into islands to stop at as well as stave off an incredibly obsessive shark.One thing I will say, is this game can feel a little bit monotonous. I strangely enjoy monotony at times, but if you don’t then this game might not offer enough to keep you interested.Positives:Raft has fairly good visuals, nothing groundbreaking but it’s certainly nice to look at (I particularly like the sunrises and sunsets).The core gameplay is fairly simple, but surprisingly well done. The meat of the game is really just using a grappling hook to pull in floating resources which you then use to make different tools and equipment to help you survive, such as water purifiers and wooden spears. It can feel a little slow at times, but for the most part it felt like there was a decent level of progression in the game.As well as fishing for resources (and fish) there are also islands that you sometimes come across. Each island has something unique about it, but they all contain some of the rarer resources required for more advanced crafting. The islands help break things up a bit and add some nice variety to the game, though they can be a little bit too challenging to get on. You also come across abandoned rafts every one in a while that also add some nice variety.The difficulty level you choose makes a surprisingly significant impact on how the game feels. The easy mode is very relaxing, little pressure from the survival elements, and you can take the game at your own pace. Normal mode requires more attention to be paid to how hungry and thirsty you are, and things can pretty quickly get away from you. The hardest mode obviously offers the most challenge but honestly it also has the least realism since you’re constantly needing to top up your survival bars. There’s also a creative mode, that’s pretty self-explanatory. Playing singleplayer and multiplayer also offer two very different experiences. Singleplayer makes you feel lonely and isolated. It’s also more relaxing and I actually found it quite meditative too. Multiplayer (depending on who you’re playing with of course) is a bit more involved and energetic, progression is a bit faster too. I’ve enjoyed playing both, but I think I prefer singleplayer for this one. In a sea (ha, get it) of survival games, Raft actually manages to have a pretty uniqueNeutral:For the main antagonist of a game, the shark is a little underwhelming. I actually ended up turning off shark attacks while I was playing because I enjoyed it more. The shark really just attacks you when you’re in the water and every so often it’ll attack your Raft and try to break some off. It definitely adds some extra challenge; I just didn’t particularly enjoy that challenge. This really comes down to personal preference though. The survival requirements can be a little intense, but changing the difficulty level really makes a difference. I figure some people will probably be annoyed that the main challenge comes from how quickly your hunger and thirst bars decrease, but I personally didn’t mind just making the game easier overall to enjoy the game more.Negatives:I really wish there was more music in the game. There were long stretches of time where the game was pretty much completely quiet. I’m sure there are plenty of people who play with their own music or podcasts, but I found the in-game music added to the immersion when it was actually playing. While I do enjoy some of the monotony, I do still feel like the game can be a little too repetitive. I often went long periods between seeing an island, and it can get pretty uninteresting if you’re an hour or two into just floating around looking at nothing but ocean. I don’t think there’s enough wood to go around. Planks are the main resource used in construction and crafting, and if you’re trying to build a decent sized raft then you need a LOT of planks. I got kind of fed up of building one new piece of my raft, going back and spending a few minutes getting more planks, and then repeating that again and again until I had built up what I wanted.Verdict:Raft ends up being a little too repetitive even for someone who enjoys monotony but it’s a fairly unique survival game and you can customize your experience with it fairly well. I’d certainly recommend it for fans of the survival genre.

review: 2018 What I hoped would be a settlement building game akin to the Cultures and Settlers series or Banished turned out to be something else entirely.First of all, the game is played on what is essentially a grid, wherein you need to scout patches of land and then spend resources to acquire them. On each such patch you can build a limited number of buildings, to which you can assign a limited amount of villagers, usually for the purpose of passively generating one of the game's three primary resources: food, lumber, and gold.Now, when I say passively, I do mean passively. Assigning a villager to a job will not make them actually perform some sort of special task, e.g. chopping wood or hunting deer, despite what the game's animation might have you believe, but will rather simply increase the plus number next to the resource counter in the resource bar and make the amount tick up faster. There is no "actual" interaction between your vikings and the map's resources.For a large portion of the time, however, instead of making your resources go up faster, you'll be worrying about making them go up at all, as you'll constantly be paying these resources for upkeep: food goes toward keeping your vikings from starving, lumber goes toward keeping them from freezing, and gold goes toward keeping your buildings from suddenly catching fire (seriously).This wouldn't be nearly as much of a headache were it not for the aforementioned building limit. Combined with the fact that you can only build food-generating building on special tiles or patches of land, and only one per such location, the very small yield from said buildings, and the increased demand for food and lumber during the game's winter period, your main focus will be keeping your settlement from falling apart, rather than building a robust economy that can sustain a large military force.At the end of the day, with no real interaction with the map, the limitation of the grid system, and the way the resource system is structured, I found myself just not having fun with this game.

2011 Portal 2 is Valve's last great game from its golden age. It's a worthy sequel to the original Portal, which was a short but sweet puzzler with a simple yet innovative central mechanic. This time around it's less of a horror-mystery and more of an action-comedy. There's new mechanics, more puzzles, more areas of Aperture to explore and even more AIs to supply witty (or not-so-witty in the case of the chief new character) banter. That, and a doozy of an ending. It's absolutely worth playing, but I would recommend playing the first Portal beforehand if possible.A separate co-op campaign - best played with friends, since that's what it was meant for and you won't find strangers looking for a partner anymore - as well as a level maker with Workshop upload capability add to the game's replayability. It's interesting to note that there is a menu option for multiplayer item trading that was ultimately never implemented, which kind of tells you about where Valve would go as a developer. There is also a good 'making-of' Portal 2 e-book for sale in the Steam store that I'd recommend as well if you're interested about the game's history.

I have been playing for a year and my purchasing is about 10-20$ per month on it. Marvel Snap is a sub 5 minute game (or ~10-30 for a Conquest game) of online PVP-only card battling featuring constructed decks of 12 cards from the hundreds and hundreds of cards in the total pool which feature Marvel characters big and small. The game is fast paced, and it manages to keep each new match fresh and interesting, even if you're sometimes facing the same card compositions, due to how 'lanes' get randomised each game.Snap is NOT pay to win, just to say this out the gate. The game respects and is kind to your money and time (/daily/weekly missions/conquest mode and such all have generous time limits and allow you to 'miss' doing some). However, there are some a core tenants to the game, as reinforced by developer communication, which may sway people which want to go hard into it.1) The game is treated as a truly living card game with ebbs and flows in the meta, cards getting changed and adjusted frequently, sometimes drastically. The meta is kept dynamic and on edge by also 4-5 new cards per month, which sometimes release 'on the high end' of tuning to make them exciting and to allow them change the flavour of meta for the immediate period of its release. This has upsides and downsides, and overall the game balance rarely 'breaks', but you have to understand that this isn't Hearthstone or Magic. The experience of constantly changing conditions, cards and 'chasing' the optimal solution is key to the experience. Your favorite deck may get nerfed, you may discover a new favorite deck with a new card. Expect this ebb and flow.2) As often reinforced, the game's progression systems are tuned to a specific goal. While allowing generally high card acquisition rates, from 4-5 a week initially to eventually around 1 new card each week, the way the progression works, it's /extremely/ hard, barring putting in money, to 'have all the cards' at any one time, and keeping to 100% having all the cards all the time. Everyone can get the hot new card at any point, there's no gating, but you can't afford to use ingame currency to do that for /every/ new card. The system is still shaking out even 6 months later but expect that after you've unlocked all of the Pool/Series 3 cards (aka, about 5-6 months into your journey in the game) and gotten into about half of the Pool/Series 4/5 cards, for progression to slow and to realise that you'll always be missing around 10-15 or so cards, that number going up or down depending on various factors.3) Game respects your time. Daily missions stack up to 6 and that covers a 24 hour period. Play 15-20 minutes each day and you can reasonably get through all your dailies. Each daily mission counts to the total 25 daily missions for the weekly mission. Given you get 6 a day for 7 days, you can miss a few daily missions and still do the weekly mission. There's a week-end mission system which can vary, but you have about 4 days, starting friday to tuesday to complete them. Conquest mode monthly reward doesn't need grinding and while it does require a bit of play, can be done reasonably easy once you have a grasp on the game, plus how the game issues out Gold tickets very often. The only reward which is somewhat gated by skill is the infinite track, as the 90 reward for gold can be challenging to get without persistence and time investment.3) Money. The game can entirely be played f2p, without feeling at a loss, and you will be able to get the exact cards you want in time. You mostly pay money for fast-tracking progression and aesthetics/variants of cards.Season pass. If you're going to spend any money, it's recommended for you to buy the season pass for 10$/eur (for example as of right now, free gets 2300 credits, 300 gold, 1 variant, 1 title and 1 card back, and buying the pass gets you a new card, extra 300 credits, 900 gold, 6 variants, 3 avatars, 2 titles and 1 card back). There's no real reason to buy the 'premium' season pass for 15$ which gives you +10 levels progression. In a regular season you can end up to going over the 50 for the max reward, up to 60 or 70, playing normally and doing daily missions. The rewards past 50 are randomized and aren't worth paying money for. Bundles. The game offers recurring and special bundles. The recurring are always paid with gold and are of moderate value. The special bundles are often money based, some at RIDICULOUS prices (100$ bundles aren't rare), but a measure of them are gold based. If you want to optimally play your game for maximum gameplay benefits you will be buying special gold variants with the gold you make in the game. To note, new players get a few new player specific bundles. Those are often very good value all things considering.There's also sometime webstore specific offers which aren't in the game, weirdly, but it is what it is, they can be found on the Marvel Snap official website.All in all, for casually enjoying the game and without whaling, personally, i spend about 15-20$ total monthly on the game, for the 30ish hours i play it monthly. I feel it's fair, ymmv, and i don't feel like i'm missing out on not putting in /more/ money into the game. However, if you /want/ to spend money on the game, there will always be something shiny or cool around the corner, or "good" reasons to make big purchases (mostly aesthetics end of game).4) What not to do. Pay for 'fast tracking' in the shop. Buy boosters for gold upgrading. Buy gold for money outside of a bundle deal which features gold. Trading gold for credits in the shop. Buy a bundle before checking fan sites if the value is worth it. While there aren't '♥♥♥♥' bundles', there are often bundles which are more worth your money than others for the amount of ingame progression you get.Also don't play Alioth or Galactus. :p

2021 Dead Cells is a fantastic, Rogue-lite, MetroidVania, Hack-n-Slash, Platformer hybrid frankenstein's monster of a game I don't have many hours, but I've owned the game on Switch for a while now, since initial release on the platform. I've sunk over 100 hours into that version, so I'm pretty darn sure anything I say about Dead Cells there applies here, and then some, cause this version gets the new updates first, has higher frame-rates, and GLORIOUS MODS! The Good The game has gorgeous art-direction, managing to not only be quite colorful, dreamy, and imaginative, but also somehow disturbing and macabre. Truly a revolutionary point in gaming, I say; we've gone from M rated games being dark and drab, gray-scaled generic shooters to fantastical games about a disease that infects every part of an island to the point of no return, but yet still somehow manages to be beautiful, encapsulating, over the top and self-aware. This also goes for the music and sound design, which only add to the games more superficial charms (art-direction, sound design, and music can go a long way in making a game good, but we all know the gameplay is where it's at).Dead Cells manages to keep the gameplay refreshing NEARLY EVERY SINGLE RUN, since level generation, gear, monster spawn locations, and secrets are all randomized. The player is encouraged to experiment with the weapons and skills they obtain, mix and match, and discover their preferred playstyle(s) as they go along. Of course, this game is also a rogue-lite, so death is 1.) common/intended but also 2.) not as big of a deal as the player would think. All progression the player gains while playing is saved any time you pass through a stage transition, letting the player rest easy knowing they don't have to go through all the hard work of obtaining weapon, skill, and costume blueprints again, on top of normal progression items as well. Once you've unlocked something, it's unlocked, unless you play on a different save file of course.Furthermore, the complexity and nuance in the actual combat and mobility of the game is staggering. There's 3 categories of gear; Brutality, Tactics, and Survival. Each come with their own unique weapons and skills, sporting their own unique usage and mechanics. Some of these categories share weapons, allowing the player to mix a Brutality build with a bit of Survival, or Survival and Tactics, etc. On top of this, there's Mutations, which FURTHER augment the player's playstyle (determined by build). There's builds the player can create that are orientated around skill-cool-down reduction, using weapons with critical hit synergy and parries. There's builds that are focused around crowd control, keeping enemies slow, stuck in place, or frozen, so you can unleash slow, but devastating attacks. There's builds that are focused around playing Dead Cells like it's some Megaman X love-letter, runnin' and gunnin. There's builds focused around speed. Builds focused on stealth. Builds focused on eliminating mobs in levels over bosses, or bosses over mobs. There's simply too much to go through to do it justice.And if there's anything the player DOESN'T like about Dead Cells, well guess what? There's a "custom mode," that allows the player to affect not only level generation, but also what weapons and abilities spawn, how much gold they have, how many mutations they can have, and other game modifiers that spice up the gameplay. If the base game isn't for you, then maybe a "remixed" approach is better? The Bad The randomization of Dead Cells makes the progression to not only obtain blueprints but also unlock the stuff themselves with cells is a rather slow, arduous process that would benefit from being expedited further, even more than just going up a tier in boss cells. To make matters worse, 2BC, 3BC, and 4BC are not comfortably beaten (and that's me putting it gently, because even then it's not comfortable) without having unlocked more reliable weapons, skills, and mutations prior. I could not imagine beating 5BC without my Open Wounds mutation, fully upgraded shops, S tier weapons, let alone beating 3BC without the Swift Sword, Rampart, and Tonic. This would be fixed if the time it took to acquire all this good stuff, which makes the game more fun with more options to experiment with, less time consuming. Some mutations and gear have less than a 1% chance of dropping, requiring run upon run upon run upon run to get them. There is a skill that guarantees blueprint drops, but it doesn't really help much. The grind is real and it is a slog, especially for someone, such as me, who has already unlocked everything on a different console. Players coming from a different version, or players looking to play it all over again from the actual beginning, beware.This section below was complaining about how much it took to get to the spoiler boss JUST to practice fighting him. This issue has been resolved with the latest patch. However, this leads to a new issue; the practice zones for bosses do not take into consideration scaling abilities/weapons.As you progress through biomes in Dead Cells, you obtain "scrolls" that increase your health, damage (for certain weapons, like tactics buffs tactics weapons, etc.), and improve the effectiveness of mutations. These are not present for the practice rooms. So you're left with fighting the bosses at base level 1 for brutality, survival, and tactics, and on all of your weapons, and there's no additional amulets to wear for things like additional jumps.Basically, fighting the bosses to practice in the practice rooms is harder than actually fighting the bosses.Why is this point in the "Bad" section? Because some builds become pointless to use. That's why. Any non-crit build leaves you wailing on the bosses for ages (and even then, it still takes forever, and some of these builds really only become viable with scaled stats, namely the mutations). You're going to lose because you simply cannot do enough damage to outlast them. The player should eventually be able to "defeat" the bosses in the practice rooms so they can feel confident about taking them on in an actual run, but because some builds aren't even capable of doing that in the practice room, they might end up not bothering experimenting. The Ugly? At this point in Dead Cells life as a game, the DLC is 100% required to truly get the best out of the game. This isn't a "pay 2 win" notice as much as it is "you can play the base game, but it gets SO MUCH BETTER when you have the DLC levels and gear". So that means, unfortunately, you dear reader, will probably need to shill out some more money. I'm sure some people are stingy enough for that to be a turn off, but the base game, I can assure you, will probably get you to WANT to give the developers more of your hard earned money.That, and the developers really give a damn about the game, put a lot of hard work and time into developing not only paid content but also FREE content for the player-base, and genuinely care about the over-all experience and balance of the game, almost to fault.Yeah, the game balance is a bit shoddy. It's alot better now than what it was during initial release but still. Some weapons are complete garbage, best left to sell for money, and some skills are better off not even unlocking.The latest patch removed multi-binding. While I agreed with disabling the ability to put everything on 1 button (which caused a lot of busted builds), I do not agree with the loss of dual-binding. I don't like this change! >:( Verdict If you like action games with lots of depth, complexity, and replayability, while also packing a respectable, challenging experience, then Dead Cells is the game for you. If you like action games with mindless blood and gore and just need a game to play for 30 minutes before going to the store or something, then Dead Cells is also the game for you.

2020 Originally when I heard about Rimworld ages ago I thought to myself that it was probably a game like Dwarf Fortress (which I have never played so I don't know). My impression of Dwarf Fortress was that it was some huge game with a lot of deep options to do stuff but really crappy graphics. One of those games where looking at screenshots you'd think it was closer to a spreadsheet than an actual game, and needed a huge manual to explain everything to the unwashed masses who might want to play it.Well, I still don't know about Dwarf Fortress but I can say for sure my impression about Rimworld being unintelligible to the uninitiated is wrong. Also after playing it for a bit I can honestly say it looks like Prison Architect and plays like one of those survival games where you start off with nothing and try to build up an empire or whatever. In fact I'd put it in the same genre as Don't Starve, Factorio, Oxygen Not Included, "Towns", Banished or any other game where you build up a base against invaders. (Note I'm not saying it's the exact same as any of these games, just that they all scratch the same itch).So you basically start a new game, pick a small selection of 3 starter survivors and then pick where you're starting out on the planet. Just about anywhere you choose will have lots of enemies around, so you basically are looking for the best resources to start out with. After that, what happens next depends on the game's AI storyteller. One may ramp things up nice and slow, another might throw random stuff at you with no regard for the player's survival. There's also the option to go peaceful if you're just wanting to build.There's lots of options and a tech tree to research, and every game could go drastically wrong (or right?) at any time if you're unprepared for what the game throws at you. It's the kind of game you can easily spend 5 or 6 hours at a stretch without realizing what time it is, and I'm sure you'll find a lot of reviews from people who have already invested thousands of hours into this game. The one caveat I'd like to put in this review is that there's an option for spending extra to put your name in the game. It's probably not worth it and the devs seem to not care about making sure everyone feels like they got their money's worth here. If you just want to see your own name in the game, you can do that without paying extra. The option is there for everyone ELSE to see your name in the game. So why is this a caveat? Well I went through the submission process and then checked the forums, and it seems like it can take a long time before they put the name in the game (which you're not even guaranteed to see). There were a couple of posts from people who said they were waiting a year for confirmation that the name had been put in the game. A YEAR. It seems like the timeframe for everyone else is on the order of 3 months or so, but they add the names in batches as the game gets major updates, so if you submit your name just after an update it could be quite a while before they add it. The devs aren't very communicative either so if you don't get confirmation that it's in the game from their submission form, then you're just left out in the cold completely.I'm sure it's a small dev team and they're not taking time out to answer questions or complaints on the forums, but at this stage in the game's development they really should hire a flunky to answer the forum posts asking "It's been a year, what's the status on my name submission?". How long would it take to figure out if it got put in the game or not and then say "We took care of you"?tl;dr the game is great but unless you just love the game so much that you want to throw extra money at the devs, don't waste your money on the Name DLC, and if you have any problems, good luck with that too since they're not going to answer any forum posts.

2022 Northgard takes a while to learn, but once you've reached the point where you can somewhat confidently build up a stable economy and sustain your population while commanding a handful of warriors, the frustration goes away (for the most part) and the game becomes incredibly fun. On higher difficulties it's pretty fast-paced, but you don't have to make good use of every single second. The game can actually be pretty relaxing, and the cute graphics and nice score greatly contribute to an overall pleasant experience during the hundreds of hours you will likely end up playing Northgard for.Random negative events throughout the game, such as rat infestation or blizzard, add a welcome variety to the gameplay, and so do the various scenarios in the conquest mode with a wide range of objectives and special conditions and bonuses. In fact, the vast majority of my game time has been spent in co-op conquests with my fiancée, as I personally find it more engaging and varied than ranked multiplayer games. Kudos to Shiro for including this game mode! That being said, story mode is probably the best way for new players to gradually learn the game mechanics and try out different clans, while at the same time becoming a bit more immersed in the Viking world through a simple but enjoyable story.There are by now more than a dozen clans you can play for, each offering a sufficiently different experience, giving the game pretty much an infinite replayability. Among my favorite clans are the simpler ones, e.g., Wolf, Boar, Stag, Ox and Horse, as opposed to those that require tedious micromanagement, e.g., Raven, Dragon or Rat (one exception for me is the clan of Lynx, which requires a certain amount of micromanagement, yet I still find it fun to play for). Anyway, with the current selection, you're guaranteed to sooner or later find one or more clans that suit your playstyle.The only gripe I have with Northgard is the AI, which lacks any intelligence whatsoever and relies blatantly on cheating. On extreme difficulty, their cheating can be extremely frustrating – as you can see in the post-game stats, their resource income is several times higher than yours right from the beginning, which gives them virtually unlimited resources, which in turn allows them to sustain a large army at all times and prevents them from suffering during blizzards and other events. In a co-op conquest, you have to typically deal with six such opponents, often as a single team, which can be a total nightmare. At the same time, the AI enemies often just hang around with their armies or harass your edge territories and then withdraw, whereas if they wanted to, they could just make a push for your town hall and decimate you in a matter of minutes with those armies of theirs. Nevertheless, at the second highest difficulty level, the game feels boring at times.So, while I greatly appreciate the amazing job Shiro has been doing balancing the game mechanics over the years, regularly adding new content and now even planning to extend the story mode, I think investing time into substantially improving the AI would be in order.◆◆◆◆◆ Gameplay◆◆◆◆◇ Story/Campaign◆◆◆◆◆ Engagingness◆◆◆◆◇ Atmosphere/Immersiveness◆◆◆◆◇ Visuals/Environment◆◆◇◇◇ Ease of Mastery◆◆◆◆◆ Replay ValueOverall: ⭐ 4.5/5

2021 American Truck Simulator, in theory, is a game that should be « killing it »: some of the scenery on the map, whether it be Interstate 70 in Western Colorado, or US Highway 95 in Idaho, is absolutely beautiful. It definitely adds to the overall experience of driving a truck, and sometimes you just have to stop on the side of the road in order to appreciate the scenery that SCS has put into this game. There are some exceptions however, as SCS has refused to finish the New Mexico DLC, nearly 4 after its release- you are left with a state which has an unfinished road network and that’s a pain in the ass to drive around. However, the beauty of the graphics has come at the expense of an actual simulation of driving a truck. The feeling of using brakes while driving is like that of a cheap iOS trucking game for iPad, and some of the truck horns used in-game were horrendously recorded; it’s as if SCS recorded the sound using 1960s sound equipment. The economic company management system is a joke, and there’s clearly been no willingness on the part of the developers to improve on this aspect of the gameplay; other than the update that years ago allowed players to own their own trailers, this is the sort of system that was designed by a bunch of 90 year olds without any imagination at all. Why are there no contracts that last more than 1 delivery, or actual levels of insurance? Truck brands don’t mean anything, it’s the same experience whether you’re driving a Kenworth or a Volvo.Many players would like to say how American Truck Simulator has been constantly improved since it’s release, nearly 5 years ago. Well other than « fluff » that keeps only the most die-hard fan of the game engaged, there has been no improvements made to what is supposed to be an actual simulation. Just pretty graphics to make players forget that SCS treats this game as nothing more than a cash-cow; new « lighting » and truck brands are just there to give off the impression that SCS is somehow « trying » to fix their game. It’s sad because if they really wanted to, they could make American Truck Simulator into an actually good game, but instead greed and being cheap is more important to them.

2021 Sea of Thieves is a pirate fantasy sandbox with an enormous amount of things to do, made unpredictable and exciting by the addition of other players. Coordinating together across the deck of a massive pirate ship is pure chaos at times, but it’s also endlessly entertaining. The cosmetic-only progression system doesn’t give you as much incentive to keep playing as I’d have liked and its free-form nature left me feeling lost at sea at times, but if you’ve got a good group of two or three friends to play with, it’s hard to find a game as entertaining to jump aboard. It’s important to understand that even though Sea of Thieves is a shared-world online adventure game, it’s not actually an MMO with a persistent world. This means that each and every time you log into Sea of Thieves you’re given a brand-new ship in one of three classes based on the size of your crew– Sloop (up to two players), Brigantine (up to three players), or Galleon (up to four players); and everything except your long-term progression goals are reset. All of the supplies you accumulated last time, the row boat you found, the storage chests you saved, all of it’s gone. Great game. It's sad if you don't have any friends to play with.

2023 A Devilishly Good Time in the Underworld…» Hades, developed by Supergiant Games, is a roguelike action game that plunges players into the dark and treacherous depths of Greek mythology. With its exquisite art style, dynamic combat, compelling narrative, and engaging progression mechanics, Hades has garnered critical acclaim and an ardent fan base. Let’s delve into the underworld and uncover why this game is a complete masterpiece, and how it has solidified its place as one of the best titles ever introduced to the roguelike genre.Gameplay and Combat» Hades takes the core elements of a roguelike game and infuses them with a level of polish and fluidity rarely seen in other titles. As Zagreus, the defiant prince of the Underworld, you embark on a quest to escape the realm of Hades. With each run, players must navigate their way through procedurally generated chambers, battling hordes of mythical creatures and fearsome bosses. Paired with a combat system that is fast-paced, responsive, and deeply satisfying, the game welcomes a variety of playstyles through the use of different weapons, upgrades, and abilities.Though what truly sets Hades apart is the strategic depth of its mechanics. The seamless combination of tight combat mechanics and the progression system strikes a perfect balance between challenging gameplay and rewarding advancement. Each death feels like an opportunity to learn, improve, and experiment with different strategies and weapon combinations. The extensive range of customizable aspects, such as the vast array of boons from the gods of Olympus, offers distinct abilities that can be combined for powerful synergies. This depth of customization ensures that each run feels fresh and provides a wealth of strategic choices.Narrative and Characters» Regarding the plot, Hades weaves an enthralling narrative that explores themes of family, rebellion, and self-discovery. Through masterful writing and exceptional voice acting, each character feels authentic and deeply layered. The meaningful interactions and dynamic dialogues between Zagreus and the other denizens of the Underworld gradually unravel the complex web of stories and connections between the characters. This intricate relationship system allows players to build friendships, rivalries, and even romance. What makes the storytelling truly remarkable is the game’s roguelike structure. Each failed attempt to escape the Underworld uncovers new storylines and character development, making each death a narrative advancement rather than a setback. This unique approach to storytelling maintains a constant sense of progression, even in the face of defeat.Art and Sound Design» Another notable characteristic of Hades is that it boasts a visually stunning art style that effortlessly blends hand-drawn artwork with vibrant colors and fluid animations. Each character, enemy, and environment is thoughtfully designed, vividly animating the world of Greek mythology with an enchanting and distinctive allure. From the grand halls of Olympus to the foreboding depths of Tartarus, every location is filled with rich details, evoking a sense of awe and wonder.Complementing the stunning visuals is a compelling soundtrack that perfectly captures the intensity and emotion of every moment. From the thunderous clash of weapons to the haunting melodies that accompany your journey, every audio element is expertly crafted. The voice acting is exceptional, with each character expressing their personality and emotions with conviction. The soundtrack also perfectly captures the game’s atmosphere, blending epic orchestral compositions with modern rock and electronic elements.Replayability» One of the hallmarks of a great roguelike is its replayability, and Hades excels in this aspect. The game’s branching narrative paths and multiple endings provide additional incentives for multiple playthroughs, encouraging players to explore different choices and consequences. With its addictive gameplay loop, diverse combat options, and the promise of uncovering new narrative elements, Hades offers a roguelike experience that remains captivating and fresh even after countless hours of play. Even if you’re aiming to master every weapon, unlock all the character relationships, or discover the hidden truths of the Underworld, Hades rewards dedication and exploration, making it an absolute joy to revisit time and time again.Conclusion» In summary, whether you're a fan of the roguelike genre or simply seeking a gripping and immersive gaming experience, Hades is an absolute must-play that will keep you hooked from the first escape attempt to the last. Prepare to embark on an unforgettable journey through Greek mythology, where each run is a new adventure filled with danger, discovery, and devilishly good fun.Score: 9.6/10Was this review helpful?» If so, please leave a rating. 𝙈𝙮 𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙨𝙤𝙣𝙖𝙡 𝙑𝙞𝙚𝙬𝙨/𝙀𝙭𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨/𝙀𝙭𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙞𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙚 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝 𝘾𝙤𝙢𝙥𝙖𝙣𝙮 𝙤𝙛 𝙃𝙚𝙧𝙤𝙨 3I had such high hopes for Company of Heroes 3. I’ve been a huge fan of the series, and when they announced it, I thought, "This is it! The ultimate World War II strategy game." But after playing it, I’m left wondering—what the hell happened? This game feels half-baked, and it’s honestly disappointing in so many ways.Let’s talk about the sound first. Gunfire and explosions? Completely underwhelming. I don’t know how else to put it—this is supposed to be a gritty WW2 game, and the sounds of combat should hit hard. But they don’t. The gunshots are weak, and the explosions sound like they're coming from a toy set. Where’s the punch? Where’s the chaos? It’s just not there. For a game that’s supposed to make you feel like you’re in the middle of a brutal war, the sound design totally falls flat.Then there's the graphics. I’m honestly confused. The visual style feels like something out of a comic book or a lighter strategy game like Age of Empires IV, not a game about one of the most devastating wars in human history. WW2 was grim, dark, and full of suffering. But Company of Heroes 3? It looks way too clean, way too colorful. It just doesn’t match the tone of the setting. I keep thinking back to Company of Heroes 2, where everything was gritty and bleak, and it really captured the horrors of war. This game, though, has such a strange, cartoonish vibe to it. It’s honestly baffling that they went in this direction.And here’s the kicker—they already had the perfect blueprint with Company of Heroes 2. That game was the WW2 RTS, setting the standard for how a war game should feel. Dark, heavy, atmospheric, with intense battles and strategic depth. So, when they announced Company of Heroes 3, I thought we’d just get more of that, but better—new factions, innovative mechanics, a fresh campaign, and some upgraded visuals. What did we get instead? A step backward. Sure, there are some tweaks here and there, but nothing that really pushes the series forward. If anything, it feels like they tried to simplify things.The battles? They just don’t feel as immersive or intense. I wanted hardcore, edge-of-your-seat combat, but instead, everything feels a bit too tame. The unit clashes don’t have that same brutal, chaotic feel that made the previous games so exciting. It’s like something’s missing—it’s hard to get truly invested in what’s happening on screen. Instead of feeling like I'm commanding troops in a life-or-death situation, it feels… casual. And that’s not what this game should be.Honestly, the only reason I bought the game is because I still want to support the developers. I’m holding onto some hope that they’ll fix this with updates, because I know they can do better. They’ve done it before, and they can definitely do it again. But man, this game is a far cry from what I expected. They had all the tools and examples to make this a fantastic follow-up, and instead, it feels like they missed the mark.Here’s what needs to happen: they need to ditch the cartoony graphics and bring back the realism. Give us that grim, dark WW2 atmosphere we loved from CoH2. Make the battles more intense, more hardcore. We don’t need a watered-down version of this franchise—we want the full, immersive, gritty war experience that made us fans in the first place.Right now, Company of Heroes 3 feels like a rough draft. But I’m still holding out hope that it’ll turn into the game we all wanted with some serious updates. Until then, it’s a pretty big letdown.

2021 Early Access Review Enthralling world building coats in chrome this dangerous and complex RPG. Much like Dwarf Fortress, I feel this game best sells itself through morsels of experiences. Spray sentience into a concrete wall, and befriend it. Call him Pumice. Buck naked, Pumice has 40 armor. Pumice's equipment slots are named thoughtfully by a detail-obsessed development team. Pumice wears sandals on his foundations, a cloak over his molding, and carries a carbide warhammer in his left crack. Pumice follows you around. Like you, Pumice gains xp, he mutates. Submit Pumice to some friendly mind control. Give him extra arms (cracks), maybe a teleportation spell? Pumice teleports in front of my enemy. Pumice Pummels.This game rewards all attempts to break it, it contains ecosystems of puzzling enemies. In the late game, it does not suffer fools. Wander too quickly into a new map? The enemy wizard across the map has sensed your presence. He creates 4 clones of himself, with all his stats, abilities, and equipment. His four clones teleport to your location. The throw ice grenades at you until your temperature rises enough that you freeze solid. Effectively, you are dead here, in exactly three turns. Maybe instead, you killed him? Good job, but somebody like him will always return. I love this game. My only complaint? A marriage of two UI philosophies that desperately need a divorce lawyer. Many of the menus are from the old system, with huge lists of text. Turn on the 'New' UI elements. For most instances, especially the main overlay, it is far superior. But, for a game swimming in Matrix code, it desperately needs font size options for it's menus, especially the inventory.Live and Drink.

2021 Early Access Review I'm a big fan of creative/survival games, of all types and flavours, but Valheim is the first in a while to really grip me the way it has. While it is in early access (and this shows in some of its parts) the basic building blocks of this game create a fantastic and fun experience, especially if you can wrangle a group of buds to play with you. Build your very own settlement, conquer enormous godly monsters, and defend your new found home from random sieges from monsters. Theres a surprising amount of content already available, and with the upcoming Hearth and Home update this will only expand. The worlds are vast, there are already a great variety of biomes, weapons, monsters and this will only get better as time goes on.HOWEVERWhile the game is beautiful, and extremely fun (especially the building system, which makes it very, very easy to quickly build all sorts of beautiful buildings and structures) there are a few nitpicks present that can slowly chip away at your good time. For the most part, this revolves around combat and the stamina system, especially in the early game. Combat is something of a chore since running, dodging, and attacking all use stamina, and the regeneration of stamina is laughably slow. Food can increase your maxmimum stamina, but increasing the regeneration of stamina (the most important stat imo) relies on mead items with massive cooldowns and very short windows in which they are actually active, or on a buff that has to be continually refilled by resting. This means that you have to build bases all over the map to keep your rested bonus up, and that frustration free combat and exploring is limited to the time you have left on that buff. This is only multiplied as well by the fact that enemies are all quick and have infinite stamina, meaning they can just endlessly chase you up enormously steep mountains that you struggle to climb, or swim infinitely across rivers to chase you as you basically slowly drown. Stamina in general is a HUGE fun killer, since it also applies to building. Nothing feels worse than having to use stamina food just to be able to sit and build, since placing, destroying and repairing building parts uses stamina for some bizarre reason. This means you'll build a small part of building, sit and wait for your stamina to regen, build another small part etc and so on. Stamina also makes other tasks like wood cutting, mining etc a chore as well, since again, you will do a small amount of work, wait for your stamina to regen, etc etc. And this is only compounded by the fact that you often get swarmed by monsters while you're trying to work, and are often left to awkwardly walk around trying to dodge the monsters until your stamina regenerates again. The game is also surprisingly grindy in its progression, since gear and gear upgrades require large amounts of resources that usually must be manually hauled across the map. This means mining stuff, loading up a boat and setting sail back to your base (this is because the actually important items like metal ores cannot be transported in a teleporter). And to be honest - this can be and is extremely fun at first! You have a merry ole time sailing across the seas with your buddies. But then you realise that you will need hundreds of ores EACH for fully upgraded gear and the amount of ore you crammed into your puny boat hold is maybe enough for one or two bits of gear, and that there are four or more of you who will ALL NEED this gear to be able to meaningly contribute to combat vs the games bosses. This is mitigated once you gain access to a larger vessel (and I would really honestly like an even larger one) but it is still something to bear in mind - logistics and transporting ores is going to be a huge time sink.I would like to make it clear however, that the game is still extremely good in spite of these frustrations - these are just things you should keep in mind as you play. You MUST play around the stamina and rested system, and you MUST develop proper sailing routes and roads - these aren't necessarily bad things, even if they can be extremely frustrating, these are just Things that make up the core of the game. If you take things slow, play with friends, and remember to eat good buffing food and mead and keep well rested, the game is an absolute joy that you can enjoy for hundreds of hours. If you keep bashing your head against portal, combat and stamina limitations, you aren't gonna have a very good time, and while I understand the limitations and ways around them, I do hope they do more as development goes on to address these small annoyances.

I would much prefer the completion of tiers, then as you're flying around the events are now in the "pool" of things that could happen. -Not enough space battles. I thought this was a really fun part. Sadly, some of the space parts on the ship never changed (now that I think about it). Do I want larger battles with allied forces and objectives? YES please.-Traps are annoying as ♥♥♥♥ when you accidentally trigger them when trying to maneuver your character to the switches.-The warp danger from psyker powers really just kinda vanished after the early game.-Medkits in belts should automatically refill after combat if there are more in the inventory.-Should've been more exploration to be had. Events with just flavor text and lore are absolutely okay with me. Each system doesn't need a landing.-Did not get enough dogmatic points to reach tier 4+. That really bothered me since there is no way to get them past a point. As I was determining who I wanted to be in the RPG, I clearly spread some choices out and ended up ruining the later parts of this system.Those are all the talking points I can come up with off the top of my head. Took me 100 hrs and I wanted to keep going. I will replay this again when there is another steam sale and the DLC's have come out.Buy this on sale or not. Either way you will get a tonne of gametime out of it.

Unfortunately their publisher on the premium version is a shambles. There are also multiple game disrupting bugs that have not been addressed in a long time.On balance my overall recommendation is to buy the premium version on sale, and not sink the time in here unless you are prepared to spend a lot more.If cash is no object then get this version, and subscribe to premium etc so you are not as limited by the paywalls.

2023 EDIT: After finishing chapter 3 and with the new roadmap, I think this review is complete. If anything else changes, I'll edit accordingly.Limbus Company is good and fun. In spite of all its problems, I don't see this game as lesser than its sibling games of Lobotomy Corporation and Library of Ruina. If you enjoyed the previous works, this game will be good.Gacha and CurrencyI'm starting right with the gacha because that's probably what most people are going to focus on.It's okay, but certainly not generous right out of the game. Rerolling on mobile devices is fast and gives you 30 tries to pull. With rates considered, it's about 8.3% chance to get a specific 000/SSR Identity. Looking at what you pay for, it seems to be about 16 USD per 10 pull, not accounting for first time packages. There are monthly packs at 3 and 7 dollars that give a small daily amount. And the battle pass is 11 dollars.A lot of people seem to be hung up on the day 1 battle pass, but I'm personally numb to it. Mind that they have already confirmed that all Identities/EGO from the pass will become available once the pass expires, so the arguments of FOMO feel like they fall short here. Each season lasts for 3 months, meaning the 11 dollars is more akin to less than 3 dollars a month, the equivalent of a monthly currency pack. People who don't want to pay for live service games are justified in their concerns, but compared to other expoitative gacha games on the market?? Limbus Company is not one of those games, and I feel comfortable spending small amounts on it knowing I won't be squeezed out for every nickel and dime.For the people who don't want to pay for their pulls, the story is a bit more complicated. Lunacy, the currency for gacha pulls, is very limited. Story missions and chapters are not particularly generous at the start of the game past the initial 30 pulls, so you may find you have to reroll or work with what you get. Upgrading gear for their third skills and passives require turning shards, the dupe currency, into upgrade materials, which eats into one's ability to craft Identities. I was worried about this, and it does seem like the 400 shards needed to "spark" an identity you want is not going to be as accessible as one would hope. EDIT: As of the announced roadmap, March 16th will add farmable content that gives Identity EXP and threads for uptying, as well as adding lunacy to the weekly rewards for Mirror Dungeons. While the Lunacy is only one third of a free pull per week, the fact is that f2p players will no longer have to decide whether to use their mirror dungeon farming to upgrade characters or to save for a spark. Free to play Limbus is certainly feasible, but I worry that new content and the frequency of new gacha banners will alienate those people who can't spend.Story and WorldBoth Lobotomy Corporation and Ruina were known to have incredibly stellar writing. Ruina especially was good at giving a detailed look into the world of the City through its piece by piece storytelling. Limbus Company has large shoes to fill, and I don't really blame people for finding the initial writing lacking in comparison. It's slow starting out, and the length of each chapter is not used quite well. As opposed to the short yet potent snapshots of reception stories in Ruina, the early chapters really do feel mostly filler even from the perspective of narrating and explaining the world.Moving on from Chapter 2 onwards, the story picks up immensely. Once the game familiarizes the player to its setting, it takes off with typical Project Moon intensity. New areas are brought in and the factions within the regions are as fantastic and wild as we'd expect. One thing I have to note as well is the way they pace their cutscenes. Limbus Company feels like they actively want to avoid the bloated wordcount in cutscenes of other story-intense games like Arknights. Cutscenes are fairly short in comparison to those, and are often split up between multiple different chapters involving fights. While the fights can be seen as filler, I personally think it's a good call to help break between the monotony of story and character dialogue. There's a lot of thought put into the story and writing of this game, Limbus Company certainly continues to uphold Project Moon's rich story and world building.GameplayLimbus can be described as "Ruina, but watered down", but I think that's both misleading and also not even that bad of a thing. Ruina was lovely, it's huge and in depth and once one gets a hang of the system each floor becomes a sandbox for a mess of builds and strategies. But it's also confusing as hell, preparation takes forever and often requires shuffling through massive amounts of UI hell, and actual gameplay slows to a crawl as single turns can take 5 minutes to plan and execute. I've spent a large majority of my time in Ruina rifling through different builds, discovering ways to loop pages and find secret synergies between mechanics. But I also know when I talk about Ruina to most people, they resort to 2 to 4 primary builds on 1 floor and rarely shift their strategy. I don't think it's a bad thing for Limbus to not want to repeat Ruina in that regard.This game is not Library of Ruina, and the people who keep comparing it to Library of Ruina will be constantly disappointed. Targeting is automated compared to Ruina, but the order is consistent and encourages using defense dice to deal with attacks that you can't directly clash with. Clashes now use coins, and determining potential values of heads/tails flips creates more predictable results compared to the dice rolling of Ruina. Teams often have synergies built into each other and expects you to find ways to make Sinners work with each other. The game is difficult, just as Ruina was, but at the end of the day it's a functional and playable game. Most people need to learn how to play it instead of trying to play the game as if it's yet another Ruina mod.Even so, I agree that the main problem with gameplay is the inherit lack of control in the targeting system. Perhaps it's because the game's still new and we have to get used to the AI's targeting, but the lack of control feels like it limits a lot of strategic planning. Even if we aren't able to have full control over our team, I think being able to give some kind of general command to influence Sinner's targeting would be more interesting. Limbus is a one of a kind game, just as all of its previous games were. I think the gameplay requires a lot of hands-on learning and hard beats, but it's the kind of difficulty and learning curve I've come to enjoy. Last ThoughtsI think most people will enjoy what Limbus Company has and it's worth looking into if you want to see more of what the City has in store. The gacha aspect is disappointing to most people but believe me when I say that Limbus Company truly feels like a fully developed game firstmost and a gacha secondary in the best way possible.I've been following these games since Library of Ruina's initial release. I remember when Ruina first came out, when we had to level up our pages and passives were functionally randomized. I remember how long it took them to change major gameplay mechanics and how the difficulty spiked, and spiked often. The game only got better as it kept developing, but even then still had its mechanical bloat and difficulty and it still takes hours to load. Compared to Ruina, Limbus Company's initial release has been almost dream-like. Minus the initial bugs and server issues, I can say Limbus came out with far more than Ruina did, which only gives me more excitement for what more they'll release.

review: Once Human: A Witty Review of an Outlandish Adventure!Character Creation: Sliders Galore!Ever wanted to create a character that truly represents your wildest dreams or nightmares? In Once Human, the character creation is as deep as the Mariana Trench! With enough sliders to rival a fast-food joint's condiment bar, you can tweak, twist, and turn every aspect of your avatar until they're perfect. Or hilariously imperfect. The only downside? Hair colors are as limited as my dancing skills. Seriously, there's like five options. Rainbow Mohawk, where art thou?One Character, One Love...Until Now!Initially, Once Human allowed you to create only one character. One precious, singular being to pour all your hopes and dreams into. But fret not, my fellow gamers! The devs heard our collective groans and quickly pivoted faster than a cat spotting a cucumber. As of today, you can now create multiple characters across different servers. Yes, that means you can finally experiment with that blue-skinned, red-eyed monstrosity without deleting your main!A Letter from the Devs: An ApologyIn a heartfelt message that reads like an apology letter from your dog who just ate your favorite shoes, the devs said: "Based on player feedback, we have urgently opened up the functionality for multiple-character creation. You can now create characters on any server and embark on adventures with your friends. Our initial decision to close multiple-character creation was due to the imperfect experience of playing with multiple characters. We had originally intended to update it after perfecting the multi-character play function by August 1, but unfortunately, it led to a poor gaming experience. We sincerely apologize for this."It's a refreshing, quick and humble response, admitting that the initial decision led to a subpar experience. Kudos to the dev team for listening and acting swiftly.Gripping Storyline: The World AfterOnce Human isn't just about creating the most outrageous character imaginable. No, this game drags you kicking and screaming into a gripping storyline set in a post-apocalyptic world where enemies can be anywhere or anything. From mutated creatures to rival survivors, danger lurks around every corner. It’s like your favorite dystopian novel, but you’re the star of the show!Open World, No Tab-Targeting: Pure ImmersionForget tab-targeting; Once Human offers a completely open world experience where you must aim and attack manually. It's like playing an action movie where you control every thrilling moment. Wander through desolate cities, explore eerie forests, and scavenge through abandoned buildings in search of resources. The freedom is intoxicating, the danger is real, and the adventure is endless.Final Thoughts: Adventure Awaits!Once Human is a PVP/PVE MMO that's got the bones of something great. With its incredibly in-depth character creator (minus the hair color faux pas), engaging gameplay, and now, the ability to create multiple characters, it's shaping up to be a wild ride. The storyline is gripping, the world is immersive, and the enemies are as unpredictable as they come. So grab your sliders and get customizing, because the world of Once Human awaits your unique touch. And hey, maybe we'll get those extra hair colors in a future update. One can only dream...or slide.

2022 TL;DR If you're easily frustrated, hate platforming, and/or suffer from chronic pain or mobility issues with your hands, you're probably not going to enjoy playing this game. Read on.I don't usually do such thorough reviews, but I feel like I need to here, to justify my not recommending it. Don't get me wrong; I adore this game and the entire franchise, the characters, the designs, the music and sound, the little details that make it spooky. And this game is largely perfect, except for one particular aspect.Sound and music: ★★★★★Make sure you have headphones on, and on my headphones at least, there's significantly more bass when they're in wired mode as opposed to wireless, and there's some GOOD bass in the sound at times. The music is fantastic, and I have a couple of tracks in a playlist for when I need a boost. Little details in the sound like Mono's voice echoing slightly when he has the tin can hat on are delightful.Graphics: ★★★★★The rain that dominates two thirds of the game is gorgeous and realistic. The depth of field works in really magical ways, highlighting just how small you are in this world, and how big and scary everything else is. I like the handful of times where the game uses the lack of a front to the set, so to speak, so that you can see floors above or below you if you move close enough to the front of the area, it makes me feel like I'm in a dollhouse or something.Story and character design: ★★★★★...such as it is. Like the first game, this one is stellar for showing how a story can be told without any dialogue, just through the environment and events. There's a lot to puzzle through with this one and a lot of questions by the end that you have to come up with the answers for yourself, or just accept that maybe there aren't any answers. The theorists on Youtube can give a more concrete idea of what the story is. But some of the twists near the end are still mind-blowing and gut-wrenching, even with watching multiple people play through it before I even bought it. None of the enemy designs really sunk their hooks into me like they did with the first game; I'm on record as being frozen in fear for most of my first watch of the first game, with my shoulders up around my ears because I was so uncomfortable with some of the designs. (Claymation makes me deeply unhappy, but I can put up with it for a good story, and in this instance I was so fascinated by my own reaction that I oversaturated myself with the enemy designs trying to figure out WHY I'd reacted that way.) From the first game, the Chefs still upset me, but I adore the Janitor. Nothing in this one really did that for me, though they were certainly all grotesque and weird.Gameplay: ★★★★★The puzzles are all managable, nothing too hard to figure out, although ymmv; I remember watching a couple of different people get stuck on puzzles that were extremely straightforward. If you're a completionist like me, you'll be happy to know that you can 100% this game in a single playthrough. There's an excellent guide on the Steam Community. The checkpoint system is enormously better than the first game, which is a damn good thing, which leads into my last section.Controls: ★☆☆☆☆Here's where it gets stinky. The first game suffered from this as well, and I was really hopeful they would have improved for this one but they did not. The main problem is that this is a game with a 2D camera, and 3D controls, combined with lots of platforming and chase scenes. I can't tell you how many times I fell off of things or missed a jump because I was too far back or forward and couldn't tell the depth of where I needed to go. In chase scenes, it's a combination of depth (getting caught on doorways or misjudging where a gap is that you need to crouch through) and the timing for succeeding being so incredibly precise that it's very easy to mess up. Additionally, there's momentum to the movement, which is always pretty hit or miss in games for me, and Mono does like to get stuck on things. I started out playing with controller, but my wrist and hands started hurting about halfway through, so I switched to keyboard, which was much easier for me but still hard. I've never had my index finger lock in the straight position before! (I have health issues that give me chronic pain and hypermobility, so my joints are crappy and do things like that.) The Hospital chapter nearly killed me, I had to redo so many parts so many times because I kept flubbing things; getting timing wrong, not aiming the right way, getting stuck on geometry, not allowing for the fact that Mono doesn't stand up from a crouch or let go of an object immediately, etc. If the scares and adrenaline are coming from the controls being unpredictable, that's not scary, that's frustrating, and it detracts from what would otherwise be a perfect game. I watched probably three or four different people on Youtube play this when it first came out, and it was always interesting to see who figured what out easily, how people reacted to the story beats, etc., but many of them had the same issues I have with the controls. Your controls in a game should be invisible and fairly intuitive. The fact that they REALLY aren't in this are why I can't really recommend this game. It's a great game! But.

review: 2018 Northgard is a great game if you want an RTS that has a slower pace and plays more like a boardgame. You'll read reviews about the game not having a lot of strategy or depth, but in any given game (and I play PvP), you need to make a lot of decisions about your economy -- THAT'S where the strategy is. This game is about 80% economy and 20% military -- very opposite of Starcraft if that was your jam. There's no one unit countering another unit in this game, it's more about which tiles you want to colonize, how to choke your opponent out of certain resources, when to make a surprise attack, and which victory condition to go for in any given game based on clan and tile layout. Northgard is great, and challenging. If you only want to play the story and then play against bots, I wouldn't recommend it. Bots are pretty boring, and they cheat. Hard bots get free iron and their economies hardly ever suffer. You need to play this game as PvP to enjoy it. Watch some Let's Plays to decide if it's your thing. Also disregard any negative reviews about the DLC, which is not essential to playing the core game, the DLC is only for a clan, not different victory conditions or special buildings. Shiro Games has done a great job developing this game, I bought it over one year ago and they have released consistent patches and content, and the balance has always been pretty decent, nothing like the pendulum swing that you find in MOBAs. You can tell they are a great little indie company that their employees enjoy working for because it shines through in their development. Northgard is fun, not too serious, has just the right amount of depth, is very replayable and challenging, and has many little eastereggs and references to pop culture, that again, are fun.
