2020 This is a Need for Speed game with some what of an identity crisis... I don't think it knows what it's trying to be other than just an Arcade Racer with a bleak storyline. The customization is there and there's some cool stuff, but I feel like it's somewhat lacking from what we had in "NFS:Underground". Police chases are present, but they're not as engaging as they used to be in "NFS:Hot Pursuit" from 2011-12. They kind of picked and pulled things from many past games, but did not perfect anything.As usual, the music is kind of a toss up... About 40% of the music is alright, while the rest are skipable at best. None of them stand out to me as great tracks though. It's more or less what you'd expect out of a NFS game, I guess..The story is lackluster. Kind of feels like they wrote it in a day or two and just went with it. The people you engage with feel lifeless and that's unfortunately all due to the horrendous voice acting. This is what I consider the worst aspect of the game and is largely what makes the story line not very engaging or exciting. Some of the storyline missions almost don't make any sense.. One mission has you drive clear across the map to meet up with someone, but then when you get there, a cut scene starts where you make a call to someone and then you drive back to your garage... Couldn't I just make the phone call at the garage instead of wasting 5-6 minutes driving? Graphics is where this game shines it's brightest. This game is B-E-A-UTIFUL. The environment, the cars, the city, it's gorgeous. Day time, is about what you'd expect, but the city really comes to life at night. Races and buildings are lit up very nicely with blue and magenta neon colors and it does a great job of keeping you on the road to prepare you for tight turns and drift points.The selection of cars is a little weird to me. There is a very strange selection of old pointless cars, 90's Japanese cars, some SUVs for whatever reason, and your typical selection of super cars. All have varying levels of visual customization while some have almost none.Controls are fine. Driving/Racing is not very fun for the first couple hours until you get a better car and can start upgrading. My only gripe would be that drifting doesn't feel as fluid as it has in previous NFS titles...Bottom line, the game is mindless racing fun. If you can get beyond the bad storyline, there's some fun to be had here. Do I think it's worth the $60 price tag? I'll give it a solid MAYBE. I guess it depends on what you're expecting out of it. But, me personally, seeing that this is kind of a jack of previous NFS titles, but a master of nothing, then No. I could see it being worth $40 now in it's current state of being still a new game. The foundation is there, it just needs a little more.

This is now my second Final Fantasy game ever after XV in anticipation of XIV, so I can only compare my experience to those two games (well, the demo in XVIs case). I did enjoy XV quite a lot, but it was a mess in almost every aspect. Though I really enjoyed how it concluded, but I just wanted a better game throughout. So how did this one fair, as it is a remake of probably the most legendary one?First up: possibly my biggest gripe with XV. Gameplay feels very nice, but I kind of miss how much more movement there was in XV, like jumping for exemple lol as in this one you are basically glued to the ground. But the combat system felt way better than XV and after both the tutorials and a few encounters I got the hang of it quite well unlike XV which never really clicked and was very confusing and underexplained. I very much enjoy the mix of turn based party combat with character action gameplay and it looks really good in action. Everything feels very intuitive, impactful and is just very fun to engage with. The bosses are also an absolute spectacle to behold, and even fighting the regular "fodder" enemies just feels cool. The design of all of these are also super varied and really cool and unique looking. I also liked the ability system where you slot in different "materia" that grants you new abilities to use in combat that also level up as you use them. It feels intuitive to switch out what you want your party members to focus on in combat. Complaints would be that the roll feels kinda pointless as it has no i-frames and feels a bit too short, and also would have liked more info about what other enemies are doing around you that you are not locked onto. Other than that it is solid.Visuals and sound are both absolutely fantastic. The artstyle of this world is absolutely stunning and Midgar looks incredible and is such a well realized place. I absolutely love this kind of fusion between fantasy and sci-fi where they use guns along with swords and even basically medieval armor. And also a thing that helps me get immersed in the setting is all the banter among the population that reflect both what is going on in their everyday life but also what you have been doing during gameplay. Also adore the camerawork in cutscenes (along with stylish animations). It is so dynamic and has so much energy which was also the case for a few in XV but here they are way more common. Nice to see some camerawork that takes inspiration from animation rather than film which is very common in the AAA industry. Both are nice, but some variety is greatly appreciated, especially when it looks this good. But the true standout must be the soundtrack. I already loved XVs soundtrack and this is no different in quality. It is in fact true that this series has some of the best music in the industry.Both the writing and acting is kind of strange, stilted and corny BUT it actually has a lot of charm and I like how committed they are to it. It did take a little time though to get used to it, but I do think that eventually it all comes together and the characters are all very loveable. What also helps is how well realized the characters are and how iconic they look. Sure sometimes they can feel exaggerated but as I said: it actually works and I think they are all great.And now to my second biggest gripe of XV: the story. So what this game is probably most known for, or at least the original, is the story. I already knew that XV was going to be kind of a mess due to its development time, and it definitely was, but my expectations of this one were a bit different. I do realize that this remake is basically the first of three acts but waaay expanded into a new trilogy of games. But how was this 30 hour first act? Do remember that I have not played the original, so perhaps the story is even better there (perhaps tighter). I really enjoyed this story overall. It has some pacing issues for sure as it is a very stretched out first act, but wow if it is just not super memorable and just really good. So many iconic moments (Honey Bee Inn was amazing and all surrounding it) and alot of variety. They solved the biggest issue with XV where it was hard to care about what was happening due to there not being enough time or info (until the ending that is). Here there is almost too much time spent with certain things. I do like it, but it really feels like there is way more to come which is both good and bad. Bad because this game suffers not having a real conclusion (which XV definitely did not lack) or answers. But it is worth it and I hope they keep this high quality in the whole trilogy and I am hooked (which is the good part lol). Idk what more to say as I do believe this is worth your time. Great stuff, but almost all setup with little payoff. Also seems like "remake" refers to more than just remaking the game which is really cool and meta. Will play the og after this trilogy is done.Ok but enough good stuff as there are a few things i dislike, and may (I do lol) repeat myself.The pacing can be off and the main reason is padding. In some missions is super apparent and messes with the flow of missions. How they do this is by either extend slow gameplay beyond what is enjoyable (make you walk or proceed really slow, doing really mundane tasks over and over etc.) or by having characters constantly repeating themselves in (skippable, but did not want to miss anything) cutscenes and being overly detailed about obvious stuff. It just feels too obvious that they tried to artificially extend the playtime to probably justify this only being act 1 and for that price (holy moly). It just feels strange as other parts are very well paced. I did state how I found the poor acting and writing kind of charming, but I still want to be clear that it just is however you put it, kinda poor that is. It can be very distracting at times as the quality tends to fluctuate a lot. This may be something that completely takes you out of this game, but personally I find it mostly charming. One other thing that I kinda dislike as well is how they sort of expect you to immediately fall in love with some characters. It feels strange as a first time player as they seem to rely on that you already really like certain characters and do not really introduce a relationship between Cloud and them "properly" or in a convincing way. I get it, they are iconic and are loved alot eventually, but as a new player it can feel a bit off. Also there is too much "anime groaning" for my taste. But as I have said concerning the story, it all falls into place eventually, but it can feel like you have missed something at times.The combat is great as I have stated, but I really think the friendly AI could have been a bit smarter. In certain battles they feel utterly helpless and are no help at all. I get that they want you to switch characters and be very tactical with who you play as along with abilities you use, but it does not change that they are just dumb. Can be a bit frustrating and a drain on your resources. I am in no way the best gamer ever, and I am especially not great with tactical and turn based games so a little bit more help would have been nice. Also would have liked if the camera followed the action better.There is also just waaay to many "squeeze through" animations that we see quite often now in AAA games. I have never really been that bothered by them, but this game must have the record of how many I have encountered. Just slows down gameplay to a crawl and is just annoying.Overall I really enjoyed my time with this game and I am looking forward to see where the story goes in the coming games in this new trilogy, and I hope Rebirth comes to steam sooner rather than later. Also getting me even more excited about XVI. This was a way better introduction to the franchise for me and I now really do see why so may people hold it to such a high regard, which also goes for this particular entry as well. Great!8.5/10

War Thunder is an immense tale of wasted potential. A game whose real capability likely will not be realized until the day it runs out of steam, its official servers close, and it gets rebooted on private servers like has happened with several other once-popular MMOs (EnMasse's TERA and Capcom's Monster Hunter Frontier as examples).First of all, the game is increasingly trapped by its initially-advantageous business model - the "F2P" or "Freemium" model. It's an easy way to get lots of players on board initially, but the longer said model exists, the worse it gets. For example, the Combined Ground mode is loaded with wheeled light tanks running around like they own the place, so adding a few more doesn't really change much even if one gets a fancy missile here and there. Furthermore, as a direct result of trying to get the most mileage out of the F2P model, the devs try to play halfsies with every sub-faction of the community, and end up leaving everyone feeling unsatisfied. Ultimately they are ordered to do awful things by the Board of Directors for the company, so its not even the Dev Team's fault necessarily. When you're under pressure, the first thing you look for is the simplest solution out, often without thinking whether or not it is the right one. Long-standing issues with the game as a result fester and go necrotic. The general worthlessness of Bombers and Attackers in every single "Classic" Air Battle map. Why even allow people to use planes that aren't Fighters if the win conditions of the game mode are such that Non-Fighters only get to matter under extreme circumstances of someone becoming a satellite or humping base AAA?Map design in Combined Arms modes is atrocious and getting worse by the update. The "sit in circle Simulator" beta feel of the Combined modes has not been really updated in any sort of good way. And instead of adding diverse new objectives to encourage the average player to use the entire map, they cut off large swathes of maps, thereby wasting the dev team's time spent modeling them in the first place.All modes trending towards sub-5min MOBA shooters with planes, tanks, and boats/ships, where near-zero brain power is needed. Match timers were shortened from 1hr to 25min a couple years ago. Many ammunition types for tanks and ships being finicky with their damage output. Some like HEAT are a total dice roll whether they will work as intended or go POOF and do nothing upon impact. Extreme Battle Rating compression that is visible even at the entry levels of the game. You cannot tell me with a straight face that a Gladiator biplane stands any reasonable chance against an I-15. Nor does a Chi-Ha stand any reasonable chance against an M2A4 Stuart with one brain cell. Nor does a coastal boat with only 7mm machine guns going against something with 15-20mm cannon(s). And the high echelons of the game are even more compressed still. But the biggest letdown has been its supposed key selling point - Combined Arms gameplay. The topic of CAS has been contentious for years. You have one portion of the community wanting to go all-in with it, one portion wanting tank-only mode at all costs, and the rest trying to be quiet while the extremists on either end scream at each other. The dev team utterly refused to firmly pick one direction here, leaving everyone unsatisfied. CAS is implemented currently as a half-baked killstreak revenge powerup. Its counters in many cases either don't work or have exceptional learning curves that few will undertake. CAS lacks all its real objectives, forcing it solely into direct antitank or anti-ship duty. Dumb game mechanics like the kill camera encourage its use in revenge bombing someone. Instead of addressing any of those, usually what happens when screaming gets out of control is a heavy-handed nerf to ordinance, which comes with the "bonus" of being applied to all the Air modes too, thereby making already-irrelevent Attackers and Bombers worth even less than before. War Thunder will always have the potential to improve, but in order to do so, it must admit that it cannot make everyone happy, and instead must firmly decide what it really wants to be. It can be a MOBA shooter or a Simulator, not both. It can have CoD Killstreak CAS or feature novel objectives for CAS other than popping tanks, not both. Ammunition can either do reliably large amounts of damage or act like near-total dice rolls if anything happens at all. I foresee the game eventually stabbing itself to death, then being resurrected on private servers, after which it will begin to realize its unseen potential. It is trapped in the F2P economic system and the constant ever-increasing flood of "new vehicles" that model demands, leaving ever-more-limited time to work on the necrotic core before it all collapses. How many years will it take for it to all implode? No idea. It's already going for 12 years this November. I would be surprised if it lasted 20, but because the bones of the game are still pretty robust, with enough churn in the development department, it could still always turn a new leaf at any time and truly begin to grow by leaps and bounds.

review: 2022 It's a pleasant game although the progression is pretty boring. The biggest aspect of this game is micro-managing worker assignments, and that is more about transferring units between tasks during different seasons. I had a relaxing time, but there is little replayability.The simplicity of it all and the lack of depth really makes this seem like a nice mobile game. A lot of gimmicks, but nothing that goes beyond micromanaging worker assignments and clicking a few menu options to trade. It's a very simple, basic, and easy city builder. I would not call this an RTS, you just mob up units and run at the enemy.The PvAI is very, very poorly developed. The AI has unlimited resources and reads your mouse clicks rather than your actions. Check Reddit out, the meta of gameplay is how to glitch the AI by tricking it with it's own cheats (clicking on territories to draw the AI army there) in order to take the territory you did want. So a "feature not a bug" situation. Plus, the DLC factions are "designed not a cash grab" to be hard to manage with resources, so the AI as these factions is ridiculous with unlimited resources as they can field 30 over-powered units of something you can scrounge 5 of as a player. Single player is not satisfying, as it is just glitching the AI to win or else be overrun by unlimited mob armies of AI led by RNG generals. Some of the DLC's are cute or add a slight bit of variation, but many of them are just cash grabs with no design.In the end, I find the early and mid game satisfying and serene to play. The late game is a wreck as you must wait X amount of time to take each territory before you can go to the next one. While you can win, it is a joyless slog of taking one tile at a time and waiting . . . waiting . . . waiting . . . rinse and repeat. The game has a semi-obvious meta designed to create a stagnation of how much land you can have and how far your armies can be from your land--this has me wondering if this wasn't a mobile game idea that got changed over to "RTS"/Citybuilder (It is not an RTS).

2019 Gameplay: 9/10Story: 9/10Graphics: 8/10Performance: 5/10Overall: 8/10There is a reason Stellaris is the only space strategy game I've had a reasonable amount of invested time in. It is the space-everything strategy game. Forewarning though, Stellaris is less of a 4x strategy game and more of a space empire simulator. You can be doing everything right with your empire and still lose simply because you were locked in total war with your opponent and suddenly invaded by extra-dimensional beings intent on colonizing the known galaxy. Hence, why Stellaris allows you to make victory conditions optional. If you're looking for something that's more game-y or closer to the Civilization series, then you may be better off with something like Galactic Civilizations or Endless Space. But you may be asking yourself, why play Stellaris? What does Stellaris have that Galactic Civilizations or Endless Space doesn't? Stellaris has scale, and not in the sense that you can have thousands of planets and stars generated (because Gal Civ and ES have this too), but scale in the sense that you control and command everything from the lowliest group of slaves to the Emperor of your empire or president or shadow council, if you choose. But it doesn’t just end with deciding what your citizens or leader does. You can decide what entire planets do. Want to have a planet dedicated entirely to housing your empire’s prison population as a sort of space Australia? You can do that. Want to have a planet dedicated to building robots because your citizens are too lazy to work? You can also do that. Or how about a planet so beautiful that you want it to be a resort world? Yep, you can do that too. Diplomacy also has a sense of scale that other space strategy games never come close to achieving (and this is without the future diplomacy DLC). Stellaris takes the notion of “diplomacy is war by other means” to heart. Allies in Stellaris can be genuinely helpful and more than just buffers against potential invaders. With allies you can form federations and combine fleets or unite to fend off a mutual invader. The AI isn’t prone to ganging up on the player like other space strategy games. Speaking of war. Combat in Stellaris is simplistic. But also possesses a sense of scale with Stellaris being a real-time grand strategy game. You won’t be waiting several turns for a single battleship. Instead, you can start producing very small fleets from the very start of the game! Visuals and sound in Stellaris are also adequate for a strategy game. Not as good as Endless Space, but superior to the dated engine of Galactic Civilizations. Planets and anomalies look beautiful. Ships look relatively detailed if you can get a good look at them, and alien races are animated. I recommend Stellaris if you are looking for a space strategy game that does everything. It’s difficult to get into if you’ve never played a Paradox strategy game before, but with a few walkthroughs and some patience, you’ll be purging xenos in no time!

2018 Rainbow Six Siege is a tactical FPS shooter that takes the 'tactical' concept to a whole new level. I LOVE this game, I have put alot of hours into the game and do not regret it at all. I started playing back in Operation Health, when I decided to download the game during a free weekend, initially before I decided to try the game, I couldn't seem to grasp the concept of the game very well, I just never thought I would find it interesting because of how different it was to other FPS titles. Which I can still understand my reasoning today as it really is a very different game to most FPS games. BUT MAN WAS I WRONG TO WAIT SO LONG TO GET IT. I've have never been happier playing a game, and will probably continue to play the game until I literally can't play anymore. Now that doesn't mean it doesn't come with some flaws, but in my opinion the pros weigh over the cons. I will go over both the pros and the cons of the game, so that anyone that is looking to buy the game has a better idea of what they will be getting.Pros:- GameplayOh boy, I can go on and on about the gameplay style of Siege. It's so fresh compared to alot of FPS games out there on the market right now. Most FPS games right now are mindless shooters, where you spawn in, get some kills, die, then respawn and continue doing this until the game is up. Now i'm not saying all games are like this, for example Battle Royales, they definitely added something different to the FPS genre, but to be honest, they are getting a little worn out. Siege on the other has never lost my interest*, this being because every game is so different from the last. How it works is that once you've loaded into a match you are required to choose an operator, once you have chosen one you are then one of to things happen when you load into the map, either you are on defense and you have to prep the site, this either being Bomb, Secure Area, or Hostage. If your on attack, you are put into the drone phase where for the first 45 seconds all the players on your team are trying to find the site. Then the attackers load in and the game begins, attackers try to take out the defenders or either secure the area, defuse the bomb, or capture the hostage, while the defenders do the opposite or kill all the attackers. Now this may seem very basic still, but it's how each situation can be done what makes the game so different. Each match is like a whole new game. This is probably the one part of the game that I honestly don't see any flaws, the endless possibilities per match just make the game so fun. - ContentSiege is absolutely PACKED, with content, and on top of that Ubisoft is constantly adding more. There are tons of different maps to play, along with so many different operators to try. Currently Siege is on it's 3 year, or Year 3, of content. In each year there are 4 major updates and multiple smaller updates in between. Each major update is split up into 4 Seasons. Each season Ubisoft adds 2 new operators and 1 map**, most of the time the new content they add is cool and really interesting and adds lots into the game. The key word there is 'most' but I'll get to that later. Along with the new ops and map, almost every week, Ubisoft is constantly adding new cosmetics. It honestly seems like that every time I come on there is a new gun skin or outfit that I can get for my operators. But that doesn't mean that the cosmetics system doesn't come with flaws, but again, I'll bring that up later. So, all in all, there is plenty of new content, to make sure the game doesn't become to stale. - Friends and CommunityFor me, one of the best parts about playing this game, is being able to play with my friends. I initially got the game on my own, and for the first few months I was the only one playing. I continually tried to get my friends into the game because I wanted to play with them. Eventually I managed to make them cave and they bought the game. And OMG the amount of hilarious moments me and my friends have gotten out of this game are endless. I have had such amazing moments with them, this ranging from hilarious accidents that most likely ended up with someone dying, or stressfull clutches where I have them giving me callouts so I can secure the win. This is by far the best part of the game for me, and I think that everyone should have a friend to play with. Which puts me into my next part, the community, the community is great, most of the time. There are lots of funny and interesting people to play with. I have also had some pretty funny games with randoms where we decided to do some dumb strat that ended up working. The reddit section, r/Rainbow6 is full of awesome people posting different things, ranging from funny moments to awesome art, to stressful clutches, I always enjoy going back onto the reddit page to see what new stuff I cant watch or look at. Cons- Content (cont'd)There is plenty of content in the game, and lots being added, but recently I have had some complaints about the recent content being added. To note, Ubisoft said about a year ago that they would strive to not put a paywall behind any new content being added into the game. Which they kept that promise, until Operation Chimera released. If you are not aware, Operation Chimera was the first update from Year 3, it brought 2 new operators, and event and this new set of cosmetic that could be recieved through special packs called Outbreak Packs, at first I was excited cause the new content looked really cool and I really wanted to get all the new skins, but when I got into the game I realized that I could only get them if I spent money on R6 credits. Which I found very obnoxious cause not everyone has the money to buy all the cosmetics that they were offering. Now at least they did give everyone at least 4 outbreak packs, but that was it, I had to buy every other one if I wanted them. After the season anded, I was really hoping that was going to be the end of paid content, but man was I wrong. Operation Grim Sky released as the second season of Year 3. This ws by far one of my most favourite seasons. The operators were cool and the map was amazing. But there was a catch, midway through the season, Ubisoft added new packs called Sunsplash packs, these were again packs that could only be purchased with real money, R6 credits. I understand that Ubisoft is a company that needs to make money somehow, I just wish they would put cosmetics behind a pay wall. They are still doing stuff like this as they did the exact same thing for Halloween. Sadly that isn't the end of the problems with content. Balancing. With every new season comes new operators, and along with that, more bugs. First I'll go over the bugs. Now I understand as a company how hard it may be to polish out all the bugs that may appear with every new season, and Ubisoft is good about getting some of the bugs, keyword 'some', there still tends to be lingering game breaking bugs that they never patch out until an entire seasons has gone by, I will say though that they have been getting better as they are adding more mid way small updates to pave out all the bugs. The other side of the problem is balancing of operators. I love how there are plenty of new operators to try from, but there are still alot of problems with plenty of operators, both new and old. The best example of this is Lion, from Operation Chimera(there seems to be a theme here with operations Chimera). Lion is an op whose ability is a drone that starts off at the beginning of every round in the sky, and at any point in the round, Lion can activate this drone which then scans the map, the problem that lies is that when it's activated it scans for any movement, and if any defense operator moves, they are lit up with a red outline for everyone to see making them an easy target. I have more to say, but I ran out of words, so if you want a full opinion, please feel free to message me, I'm always open for discussion.

review: 2021 Early Access Review I actually haven't played this in a while, but Steam awards are upon us & I nominated Raft in the "Sit back and relax" category (though one could certainly argue that it fits better in the "Better with friends" one). Did a quick launch just for the badge and... nostalgia hit. :) So I decided to briefly update my review as well.I've finished the full release story and in all honesty I had mixed feelings. The final chapter felt a little rushed. For the first time, I've encountered pretty bad bugs during a boss fight. I felt like they could've done more in terms of populating the ocean. No need to go full Subnautica, but they mainly just added a few more decorative fish groups in the shallows & it was nice, sure, just felt a little... 'low effort'? All that aside, I did continue to play, mainly to chill on easy mode while listening to music or audiobooks. It was a great way to completely distract myself after work, sort of like diving into vacation mode and melting that stress away.In terms of recommending the game, I absolutely do, though I do have some friends who got dreadfully bored within a dozen minutes or so and some who enjoyed it. Personally, I loved Raft and I'll keep coming back to this game from time to time.Oh, & if there's a Bruce plushie that I can poke with a pencil or something, I'm so buying it. :)Leaving the entirety of my Early Access review below.* * *I've loaded 2 worlds so far, one with a teammate on normal difficulty and later solo easy. I'm so glad I started with a teammate, and not on easy. The initial poking around, wasting time and a bit of survival chaos that ensued from neglecting the food/water meters resulted in a few hours of incredible fun. Nothing more priceless than that initial "oh ♥♥♥♥" moment when you're still clueless, the shark bites off a bit of the raft for the first time and you're now floating on your measly 3 tiles. Not gonna lie, when the shark started going right through them with the waves that became a little biggish and unruly, I got a hit of mild thalassophobia. \(°Ω°)/ On easy you don't have to worry too much about your food and water intake, so you have more liberty to explore without stressing about supplies. However, going solo and already familiar with the basics I did notice that a certain repetitiveness can set in, mostly due to survival mechanics. There is a minimum necessary routine, and "oh no, not THIS island again" moments can happen. But I'd say it's not too much of a problem if you just surrender to the experience and relax, fish, dive, have philosophical conversations with the shark, poke it with a spear when it disagrees. You definitely can't rush this game.Solo I can play this for up to an hour, with company it's much more enjoyable. So my advice would be, don't venture into the ocean alone, grab a buddy or two (in case you're wondering, no, you can't eat them when supplies are low :P though you can enable friendly fire, so declaring an FFA for the last bit of fish scenario is entirely possible). And don't fear the shark too much, later you can wear it as a hat. >:)Edit: I've now finished the story, it took us around 40-50 hours in total to complete. Mind you, we were taking our sweet time, stopping at every island and stripping it of all its materials. From the moment we built the radio receiver and started properly pursuing the objectives I'd estimate there were some 15-20 hours of gameplay. Once the story was over my trusty teammate mostly lost interest, while I'm still floating about, grinding achievements and enjoying the current endgame, which is basically furnishing the raft of your dreams. :)

review: 2020 There are few games that have had the impact on me to the scale this one had. I liked the first Titanfall enough to the point of when I heard they were making a sequel in early 2016 I got a bit hyped, though I was skeptical that it would be just another disappointing sequel made in order to create a bloated franchise EA could milk to death. Then the Multiplayer Tech Test dropped and it felt... underwhelming. I wasn't used to the mechanical changes from TF1 and everything felt a bit under-cooked. This led to me skipping out on the game initially when it dropped, not helped by its terrible release date which I noticed even before launch. Then roughly a month after launch I played the free Multiplayer weekend and although I wasn't engrossed yet it did feel a lot better than in August. This led me to take a chance on this game and get it for my birthday. Then I played the single player campaign, and I felt something I hadn't felt since I first played Half Life 2. This game is a love letter to the FPS genre and a damn good one at that, every mission is memorable, the characters likable and with the exception of some bad enemy AI and a slight lack of variety in the arena encounters, I would go so far as to say is perfect. The Multiplayer finally clicked with me as I got used to all the new additions and appreciating them for expanding the sandbox beyond what TF1 could offer. Respawn are one of the most talented and passionate teams EA has under their wing and this is proof of that. This game is a genuine masterpiece that I'd highly recommend anyone interested try for themselves, if not just for the campaign alone which is worth the price, and I'm so glad people are starting to see this after the game's recent appearance on Steam this year. In conclusion, go play this game, thanks

2019 I wish there was a "It really is great, but not for me" button.Being a fan of the Souls games as well as Bloodborne, I found myself in familiar territory with Sekiro, but something just wasn't quite clicking. All the new systems function well, and the setting is expertly crafted, but it's the stripped away RPG elements that leave me feeling empty with Sekiro. For me, so much of the enjoyment of the Soulsborne games came from exploring the intricately designed areas and finding strange little nooks and crannies containing unique weapons and/or armor. It felt like an interesting and satisfying reward for exploration. In Sekiro, every item you find in the world is more or less a consumable (with few exceptions), and that sense of wonderment feels lost. I feel no desire to explore secondary paths knowing that they all end in yet another pocketful of confetti. That sense that each pathway could potentially result in a weapon that changes your whole playstyle (if you want it to) is no longer present. This drawback also bleeds into my second issue with Sekiro: Being locked into a singular playstyle. Again, to reference the Soulsborne franchise, FromSoft games have always come with a variety of ways to build your character. Do you want to be a heavily armored brute with a two handed axe? Have at it. Want to be a robe-wearing mage? Go nuts. How about a holy Paladin type that hurls lightning-spears from behind a shield? Whatever floats your boat. On the flip side, Sekiro takes the approach of "learn the new parry/block system or die." Without having the previous FromSoft titles as reference, this isn't a bad thing in and of itself. The system works well and has a good deal of polish; it's the fact that it represents yet another facet of RPG-oriented gameplay that has been stripped away from FromSoft's design philosophy.The world itself also feels much more linear than that of the Soulsborne titles. To compare Sekiro to Bloodborne or Dark Souls, it's clear that FromSoft was less interested in the intricate world building they're so well known for. The levels are gorgeous and well crafted, but are much simpler and straight forward. The lore is not nearly as cryptic and expansive, and the host of characters are far less enigmatic. Again, not an objectively negative trait, just... Not what I admire about FromSoft titles.In a vacuum, this game is fantastic on a technical level. review: 2018 This is a game that I have actually played or seen played, from sharing my library, four times now, so I've probably had long enough to think about it and, simultaneously, have no idea if I've had enough time yet. Is such a thing knowable? Life is Strange comes across as something that can't really be filed as good or bad, just something that is. Which is probably because there's so much diversity between the different chapters. Some of which I was amazed by and some of which I didn't care for at all. But I'm still interested in looking at the game as a whole while not spoiling it for someone thinking about buying it.Life is Strange is kind of a third person mystery adventure game where you play as Max Caulfield, a socially awkward super-hipster, going to some kind of weird private secondary school in Oregon that you attend your senior year only, apparently. She discovers that she has a short-capacity time rewind power which serves as the base mechanic for the game. After the first five minutes of semi-tutorial out of the way, the game basically plays as a three dimensional Choose Your Own Adventure book. You are occasionally confronted by large, epilepsy-inducing either/or prompts which mildly or markedly adjust the storyline from there on. Additionally, there are minor events along the way that very *slightly* adjust the story and your relationships which you can choose to participate in or not, depending on what your aim is. All of these actions add up and there are many different ways the story can go.At few different places in the game, it definitely has the point-and-click genre's "Oh my god! I am completely thwarted by this exceptionally mundane situation. Let me find the one item hidden in this room that will help me take the laziest possible way out" trope that absolutely drives me up the wall. On the other hand, there is sometimes more than one way to complete a puzzle, or puzzles that need some innovative way to get through. Mostly, as long as you remind yourself that the game is centred around time rewind powers, you'll probably get through. Don't think about how objects can stay on your person through the time travel, or how it looks like you're teleporting to the outside observer or your brain will explode.There's a lot of visual and atmospheric beauty to the game, both in terms of the presentation and tone, as well as things as simple as lighting and colour scheme. You'll find points at which your character can just sit and look around, admiring the scenery and looking for some kind of beauty in the environment, while you listen to the soundtrack and watch them contemplate what's going on in their life. There's such a good presentation of these moments, particularly when the episodes start, that it isn't immediately clear that it's not actually a cutscene, and you can get up any time you like. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as far as I'm concerned.The episodes essentially go as follows:Episode One: Well, that was fine. I guess I can get into this character.Episode Two: That got a lot more interesting. Neat!Episode Three: Every action that you make is wrong and you will be made to feel bad about it...Which is also my assessment of Fable III.Episode Four: Welp, that got dark REAL fast.Episode Five: Here are the assets of the Unreal Development Kit / The increasingly bad things that happen to Alyssa.From those brief tag lines, you can kinda see how I feel about it. It starts extremely slow, then takes off in a hurry until the very last episode, which is mostly a bizarre LSD trip that goes on way too long. But I guess that's to help you get the authentic Oregon experience. Either way, you need to get through the end to make it to the final epilepsy prompt to conclude the game. Easily, you can play it twice and go with all of the other options that you didn't pick before and try to talk to different people to see if you can form different relationships and affect parts of the outcome. I'm not sure there's more than two good playthroughs, but there's about fifteen to twenty hours of content for each run, depending on how many journal entries you read and how many non-essential NPCs you talk to along the way. So two of those have an appropriate level of content, I think.I would definitely recommend this game as an interesting story for absolutely any player and any level of dexterity or no dexterity at all can get you through. In the end, you may think about how different your relationships would be if certain events were changed, and those closest to you, for a brief moment, knew you only as a stranger. Would you still get along with them through intrinsic similarities? Or is it based on a culmination of fortunate events that have carried you to this point?My recommendation is positive.

review: This game just makes me want to play Warframe. I have a very positive bias towards Warframe, but the similarities are endless. The modding, Descendant abilities, and leveling systems all remind me of Warframe, because they are basically copies of it; even the mastery rank system is there. There are some Destiny features in there as well, such as weapon infusion and whatnot (which is so expensive and inconvenient that I didn't even make it far enough in the game to make it worthwhile), and there are Ultimate weapons that draw similarities to Destiny's Exotic weapons, such as "The Cage", which is basically Destiny's Thunderlord if you made it an SMG. If we are ignoring my comparisons, this game feels clunky most of the time. I never use the grappling hook, I feel like I can't jump or move to where I want to go a lot of the time, the AI in this game is not impressive my any means, and the only reason why it puts up any semblance of a threat is because after the second or third area, your Descendant becomes as brittle as glass. It's an enormous difficulty spike out of nowhere and it feels painfully artificial. I called it quits after going through the game's dungeons and getting irritated at how these boss encounters usually went (keep in mind that I'm a solo player). The game will constantly spawn enemies while the boss fight is happening, which makes it really hard to get any damage in. You don't really need a ton of time, but it's annoying how the game NEVER stops the ad spawning. The bosses also typically come with some crazy regeneration, healing abilities, and have 3 "phases", which I will simply call "moments of immunity" because that's all they really are, and this combination of traits and abilities makes all of these fights insufferable IMO. The significance of this is that you have to run these dungeons constantly (it's a grind game after all), but the dungeons are not fun. I was originally gonna see how long it was going to take me to grind out one of the Ultimate skins in the game, but I don't really want to do that anymore. As I was writing this, the thought of "mad because bad" came to my mind. It's kinda funny, but at the same time, I usually like pushing back on a game's difficulty because it feels good to do so. I can't say the same for this game. Because of that, I just can't say that this game is worth a try. Hopefully it will be in the future.--- On a side note, why is this game's audio SO bad?! The voice acting is bad, the music doesn't evoke anything from me or even match the pacing of the game, the guns don't have balls, your characters don't make sounds as they're running and walking, the environments don't have any ambiance; it's disturbingly dull and lifeless, and I'm not going to give this game credit and say that it was doing that intentionally.

Casual Controller Player Review:I have some gripes with the game, but overall it's actually very solid. I'd certainly call it an improvement over F1 23. I pre-ordered the Champion Edition on PS5 and then got a nice PC so I re-purchased it on Steam, so I have experience on both console and PC versions, but waaay more on PS5, played it since the first day of early access for pre-orderers.Cons (most of which you've probably heard):- Little to no customization options at start. The base edition comes with 1 standard livery/suit/helmet set that actually looks decent, it's just a little much. There are 3 liveries/suits/helmets in the store, I believe 2 in the Podium Pass and the rest come from Challenge Careers and F1 World events. Otherwise, I imagine they'll be expecting PitCoin for everything whenever they DO decide to add it to the game.- Handling is a bit inconsistent between patches at the moment. There are lots of updates happening because the handling model, as it was released, was pretty bad. To give them their credit, they actually DID make a lot of the handling better in the release version compared to F1 23, but the few issues it had were pretty abhorrent. Now, the regular handling updates can make it a bit tricky to nail down a feel for the new model.- The usual track bugs that come with the Ego engine have not disappeared. Invisible walls, bumps of death, etc. Believe it or not, however, it IS probably for the best that EA didn't switch to UE5 given the performance of the new WRC game.Pros (which I feel have been egregiously underacknowledged):- The handling model is MILES better than F1 23 once you do have a feel for it, it's fun to drive, default setups are actually relatively decent for an AI race, I just take whatever the game gives me as the recommended default (high downforce, high top speed, balanced, etc.) and adjust the engine braking to 20%, brake pressure to 96% and brake bias to 53% on *every* track and can be competitive with 100-diff AI. All I'm saying is that you can be a casual player and still be competitive with some real tough AI opponents that'll give you a run for your money, all with just a few small tweaks to your setup, you don't have to be a nerd about the setup unless you wanna get sweaty online.- The tracks that have been given a touch of makeup look great, they feel great. The only gripe I had up until today's update was that the bigger kerbs actually didn't affect the car much at all. You could fly right over sausage kerbs with ease and with no consequence, for example. I believe they've fixed this problem in the most recent patch however.- Driver career is SUPER fun, big fan. New cutscenes, secret meetings, specialists, on-track objectives and driver radios, the list of new features goes on.- Fanzone is a thing, you pick a favorite team and a favorite driver to join a leaderboard of fellow fans and the different fan bases compete with each other, you vote on race day predictions for the upcoming irl race, etc. Kinda in the background but it's free rewards and you can see all the other fans of your favorite drivers and teams, it's nifty but inconsequential.All-in-all, I think this game got a lot of deserved criticism because of the state of the handling model and customization when it first released (customization STILL needs work). But I think it also got a lot of undeserved hate from people who were still bitter about how bad F1 22 was and weren't properly satisfied with F1 23, now they've made it a personality trait to just beef with EA and throw tantrums over everything sitting between this game and perfection. I like this year's game and I think they've made significant improvements upon last year's. Now if we could just get a MyTeam revamp and those customization items figured out, we'll be cooking. Fingers crossed for 25 🤞

After which point, you must leverage the resources of the other planets within your star system to continue to progress. Eventually, your efforts will gain you the ability to leave your star system and travel the vast expanse of space to various other star systems, where you will need to harvest the resources of the planets within them. You will then ultimately combine and utilize all of these resources to construct a highly customizable megastructure called a Dyson Sphere, which harvests the energy from whichever star you choose to build it around. You can then do this again and again, in as many star systems as you desire, all the while fighting hordes of an alien species called The Dark Fog, and learning from their technological arsenal to expand and improve your own.This game, despite being in its infancy, and at the time of this review: in early-release, is well-designed, intuitive, of great depth, and in possession of much potential. review: 2017 There's a bit of a difficulty with reviewing a game like this, because its DLC has changed its functionality immensely, and while I absolutely love the base concept of the game I do not recommend all DLC... even though most of it is in fact pretty good.It is worth noting that at the time of writing I have over 1600 hours of playtime in this game. Actual playtime. This is the game I can't leave lying around. If I have nothing else that I can think of doing, I start another game of EU4. If I have other things to consider doing, sometimes I still start another round of EU4. Whilst in setup quite similar to the Total War games, this game beats them for me by a mile because I *don't* have to do each battle manually for good results. I've played various Total War games as well and while it's awesome being able to outmaneuver the AI it also gets boring having to do that same trick over and over again. This game does not bother with the battle micromanagement and some will consider that a bonus, some a malus.Comparison aside for those unfamiliar with either the Europa Universalis or Total War series: you play a country on the map of (at the start of the gameplay anyway) Europe, starting in 1444 and ending in 1821. So, your time is limited, and your goal is to generate as a high a score as possible by turning your country into an economic, diplomatic and military powerhouse. Enter the main problem: this is not immediately obvious. In fact, I don't even recall exactly when I finally realized the game had a scoring system. I played it the way I imagine everyone plays who sees a strategy game like this: What are we going to do tonight? The same thing we do every night Pinky... trying to take over the world.And here's the immediate issue with the otherwise good DLC additions: much of the DLCs and patches that came with them, seem focused on making it more difficult for you to take over the world, but provide other methods by which you can increase the in-game scoring system. And I am not ashamed to say it was at this point that I actually realized that the game had this scoring system at all.I will touch on the eternal DLC release that Paradox obviously employs to make money in a simple statement. Yes, they aim to make money by providing ever more DLC to improve the gameplay and add more functionality, most of which is quite enjoyable. However they also provide the simple ability to play earlier release versions which work just fine, don't bother with the new changes/additions, and leave you entirely able to play an awesomely entertaining game without buying all the DLC. I never felt like the game's DLC provided functions that it absolutely needed in the first place to be fun. It was always a fun game for me.So, what's the game actually about? Well you pick a country on the map that existed in historic 1444 (or create your own if you have the DLC for it), that country has certain national bonuses that match its history, and you play through the next 400 or so years. The game follows historical patterns, in that some historical events have chances of happening, countries will generally behave as they did historically towards allies/enemies, the historical powerhouses tend to be just that... and in the middle there's you. The player. The wild card. The one who has the greatest impact on how the game will NOT follow the course of history.It is worth mentioning that I never fully appreciated the brilliance of this game until I started playing in Ironman mode. Ironman mode gives you ONE save file. You declare a war, it saves. You negotiate a peace, it saves. A month passes, it saves. You quit the game, it saves. And every time it overwrites the same file, so no backsies (unless you alt+F4 the game, a trick known as "Save scumming"). Ironman mode teaches you that your actions have consequences, and it means your playthrough can get ruined.... but that also means it's ever so much more exciting. When you don't get savepoints, when you don't get to undo things, everything you do in your playthrough just matters so much more.The basics of the gameplay is simple. You are a country (or part of one), you have an income based upon the taxes, production value and trade value your provinces generate. With this money you can field an army, improve the wealth (and thus income) of your provinces, hire advisors that help you generate monarch points (a "currency" required to improve your nation, develop technological advancements and national ideas that provide tangible bonuses), bribe allies (or enemies!) and as a result of all that expand the territory of your fledgeling empire... but beware, because expanding will anger your neighbours, their allies, their friends and their cat.At the end, Europa Universalis IV is a game that is easy to start with but hard to master. Beyond the mechanics of running your nation there's the historical mechanics, mechanics of how AI typically behaves as each country values different things/territories, a trade system that's impossible to wrap your head around in actual playthrough there is a host of other details that I am forgetting, some of which I realized far too late and left me with a sense of "Ooooh, is THAT how that works!" even after my first few hundred hours. And that is disregarding the additions the DLC parts will bring.The only downside worth noting is that you may not want to install the latest version if you don't own the DLC to make use of it. The game has the annoying tendency to introduce new features in the latest patch that you can't make use of unless you have the DLC but will affect your game as the AI can make use of the mechanics. It's a bit of a hamfisted way of encouraging people to pay, but the game lets you install earlier versions easily enough and I would recommand doing that if you do not like some of the newer systems. I will say it again, DLC brought some improvements and made some things harder but the base game is worth it either way.

2022 So I wrote up a longer review, read it over and decided I'd rather write something shorter. TL;DR: I've given the game enough chances to be fun, and it doesn't respect my time or my effort. The content is drawn out and both tedious & obnoxious instead of being fun. It's a big commitment that doesn't really give anything in return. You're better off focusing on your real life, or on a game that's better designed and values your time & energy. PROSCommunity is mostly friendly. It doesn't contain most of the toxic elements in more pvp-focused games, at least not until you start doing endgame content. Music is good, Story is fun even if the lore is messyA good amount of the characters have nice personality and life to them. MEHParkour system is mostly good, however frequently you'll get snagged on loose bits. Combat can be good, however enemies in higher content become bullet sponges. This leads to endgame content being more tedious and obnoxious so it feels like a chore instead of a game. CONSThe amount of grind is insane. It's multiple levels interconnected levels of grind to where you have to essentially grind through multiple layers of grind hell to progress in the game. The open worlds are the worst offenders of this because they frequently require resources that you grind out from previous open worlds. Progress is also further limited by daily caps and long build times, so even if you do grind out the resources, you have to spend multiple days leveling up the faction, then wait for your new gear to actually build before you can use it. (You also gotta level up the new gear on top of that) This is made worse because too much of the content exists as content islands and there's not a whole lot of interaction between each island aside from those resources you grind out. You might get a necramech or archwing, but can't use it in most missions, you might get a railjack, but can't use any of it aside from sometimes bringing one of your crewmembers, you might level up your operator but they require a significant investment to just do what you could already do. Each of these is a content island you play with, that just doesn't have any lasting appeal. The amount of BUGS that are present and get ignored is ridiculous. If you fail a mission you lose everything except for a portion of your XP, so having your mission break because of a bug means your time just got wasted. This is really frustrating if you were farming for a rare drop and GOT it, only to lose it because the mission objective bugged out or auto-failed. The multiplayer aspect is messy, and you can be kicked out (and completely lose your progress including all XP) of a mission at any time because the host's connection to the server acts up or the host leaves the mission. The difficulty scaling for multiplayer and lack of a pause feature has lead to me playing more solo missions than multiplayer ones because then I know it's less likely to break.Balance is in a whole mess right now. They were trying to fix some powercreep and cheesy strategies but ended up doing a sweeping nerf that did more harm than good. The developers are also leaning more in "make the content MORE tedious" instead of streamlining or trying to make the content actually FUN. This is doubly worse because the new content is too frequently designed to make old builds and squad setups useless. Rare resources needed for progression that only drop from doing a scavenger hunt, bosses with damage reduction that can't be removed, damage attenuation so trying to BUFF your damage actually makes your damage WORSE. All of this together results in a very narrow amount of gear that's actually any good. A lot of older content just falls off for any endgame pursuit, and any CC or status effect playstyle can't really do anything since stronger enemies are just immune. All the builds feel like they just end up being the same build, and there's no real room for flexibility or creativity. You wanna focus on being better in parkour? you need to compromise your damage or defenses then. Ultimately the game just wastes your time and doesn't give any real feeling of accomplishment or fun. The level of commitment this game requires is just insane. You're better off finding something else because the state the game is in right now is not worth anyone's time. I wish that it didn't turn out like this, because I did have some legitimately fond memories of the game and I was so excited for some of the newer content. I gave this game enough chances this month to actually be fun and it's spit in my face each time. So I'm done.

The 33.5 hours I have on record are how long it took for me to beat the Italy campaign and the German campaign on standard. Maybe you're less of a scrub than me it would be shorter for you, but I feel I got my money's worth. I purchased this on sale, if you are weary of the game because of the negative reviews, I suggest buying on sale like I did.

2021 Absolutely charming. I might be joining a chorus of praise, but that's exactly what this game deserves. It's clear that it's been a labour of love.The plot initially had me rolling my eyes--there's a lot of anime cliches, including characters that pop in and out of the plot to do little more than showcase how badass they are, a bland protagonist, and a lot of cookie-cutter shonen anime character designs. But engaging with this plot is like watching a campy 90s anime like Sailor Moon; its hit a certain point where the cliches seem almost charming and stylish. And while I'm about 20 hours in with a LOT left to go (as far as I can tell), I can already see that the campy plot is only the surface. This game has solid writing, and I hope that it proves to truly have the depth it's foreshadowing.It's the gameplay that gripped me the most. Everyone is making the comparison to X-COM, and while this looks like X-COM and in a lot of ways plays like it, it doesn't feel like X-COM. X-COM felt oppressive (on purpose, of course), and a lot of the frustration came from how valuable your turns were: if you didn't hit that 70% shot, that wasted turn could cost you a unit or two. Lucky criticals can easily one-hit-kill. But in this game, the math doesn't really work like that. While enemies can certainly be challenging, you can afford a few missed shots before it really impacts the mission. You still have to play smart, as the game punishes charging in due to the sheer number of enemies on most maps, but never once have I felt that a failure was due to poor luck rather than poor tactics.The little details and features really sell it. I'm a sucker for little subsystems, menus, and knobs to fiddle with. There's a friendship mechanic between team members (that you can influence with specific actions during missions), a simpler-than-it-looks customizable and craftable ability system, a mechanic for managing the reputation and PR approach of your mercenary/police group, individual motivation, and more. It may sound overwhelming, but the game introduces them slowly enough that you'll never have more than you can manage thrown at you at once. It's a number of mechanics and system that I dream most other RPGs had.I was also worried that with an optional online, MMO component and a crafting/loot system, there would be a fair bit of grinding involved. Thankfully, not necessary as far as I can tell--in fact, I wouldn't recommended it. On Normal difficulty and higher, the bosses scale to your level, so while you could grind to outpace their support, I don't think you'll ever hit a difficulty wall. Equipment and crafting materials are also generous enough that I've never felt the need to grind for them. I will say that I'm a little confused as to what the purpose of the online features are, but it hasn't affected my experience.This is a small team doing some great work with limited resources. It's already surpassed the level of enjoyment I've gotten from a lot of big-name studio games. Give this game a try and show the team some support!

Early Access Review I mean, its a supermarket simulator, and I would say it does its job well. Its not overly complicated, and has a few flaws, but its enjoyable.You start the game with a small store, a few shelves, and just enough money to buy a few items. You purchase the items, stock the shelves, set a price, and checkout customers to earn money. From there you get more items until your shelves are for, but what do you do with the rest of your money now that you're somewhat stable?This is where the progression steps in. As you go about your day, buying items and selling them, your'll get xp for your store and eventually level up. Hit certain level milestones and that will allow you to expand your store (at the cost of slightly higher rent after the initial payment), unlock a storage area that will hold excess stock, hire workers that will automatically check out customers and restock shelves (assuming you have the items in your storage), as well as purchase food licenses to expand on your inventory. This makes for a relatively nice, relaxing tycoon game where you can get set up for the day and watch as your workers make you money.Now, there are some issues I do have with the game, though they are relatively minor. An example is that your cashiers are relatively slow, scanning maybe one item a second. At this time you can only hire 4 of them, and you need a relatively high store level to hire them, let alone the space to warrant hiring that many. Another issue is more of a peeve than anything. Some customers are apparently hoarders and will just take 3 packages of toilet paper. Now toilet paper is relatively high margin, meaning you make more of a profit selling one package of toilet paper than selling one hand soap, the issue comes with spacing. You can only fit 2 toilet paper on a shelf space, but that same shelf space can hold 12 hand soap. So now you have to keep an entire rack of toilet paper in your storage just so you can keep restocking toilet paper after someone preps for the next pandemic. There also was an issue where stockers would not take boxes to the storage, which was a massive time sink as you can image always being the main stocker bringing items to your storage from the street, but that has now since been patched and stockers now deal with that well enough.I would say my biggest issue is that the game freezes if you tab out and only works if you're actively playing it. That may not sound like an issue, but I would like this game to function more like an idle game, where I get everything set up at the start of the day, and then the day progresses with little input from me while I play Runescape or something, but the game won't progress unless you're actively playing that game only. Just breaks the flow for me.I recommend this game highly, given its cheap price and its functionality, I can always boot it up and enjoy it for what it is as a simulator, and it doesn't break the bank in the process.

2022 Mount and Blade: Warband is one of the greatest games ever made. It has some of the best melee & ranged combat in any game ever, great commander controls, a well crafted medieval world with lots of player freedom, and a huge modding scene. This lengthy review is only a basic overview. The combat of Mount and Blade: Warband is excellent as it is easy to quickly understand, but difficult to master. The game has a large number of melee weapons that can attack from a variety of different ranges and from up to 5 different directions. The default setting is that right click slowly automatically blocks attacks from any direction, but for higher level play blocking should be set to either mouse direction or keys because players and higher level AI enemies use fake outs and attacks from angles with jumps + spins. Weapons include many different kinds of swords, scimitars, two-handed swords, axes, two-handed axes pikes, hammers, maces, spears, lances, and many different types of shields. Lances can be couched while on horseback to do insane amounts of charge damage and weapons work differently against different types of armor. Ranged combat also has alot of depth as bows can do more damage and be fired while on horseback, but require a large amount of skillpoints to be put into the Power Draw and Horse Archery skills to access their increased utility over crossbows. Crossbows lock aim in place and can be fired like snipers from the start, while bows require leveling the skill to reach that accuracy. There are also thrown weapons like knives, javelins and throwing axes that have their own complexities. Mount and Blade is not just about fighting, but also about building and leading an army made up of many different kinds of units. The army command system is very basic, but it allows for skirmishing, flanking, rotating charges, and even hit & run tactics. By default commanding is done through the F1-F8 keys and the 1-8 keys with each key linked to menus that let you command different kind of units. Units and companion characters can also be rebranded to being different types of units. There are 6 different factions modeled off of historical medieval regions that each have their own specialized units and you can use any of them and even create mixed armies. Mount and Blade is probably the best game where you lead soldiers in battle. Alot of attention has clearly been paid to developing Calradia. Before you start you have to build and design a character. Skill points, weapon points, starting items & reputation are allocated based on the many different backgrounds you pick for your character as they age up to adulthood. Gender affects how the points are allocated and how your character is treated throughout the game. Calradia is a patriarchal society that gives women a harder time, but marrying a lord can also give your character a fast pass to riches. The backgrounds can be mixed and matched and most are affected by gender. The game has alot of optional text for those who want to learn, but these traditions, economic lessons, peoples concerns, and conflicts all manifest as mechanics. Money can be made by killing bandits, trading goods between cities & villages, investing in manufacturing, doing quests, fighting in tournaments and more. Players can set any goals, from conquering the whole of Calradia with themselves as monarch to making a fortune as a merchant or installing a pretender on a throne.The game has companions that all have their own skillset, backgrounds and dramas with other companions. The sheer number of different party skills makes creating a balanced party a good idea, but picking characters you like is also an option. Mount and Blade: Warband is a game that you can pour thousands of hours into without getting bored. Its limited number of skillpoints, large number of factions and political system justifies specialized characters and many different playthroughs. It has mods that fundamentally change the game and even represent epics the Sengoku Jidai, Viking Era, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, and Lord of the Rings. Its eighteenth century combat mod had hundreds of players organizing into regiments for historical line battles and this eventually became its own DLC. This game has endless content for both singleplayer and multiplayer.

2023 Total War: Three Kingdoms is the best game in the Total War Franchise hands down. The game is based on the historical Romance of the Three Kingdoms and the game does an amazing job in bringing out the rich cultural and historical content that makes the Three Kingdoms era one of the most revered and popular period of time in Chinese history. Total War Three Kingdoms has an amazing and efficient diplomacy and economy system. It has a very strong campaign, with an interesting character-focus which I came to like a lot. Don't expect historical accuracy: the generals are quite powerful (can take on entire units by themselves). The map and environments are beautiful. The soundtrack is very pleasant. It also runs better than other recent total war games for me, while also looking better - so that's a plus. The UI is also very pretty and (mostly) very practical.What it's weak in is unit diversity. That doesn't make it's battles weak, the opinion of a lot of people on this sub is that the Warhammer games have objectively superior battles because there's more variety in units (I disagree). You probably wont even notice that issue though, since it does have more diversity than Shogun 2.The charges in 3K are generally very satisfying (especially heavy shock cavalry into light infantry), the duels between generals are a very cool mechanic, and the sieges are fun enough. Unlike Shogun 2 there are very few matched combat animations, though they are still present in general duels.You'll get a lot more out of the game if you've got a vague idea of who the characters are and how the story goes. You don't need to know much, but finding a video or two to have a quick catch-up on who the characters are adds a lot of context which makes the game fun. I really recommend this game to Total War and Three Kingdoms/DW Fans.Also, Do Not Pursue Lu Bu!

2019 Early Access Review You know it's been hard to get The Guys together for games recently, we all have different stuff we like and some people just aren't interested in some games that others are.But there's one game that almost all of us can agree on a good amount of the time, and it's this game. For that alone, I recommend it to you and anyone else who wants a challenging, semi-strategic, fun coop FPS to play a few rounds of in the evening and not feel like you wasted your time.Edit 1: Payday 2 style mission selection, different biomes with randomly generated objectives+side objectives for bonuses. You mine strains of minerals off of the caverns either for a mission or to upgrade your gear. Occasionally you'll get hit with a swarm/horde/police assault/etc and have to fight waves of enemies that punch through cavern ceilings, walls. Enemies explode and take out massive chunks of the environment, others can pick you up and carry you across the cave, some can punch you backwards (and potentially off a cliff). Combat never feels repetitive because each encounter is dangerous, but also incredibly reward as weapons are punchy, well animated, and have actual personality. You can also upgrade them through skill trees and more recently use Overclocks to change it's base functions (regular burst pistol can throw small electric mines that stun enemies, but do less damage overall. Not very useful but still fun)There's no microtransactions, just Supporter/Special Edition packs, and those only provide in-game cosmetics and flair for the Discord server. The game is still in early access but the developers have a concise road map that has been followed since release and that is been updated on time every time. Updates are big and game changing while not screwing with the core gameplay, it's seriously refreshing to see an early access game receive this level of support. $30 is a steal for the amount of fun I, and we, have had playing this. Highly recommend it!Edit 2: Only for the Steam Award. Still love this game, just a blast to play. No problem jumping in with friends to play a handful of missions. Difficulty is great, the style is fun. You may find it repetitive at a certain point but I suppose that happens with all similar wave based coop shooter games out there, I personally love how it's implemented here.

2020 It’s telling that the studio responsible for Dark Souls continues to reinvent its combat, while other studios are still aping the original Dark Souls. For Sekiro, the combat needed to be faster, more aggressive, more vertical, with a focus on counterplay and deadly consequences when one of the combatants falls a step behind. You need to feel like a Shinobi, not a plodding knight, so From Software radically redesigned their combat for this new fantasy. But don’t expect this ninja mastery to just be handed to you. From Software, bless their hearts, continues to believe that you should actually have to work hard and overcome a difficult obstacle before feeling like a badass. And paradoxically, it might even be harder for Dark Souls veterans, as the “dodge and hit” rhythm has been replaced by a more intricate pattern of attacks, parries, and dodges. There’s even one glorious boss battle on top of a Japanese Castle where the game basically says “Look, if you keep playing this like Dark Souls, you’re going to keep dying. Be more aggressive!” It took me a while, but eventually things clicked and I started to feel the ebbs and flows in the rhythm of our sword clanks. From that point on, I was in love with the combat. Besides castle guy there’s several other creative and brutal bosses that’ll test your mettle, but give you the biggest gaming highs of the year.There’s more to Sekiro than combat, the game also features an interesting setting: a mythical feudal Japanese kingdom that’s beset by war. That said, the story gets pretty convoluted. From Software tends to focus more on subtle environmental storytelling as opposed exposition or cinematics. Parts of that work well, as you can feel the decay and corruption that chasing immortality has wrought. Unfortunately, there’s also a bunch of stuff about loyalty and the Iron Code and war that I didn’t understand at all, to the point I was only 65% sure of what I was doing when making story-critical choices. The levels also feel somewhat subdued, with only a few matching the supernatural spectacle of From Software’s previous games. That said, the level design is excellent, with impressive continuous corridors that make good use of your grappling hook and stealth kills.Sekiro isn’t just ninja Dark Souls, a choice that doubtlessly alienated some fans, but it’s something really special in it’s own right. A glowing recommendation for anyone who loves action games and a challenge.

I was one of the unfortunate souls who bought the $120 forty years of WrestleMania edition and then proceeded to have their data erased when the game came out. And I'll admit... that's gotta be the biggest problem I've had with this game, and they did resolve it. And, as you can see by my playtime, I'm rather pleased about thatIt has since been about a week since it happened, and I haven't had the game crash, let alone delete all my data. And beyond all of that, this really feels like an improvement over 2K23. Technically, things are mostly the same, but there's additional bits and bobs added for both variety and QoL reasons. On of my absolute favorites to mention would be the reversal prompt is now able to tell you if your input was too early or too late. On top of that, thanks to the WrestleMania Showcase mode, certain legends like Ricky Steamboat and Ravishing Rick Rude are back on the game's roster, as well as a huge array of alternate versions of stars from different eras that DO have different stats. Maybe they could've had one or two less versions of Cena, but they also have four or five different versions of Bray Wyatt, so it does feel like they were listening to the crowd as much as their wallets. OH! And let's not forget having the ability to have CASKET matches, AMBULANCE matches, GAUNTLET MATCHES OF VARIOUS TYPES! You can have special referee matches, No Holds Barred, falls count anywhere, an entire Royal Rumble. They've really made selecting a match feel like it's 2006 again with all the options, and you can make your own preset of rules to save and select to use.If I had to give one genuine worry about this game, it would actually be the MyRise story mode, specifically the male side in Undisputed. Don't get me wrong, I adore the idea of letting the player become the Universal Champion and prove themselves and all that... but that does bring up the question of what the hell the story would be for a 2K25? I'm sure someone will think of something good. Personally, I'd like it if we got a MyRise mode that took place in a past generation of wrestling with past legends as main points of the story, but that will only happen in my hallucinogenic dreams. Outside of that, though, the biggest takeaways from the game are common lag issues some folks have, most of which are fixable, and the aforementioned botchamania with the early access players' save data, which they have fixed and seemingly fixed well.I would absolutely say this game is worth market price if you loved 2K23, so long as you know how similar the games are to one another. However, I do think this one has enough different and interesting about it to warrant a separate purchase.
