Follow My Review Group Here! About Description 💾Graphics The graphics are kinda meh in my opinion. I know I might get some hate on this, but I feel like the graphics looked better in Fallout 4 in some aspects. The shadows and draw distance just feels lackluster at times. The map is really well designed though. I have to give props to the design team for the map. It’s absolutely stunning in some areas and blows me away. 🎮Gameplay Fallout 76 has pretty decent gameplay elements to it. You do level up and get perk cards which you can put on your character. It’s kinda like the Fallout 4 perk system, but more casual and gives you more freedom in terms of switching up builds and messing around with it, which is really nice to see. You can swap cards at any time which is good, so you are not stuck with a build you make. The shooting mechanics are kinda hit or miss (Pun intended). It’s like Fallout 4 shooting mechanics, which I liked but it just feels buggy (I’ll get more into that in the bug section of the review). The RPG elements are there in this game, so you can make many types of builds which is amazing, especially for an online Fallout game. You can build your own settlement in this game, but getting some of the cool furniture items takes “Atoms” which you can get for free in the game, but it's a huge grind to get a lot of them. If you want every item in the game, you’re gonna need to spend money sadly. It honestly feels like a free to play game. The seasons are pretty nice though and give you some really cool items if you grind like mad. 🎭Multiplayer You will always be in a lobby with people (unless you get Fallout 1st). The connection is pretty good so I never really had any connection issues in this game. You are able to do quests together (unless it’s a main quest) for the most part which is nice. The community is pretty nice but omg there trade prices would make Stalin Jealous. The PVP is basically non-existent anymore. That multiplayer has some issues, but it gets the job done. 🕛Playtime The playtime is there for sure! I put almost 100 hours into this game and that was only with my brother. I feel like once you get to that high level and you get the build you want, the interest or challenge disappears. The quest can get repetitive and boring really fast in my opinion. I highly recommend getting a friend to play with. It’s almost essential. If you want a friendly PVE Fallout game, then you will put a ton of hours on this game. 🎧Sound The monsters and bandits sound really good in this game. The voice acting is pretty mediocre in this game, as well as the music in my opinion. The gun effects are still pretty good here so no complaints. Not much to say on the sound department, it's pretty good with minor complaints. ❗Bugs❗ Okay, this game has a ton of bugs. Some quests will not show on the map, if you join your friend into a building and you are doing the quest together, that can bug your quest from not being completed (so when you enter a building with a friend while doing the same quest, you have to enter solo). The hit detection is really bad at times. You can snipe someone in the head and you will not get a hit marker at all, sometimes even in the chest and that makes me wanna scream! So the shooting mechanics can be really buggy. Sometimes enemies take a second to die after killing them, like there is a delay. Also throwing grenades are really laggy. It could be server related, but still really annoying. Also if I Alt+Tab too much, my game gets super blurry, so I have to restart the game to fix it. I get it, it’s bethesda but come on, I wanted 16 times the detail, not 16 times the bugs. Hopefully they fix some of these issues soon. 🔅Performance The optimization still needs some work. I’m playing with a GTX 1070 with a i5-6600k and I get pretty good fps most of the time, but then I get a huge drop and stutter, especially when loading in cells or loading into a city. Maybe that’s to be expected, but to me it can be annoying. I will say if you are gonna play this, you may need to lower your shadow distance, that destroys your fps a lot from my experience. ✔️Pro’s Amazing mapOnline Fallout gameMany character buildsSettlement buildingTons of questsGood enemy varietyExcellent community ❌Con’s A ton of bugsMicrotransactionsOptimization needs workShooting mechanics can be bad at timesA Lot of cool items locked behind the Atom ShopGame can feel pretty boring solo (in my opinion) 🏆Rating 5.5/10I'd pick this game up on sale for around 25-50% if possible. 🔗Conclusion I wanted to get this game a thumbs up, but with the annoying bugs and unfinished feel of the game, I can’t. Also the Atom shop just kills it for me. $10 for power armor skin is wild to me (that’s just the tip of the iceberg). If you've been looking for an online Fallout game, then give it a try and you may enjoy it. I just didn’t have a good time, the quests were a drag in my opinion and the bugs threw me off (especially the Atom Shop). You may like it, but I keep feeling more disappointed the more I play it. 2023 Product received for free A Sequel That Shines Brighter: Ori and the Will of the WispsRating: 9/10Ori and the Will of the Wisps is the next part of the Ori series which are metroidvania platformers. This time the Moon Studios made everything bigger and better than last time. Amazing locations and characters. All audio, visual and gameplay has improved from the previous version. Everything just sound and looks cool while you are doing it.Gameplay (10/10):There has bee major improvement in the combat of the game. Previously in the Ori and the Blind Forest the combat was really lacking compared to the platforming part of the game. Now the combat has been brought to the same level as the platforming was. The combat now is fun and can look incredible while you are doing it, when you combine your platforming skills with your attacks. There is now real progression with your combat abilities. You get skills that you can upgrade by buy upgrades for them and some skill get also upgraded by equipping spirit shards. At the end of the game you feel so much more powerful than at the beginning of the game. The progression is not slow either. You will be getting frequently new upgrades or skills while you playthrough the game.The platforming on this game is very fun with minor changes from previous game. This is good thing. Ori and the Blind Forest, the previous game, had already fun and nice looking platforming mechanics, so there is not that much of a reason to change it.Huge improvement in this game is that it actually autosaves and these save spots are almost all the time in very convenient spots. You don't lose too much progress when you make some mistake and die. You will be brought back quite close where you were before. I remember only like two points where I would have collected a secret and died soon afterwards and then needing to collect the secret again. Most of the time you don't need to collect the secret again, but for some reason some spots didn't save that.Graphics and Sounds (10/10):Graphically the game is still excellent. Like the previous version the game just looks phenomenal. Moon Studios have actually improved on this part too. They have fixed some issues, where some of the bright parts would get so bright that it would just become a blob of white. I didn't notice that happening in this game at all. They have also added the HDR mode, but I could not sadly test that since I lack the monitor for it.Music in this game is also very good and add lot to the storytelling and boss fights.Difficulty (8/10):The game is not the easiest platformer out there, but not too difficult either, since there is very forgiving autosaves. I played through the game on the hard difficulty and for me it wasn't too hard and the difficulty didn't affect the enjoyability of the game. I had to try some parts multiple times, but I eventually got through them.There are also two easier modes that I haven't tested, but I would imagine that they will just make the combat part easier if you are not interested in that. It would be good if there was a way to make some platforming parts easier to those that just want to enjoy the games story, but I don't think the difficulty options affect that.This game also has some achievements that require you to be good at the game, like not dying at any point of your playthrough and not using any upgrades. Those will make the game significantly harder.Replayability (7/10):There is not any meaningful choices real choices to make while you play the game for the first time. You can farm the currency (spirit light) and unlock all skills in one playthrough quite easily, so you can test all of the "builds".Only reason to play this again would be to experience the story again and try to speedrun or achieve other more difficult achievements that the game offers.There is also the spirit trials that you can try to compete in. There is separate leaderboards for them and you can compare your time against your friends times and race against them.Story (10/10):The story continues from the previous game and it is really a roller coaster ride of emotions again. I don't really want to write too much about it to not to spoil too much, but I'll just say that I liked it and it was nice to have more story content and characters in this game than in the previous one.You don't need to play the first game to enjoy this one, but I would still recommend you to do so, because it tells origin of Ori and how they got there and who are the characters shown at the start of the game.Conclusion:Ori and the Will of the Wisps is a game that I can easily recommend to anyone that likes platformers and metroidvania games, because of its story, visuals and gameplay. It has improved from the previous game a lot. It is not too easy game, but forgiving autosaves will help you with the difficult parts. It is really enjoyable experience and I would like to see more of this series from Moon Studios in the future.

2021 Early Access Review I've always had a fascination with astronomy, engineering and physics but this took it to a new level. The idea of a dyson sphere was always one of the most alluring concepts to me as far as future tech was concerned. To live in a day and age where a society can collaborate so perfectly that it could create such a structure felt like a dream to me, but this game gave me a window into that dream. To be able to exist in world where even hypothetically, as a collective we can create a theoretical concept for the future, regardless of whether humanity will ever get there, it gives me a little hope for a possible future. I never played games like this before. Builders and factory games were never something that even crossed my path, let one drew me in. But this game opened doors for me; gave me ideas. Plus the concept of being a lone individual with such a God like power to shape your part of the universe, carving out planets and owning stars, while you contribute to the whole of the galaxy along side other engineers in their own cluster is a very empowering idea. The gameplay mechanics are phenomenal. The limitless possibilities of factoring in resources from planets across multiple star systems. Planning to create massive structures with nigh infinite power at your disposal. Harnessing the power of the sun itself in the palm of your hands, then exploring further to touch another. This game has so much potential and it's still only in early access. Early Access Review This game has constantly refactored it's core loop, often for the worst, every major update. This has resulted in 12 years of development with the end result being a repetitive game with an extremely shallow pool of content. Made worst as the devs are absolutely obsessed only with how quickly you progress through what little content is actually in the game. Most of the time, the updates are focused on extending what little content the game has instead of actually expanding the game. This leads to frustrating loops where you raid high difficulty locations for your current stage in the game, and end up with tools that are either worse than what you came in with; or slight upgrades at best. Historically, the game has worked around several core mechanics, the longest running one being a "Learn by Doing" system; whereby using specific weapons and crafting items you gradually got more proficient in using and crafting said items, allowing you to craft better weapons and use them more effectively. This was removed in favor of a brand new leveling and perk system, "Learn by Skilling" essentially. Where the player gains a level and may allocate a perk point anywhere they wish to gain small percentile bonuses in a specific task and unlock better quality items and new crafting recipes. Currently, the game works on a "Learn by Looting" system which followed almost immediately after the "Learn by Skilling" update, where the player needs to read a set number of magazines which they loot from PoIs or earn by doing trader quests. The current core focus of the game is essentially a looter shooter where you raid points of interest for supplies in preparation for a horde night at the end of every 7th day. The actual survival elements are slim, with each subsequent update continuously paring them down. Being able to jar your own water was removed, farming food was nerfed, crafting better quality equipment was heavily restricted and gated behind looting PoIs, even the cost of cooking recipes was increased to minimize the survival crafting element and cater the game more to looting and action. The most recent update has (at least temporarily) removed weather effects to my knowledge to make way for the new armors.The actual content in the game essentially revolves around roughly 10 or 11 different weapon categories and 4 tool categories, each following a 3 tiered system of progression; stone, iron, steel with each progressive tier being a statistical improvement on the last at the cost of increased stamina usage. Though a slim few of the weapons are unique within their category, like the SMG in the pistols category or crossbows and bows being grouped together. This naturally leads to the game feeling extremely samey every play through as most skill trees are allocated 1 melee weapon and 1 firearm, though a select few get 2 of either one or the other. Due to the loot progression dragging it's feet and being hyper focused about extending the 40 or so odd items that you can use as weapons or tools across the game; you can often find neolithic stone spears and wooden clubs inside of a military base's armory if you make the mistake of looting it before you level is high enough to get you over the invisible "loot stage" hump, which determines if you're even allowed to roll on a table featuring an item of a higher tier than you currently have. With some luck, you can progress decently through looting. Though often times most loot is basic food, trash or raw resources. Making the majority of spins on the loot roulette immensely disappointing.The bones of each update have carried over with each iteration, often for the worst. Besides the perk system from the previous update (which to this day is horrifically balanced with multiple useless perks), jars remain in the game as dummied out code and a highly granular quality system (separate from item tier) from the earliest alphas persist to this day. Rolling random levels in 10 point range from 1-60 for each level of item you make. Quality 1 is 1-10, Quality 2 is 11-20 and so on up until Quality 6, ranging from 51-60. This is completely hidden from the player, but has a major impact on stats. You could craft a Quality 4 item that rolls a 40 that out performs a quality 5 item that rolled a 41. The current "1.0" update, which is just another Alpha version being sold at full price with a 2 year road map, has gutted the former armor and clothing system instead for fixed outfits with unique stats that scale with quality level. Significantly downsizing character customization and enforcing a strange metagame where you have to constantly hotswap pieces of your outfit to maximize productivity. This is in addition to further slowing progression by essentially making trader rewards useless and adding zero new content to the game, not even following up on the promised "improved optimization" which the game desperately lacks.In short: 7 Days to Die was an extremely promising game that has been jerked around by it's developers for 12 years, as they gradually lost the vision they had and began instead trying to micromanage how their players play their singleplayer survival crafting game.

Balatro is one of my new favorite games of all time. I am nowhere near done playing this one, despite 100%ing everything in the game except for grinding the Gold Stake difficulties; I'll be doing that for many months to come, and even after I'm done with that I won't be surprised if I come back for even more.As for my actual thoughts, this is, no exaggeration, the perfect roguelike experience for me. Every single time you start up a run, it is a completely different game. There is so much content, so many different combinations of things you can do. From 15 decks with 8 difficulties each, 150 unique Jokers to cheat your way through poker, nearly 30 different bosses, and 20 unique and difficult challenges flipping some of the mechanics of the game on their heads, this game is packed to the brim with addicting gameplay. Even compared to Slay the Spire, the gold standard for deckbuilder roguelikes, this game has so much to do.My absolute favorite part of the experience, especially compared to something like StS, is just how fun it is to get something going. You don't need to know too much about all of the different Jokers available or card variations to deduce some insane synergies. Almost all of my runs started with a Joker that I hadn't started with before, and I tried to build everything around it, which was incredibly easy to do due to all of the different combos. Flushes are easy and consistent, straights are a bit harder but satisfying to pull off, high card decks with a lot of planet upgrades and steel cards are so much fun, and I love the secret hands like 5 of a kind and flush five. Everything feels viable given enough skill and luck, which I certainly can't say about other roguelikes I've played. I love pulling something off with a Joker that I saw in the shop on a previous run and thought "there's no way that could ever be good" and then it takes me to the end game.My other favorite part of this game: endless mode. Sometimes in Slay the Spire, I would have an absolutely insane deck, crush the heart in 4 turns, and then just have to start from the beginning again, when I just wanted to keep using that deck. Well, Balatro just has that baked in, making runs feel so much more exhilarating. Sure, the "final boss" is on ante 8, but ante 12 ramps up to 300 million points, which feels much more threatening a lot of times. My highest score happened in ante 17, past the SECOND "final boss," which involved numbers so large that scientific notation was required to display them. Every time you think you've blown the game wide open, it throws another insane milestone at you, which I absolutely love.If I had to complain about anything, it would be the hardest difficulties and challenges. Most of the challenges I found very fun, but I spent way too long on the final challenge: Jokerless. It felt far too luck based and unfair, but it was still addicting and kinda fun to grind. My run that ended up beating the challenge got to ante 13, with a bunch of red sealed, polychrome glass 5s of spades, which was scoring billions by the end game. All that with none of the 150 Jokers in the game gave me a true appreciation for how well balanced this game is, and how, as I claimed before, everything is viable. I am hoping that going through that challenge makes the rest of the gold stake difficulties feel a little bit more manageable, because the first one I did was a grind fest that was very hard to get off the ground. I'm glad that this game is gaining the traction it deserves, and I really hope that LocalThunk, the SOLO DEVELOPER (HOW) of this game, continues to make great work. The patches and demos and community surrounding this game has been incredible, and I just want to continue playing Balatro forever now. Even if Persona 3 Reload and Final Fantasy VII Rebirth have the greatest stories, visuals, and gameplay of all time, I think that this is my personal game of the year, and in my top 5 games of all time.

2018 Early Access Review TL:DRDeck Building ✓Setting and Graphics ✓Gameplay ✓Metaprogression -Rating: 8/10Full ReviewSlay the Spire is a rogue-like deck building game that is becoming the baseline of the genre. Every other rogue-like card game is now compared to this one almost as the gold standard. The goal is to defeat the boss at the end of 3 levels by traversing maps of battles, shops, and encounters to build your deck and gain passive abilities and gold. The maps consist of multiple different locations that you can go to. There are average monster battles that beating them result in gaining gold and adding 1 of 3 random cards to your deck. There are hard monster battles that beating them result in the same as an average monster but you also get a relic. There are shops that you can go to in order to buy cards, potions, relics, or to remove a card from your deck. There are mystery spots which can result in a shop, free item, item trade, or monster battle. There are campfires that allow you to either rest at to regain health or to upgrade a card. There are boss rooms where you challenge the floor boss and upon beating them get rewards, your character gets healed, and you move to the next of the 3 levels. When you start a new level you can see the whole map and have multiple starting points. You are able to plan out your most desired route to optimize your resources for the campaign.Players have the option to choose from 3 different classes to take on the campaign, either a knight style that specializes in having lots of block and physical attacks, a rogue style that specializes in poisoning their enemies and being able to have a large amount of cards during a turn, and a mage style that focuses on strategically setting up attacks with passive damage dealing powers.While going through the campaign, the player has many customization options for their deck as long as they land on the right spaces. You always start with the same small deck but as you go through the game you have the option to gain new cards, upgrade a card in your hand, exchange cards in your hand for others, or remove cards in your hand. At first it seems like you want every card possible but after playing for a while you better understand how to optimize your hand for the specific character you are playing.The passive item relics vary greatly in what they do and add another fun layer to the gameplay experience. Each character starts with one of these relics and can gain more from beating more difficult enemies or from purchasing them in the shop with gold. The relics range from increasing the amount of cards you can play in one turn but removing another aspect of the game to adding an additional point of poison to evach enemy that gets poisoned by you. They can make for some crazy combinations to make each run a new and fun challenge.The only area I am not too thrilled about is the metaprogression for the rogue-like style. Each of the 3 characters has a total of 3 unlocks for new cards and and items. These are unlocked by gaining experience from going through the game. Even if you lose you still receive the XP so it does not take too long to unlock everything. After that the only things to unlock are ascension levels. These are basically difficulty levels ranging from 0-20. To unlock a new ascension level all you have to do is beat the game on the level before it. Each level makes it more difficult by making enemies more dangerous or reducing the ability to get new resources. While it does give you a good sense of accomplishment when you complete a new level, I wish there was more upgrading you could do for each of your characters from winning.Overall it is a really fun game and I definitely recommend it both to people who are into rogue-like/card games or to people who are trying to get into the genre. 8/10

Highest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ recommendation I can give.In 2002 a child me played this game for the first time, saw a Minotaur punt a Greek soldier halfway across the map, and thought that was the coolest thing I'd ever seen. That level of physics in an RTS was astounding at the time, from the minor god system creating dynamic adaptation situations to the global presence of god powers this game pushed SO MANY boundaries for the genre. I would have been happy with a simple remaster, just to brush everything up, make it nice and shiny for the modern era and call it a day. So I make that Minotaur, I attack that Hoplite formation, the soldier still goes flying... ALONG WITH EVERY SINGLE OTHER SOLDIER NEAR HIM.It's little things like that make me love this remake. The developers of this game seem to have approached every aspect with the philosophy of "Ok but what if it was MORE extreme?" What if single-target became multi-target, what if you could cast god powers over and over again, what if the Norse got a fiery wolf-shaped nuclear warhead? What if there was a brand new win condition where you built a Wonder and all your myth units doubled in size and damage?! When I say double the size I mean DOUBLE, if you thought the Titan unit was impressive wait until it's half your screen tall! There are countless little details and QoL improvements, ranging from each civilization getting a unique Citadel from the Egyptian God Power (Completely unnecessary, they did it anyway), Titans being able to walk through water is huge, making every naval myth unit available to every build is huge, there is a toggleable autocast/autobuild/auto-anything for nearly every aspect of the game. This very well may be the best RTS to introduce people to the genre for that reason alone! Every other aspect of this game has evolved into something so much grander than it was before, while still maintaining the classic appeal of the original. I am flabbergasted they achieved both of those outcomes, I would go so far as to call this one of the best video game remakes I have ever seen. And it's going to get even better! They've set up a perfect groundwork to build off of in the future, and I cannot wait to see what Pantheons get added down the line. This isn't just a great game that'll provide a great time, it's a great investment from a proven track record that will continue to provide a great time for many years to come.Mark my words, this is just the beginning. 2021 Tomb Raider is very much similar to Uncharted, though in some ways better and in some ways worse. Depending on what you want this could be good or bad. Uncharted has better story telling and production values, whereas Tomb Raider has much better variety of gameplay and level design.In TR there are 4 weapons you can carry on you: bow, pistol, machine gun, shotgun as well as a pickaxe for a melee weapon. Actually, the pickaxe, bow, and technically shotgun are all used in many of the platforming/puzzle elements as well. Very good design. There are also alternate firing modes for every weapon (the pistol is DLC though), skills to be unlocked, and upgrades for weapons. This game is like if somebody took the Uncharted idea, but wanted to add more gameplay elements to make it more fun.Before getting to the multiplayer section, I should note that the story in this game is more dark/supernatural oriented so be advised. Also the camera during cutscenes is unbelievably shaky which can be a little headache inducing. I think they were trying to go for the whole "someone is filming this while on their phone" type thing.Multiplayer:I'm a bit shocked that I've enjoyed the MP of this game when I rarely do for most games. Part of this is because I usually have to enjoy a good single player experience and get "attached" to a game/characters and a lot of MP-focused games may not have this. The other reason I think I enjoy this is because of how you gain experience in "stages": Obviously if you are amazingly good at the game you'll be getting experience from kills but also a lot of experience from "feats" like killing 5 enemies in a row without dying or getting headshots. If you are mediocre at the game you only get a moderate amount of exp from kills but there are certain feats that are specific to being "mediocre" so to speak. You won't get as much exp as if you were really good (duh!) but you will get some. The really cool thing though is how you still get SOME exp (though not much) if you are terrible. There are some feats that are specific to not being very good so you can still earn SOMETHING. Again, you won't get much...but at least it's not an all or nothing type thing.Some people might think this is similar to a "participation trophy" but it really isn't due to the fact that better players will get more exp than worse players. A true participation trophy is something everyone gets and therefore "equalizes" everyone regardless of how good or bad you are.Also of note for the multiplayer: You can earn exp while in private matches (which is awesome!) so you can just have fun with your specific friend group rather than fighting against max level players who've been at it probably since the game came out.Overall, TR is a really good game with an interesting MP that you might like if you aren't usually into other MP type games.

2023 Lies of P is an absolutely fantastic game. It is a game clearly inspired by Bloodbourne and other From Software games; and while many of the tropes and ideas are lifted directly from those games, Lies of P finds its own distinct niche both in aesthetic and in gameplay. This game is hard, even compared to the soulsbourne games, but like those that came before it, it is fair. If you stick with it and really try to learn the mechanics, you will find one of the best games in the whole genre.While many games that attempt to copy the homework of fromsoft fall flat in several ways, Lies of P passes with flying colors in nearly every aspect, most notably the combat. Your two defensive options are guarding and dodging. Dodging is mostly straightforward and similar to any other soulslike, if a little bit less lenient than most. Guarding, on the other hand, is very unique in the genre and is what gives Lies of P its own style of combat. Guarding an attack will drain less of your health than getting hit, and will make all of the lost health restorable, similar to the rally mechanic in Bloodbourne. Pressing the guard button just before an attack lands will result in a perfect guard, which will not drain any health and will contribute to staggering the enemy, among a few other benefits. While the perfect guard window is tight, noticeably smaller than that of Sekiro, missing and landing a regular guard still grants you the opportunity to regain all of the health you lost, which incentivizes you to use it even if you aren't completely confident.This guard system gives Lies of P a combat loop that feels like all of the best aspects of Bloodbourne and Sekiro combined into a new formula that has its own distinct appeal, where you attempt to parry strings of attacks from an enemy, and after the string ends you try to restore as much health as possible from missed parries. Of course, even if the abilities of the character are perfect, they would go to waste if the enemy design doesn't allow the to shine. Luckily, the enemy design in Lies of P is absolutely top notch.Basic enemies have a few attack varieties the keep you on your toes, but aren't fast or frequent enough to ever become ganky. As you progress later into the game, you encounter a wide range of basic enemies which become increasingly difficult and complex, which makes exploring never get tiring. While they aren't anything truly special, they are more than satisfactory and get the job done filling out the areas with plenty of variety. The more difficult non-boss enemies can honestly be a significant challenge on their own, with a relatively wide array of attack timings and patterns. Some of the later ones can even change which combo they do based on how you react to earlier hits which gives them a feeling of being a real opponent and not just an exploitable formula. Most of these can be ran past, just like in the soulsbourne games, but defeating them almost invariably gives you a valuable item as a reward.The bosses are my favorite thing about the whole game. Practically every single boss is a highlight. Every boss has a huge number of attacks and combos with unique ranges and timings which are both well telegraphed and animated beautifully. Every attack has a clear indication of where it's hitboxes are, and I could count on one hand the number of times I got hit in a manner that didn't feel like my own fault. Parrying and dodging every attack after learning all of the combos and variations elicits the same feelings as the very best From Software bosses. The scramble to recover health after failing a parry is just as exciting as it is in Bloodbourne, and the fact that it comes from blocking gives the combat an ebb and flow that I believe surpasses it. While a couple of the bosses reuse assets from earlier in the game, they gain a large suite of new moves and behaviors that make them not feel like re-fights at all. All this is without even mentioning their designs, which are awesome across the board. Many of them are also foreshadowed by notes or characters found around the preceding level, which gives meeting them for the first time a great payoff.I could go on and on about the million other things that this game does right: the aesthetic, world-building, interesting story and characters, music, weapon building mechanic, durability mechanic, fable arts, progression system, lying system, voice acting, performance, visual fidelity, etc. but for the sake of not making this review the length of a college thesis I will conclude with this. Lies of P is the best soulslike not made by From Software, and is on par with some of their best work.

2018 Early Access Review I'm a pretty casual roguelike fan and Caves of Qud is the first to really draw me in. Despite the large number of key bindings it's actually quite intuitive. The music and atmosphere is top-notch and just oozes that late 70s New Wave sci-fi vibe, and the wide variety of options for character builds ensure you won't get bored or frustrated. Plenty of previous reviewers have already touched on that, but it really does bear repeating: while there are a handful of "optimal" bulids, experimentation feels rewarding and it never feels like the game throws more at you than you can handle. It is a very text-heavy and thoughtful game, and many very dangerous situations can only be overcome by throroughly considering your tactical options. It's hard to believe that Caves of Qud is still in early access, as it's more fully-featured and nuanced than quite a few other "complete" roguelikes I have played. Little touches of brilliance like colored text to help differentiate between certain varieties of items or line-of-sight markers to show where a ranged ability will actually hit are plentiful. That's not to mention the quality of the writing, which puts most AAA devs to shame and may even rival genre heavyweights like Planescape: Torment and Pillars of Eternity. Text descriptions of even the most mundane enemies are loaded with vivid imagery which helps support the game's vibrant yet minimalist aesthetic.I'm very excited to see where Freehold Games takes Caves of Qud from here and happy to have supported them during development. Definitely planning on buying copies for a few friends to share the experience...live and drink!

Look, I want to give this game a recommendation because I don't think it's a BAD game, but I can't in good conscience recommend it to anybody else.Now I do think it does a good job of giving you the feel of living in the grimdark setting of Warhammer 40k in a way no other Warhammer game has to date. Sometimes the path of mercy just gets more people killed, sometimes you have to recognize that no matter how nice you are to that xeno lady she won't see you as equal to her, and kindness is met with suspicion and many will try to exploit it. My own character tried to thread the needle between being a good man but holding to faith in the God-Emperor, which meant I never got past rank II in either Dogmatic or Iconoclast. He tried to make friends with as many factions as possible... which means aside from the Imperial Navy nobody got enough loot to see the Rogue Trader as an ally. This is one of the major problems that keeps me from giving this game a recommend: the pacing.So about that Pacing:Alright, so here is where I was at the end of Chapter II - I had just finished a bunch of sidequests, none of my companion stories were finished but they had all had a satisfying Act I or thereabouts. I was at rank II of V on Dogmatic and Iconoclast so I was thinking that okay, so while I know I will be capped based on which one hits rank III first I'm in little danger of that not happening. I wasn't very far along on anybody's reputation except Explorators but I was about a third to maybe halfway through which, this being the end of Chapter II, meant I felt fairly confident regarding my progression.Little did I realize I was actually 75% of the way through the game. Chapter III takes you out of Koronus entirely for reasons I won't explain because spoilers, and each Chapter after that feels like it has about as much content and by extension resources and missions as Chapter I. Worse, the bridge from Chapters 4 to 5 comes more or less out of nowhere and while you are warned ahead of time you are going for the endgame and have a chance to gather stuff and finish sidequests... as far as I could tell I had done everything already.And that's the big issue - I took the massive amount of content and all the adventures I had for Chapter II to mean that the rest of the game must be like this and I've probably still got dozens of hours of gameplay left! But as it turns out, I had missed the boat on committing to an ideology already, and had also missed the boat on gaining any real allies other than the Imperial Navy. I also rarely encountered story events or other means of boosting reputation with other factions that wasn't just dumping all the garbage I had looted upon them, making things feel so very limited.All of this would be fine and keeping with the themes of Warhammer 40k if I was warned ahead of time and knew that what looked like "not even halfway through the game" was actually "almost done".Oh, if you're wondering why I was able to max the Imperial Navy's rep and nobody else's? It's because they're special and get a resource to boost their reputation with that's completely separate from everybody else and that nobody else will take meaning boosting rep with the Navy costs you nothing with the other factions. Which means if you just focus one and only one faction then good news - you can be best buds with both the Navy and the xenotrading, heretical artifact smuggling pirates! Again, I'd have been fine with the idea that you can only be friends with a couple factions if they had, oh I dunno, maybe had some mechanic where boosting one faction lowered rep with another so it basically signaled you're not supposed to be friends with everybody ahead of time. Or maybe just more story stuff that made you choose one over the other more often.Actually, about the story...So I'd say the story is overall pretty good in terms of immersing you into the setting. It does this job quite well in fact, for a while. The problems really begin towards the end of Chapter IV. I won't spoil anything but... well if you've played Far Cry 3 you probably are familiar with this pain. There is a threat you're dealing with, eventually you deal with that threat, and it turns out the real threat is something you never even saw a glimpse of once on screen until you get to Chapter V. They also tease at another faction showing up but they never seem to matter - which is funny considering they went through all the trouble of having you fight members of this other faction that I don't mention because spoilers but nope, never seen again.Basically, after doing a wonderful job pitting you against a chaos cult, xenos raiders, and all sorts of other problems the story falls flat on its face, gets tied up in Chapter IV, and suddenly you get a whole new villain and threat out of practically nowhere because I guess somebody told them they have to have FIVE chapters.The Combat:So anyway, how is the combat? Afterall it's the grimdark world of 40k where there is only war, and it won't feel like there is only war without, well, warfare. Well, the combat is bland to put it mildly. The biggest issue are the infamous difficulty spikes that owlcat is known for. This makes it critical to focus your characters and know from the start what niche they'll fill and build focusing on that.The problem is if you do this well you end up with an utterly broken character who trivializes anything you run into and all anybody else gets to do is chip in once in a while while they murder entire rooms of xenos, chaos marines, daemons, and whatever other horrors this game throws at you. Now, you could deliberately nerf your builds a bit to avoid this... at which point your backside is artfully removed from your body and served to you with garnish and a sweet, tangy sauce.Space combat is not as bad in terms of balancing but it's really tedious on the whole and that's all I've got to say about it.Regarding Bugs:So as of this time it's very possible to finish the end without encountering game breaking bugs. That said it's still buggy - the game sometimes forgets its own rules or how its own status effects work, I'm not sure how much of the damage I dealt (or didn't deal) was due to a bug and how much of it was just game mechanics interacting in ways I didn't anticipate, and actual chances of success are not always displayed accurately. It's playable, but just don't trust everything to always work the way you expect it to at all times which can be infuriating if things break in a way that makes combat far harder than it needs to be.Overall verdict:So basically, I think I enjoyed this overall but as you can tell, I can't recommend it. It scratches a 40k itch that nothing else does, but all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the way just annoys me. If I had to call this game anything I'd probably call it unfinished more than anything else. It feels like there was supposed to be more content at least in Chapter 4 that just never made it into the finished product. I'm sure some are hoping for DLC but, well, even a small studio like Owlcat doesn't get to get away with selling an unfinished game and then making us pay extra to get the cut content. Granted it's not as insulting as Day 1 DLC would be, but I'm still not so inclined to forgive them on this.

2018 Early Access Review Dead Cells, while boasting fluid and enjoyable combat, faces a significant hurdle in the current implementation of the game's progression. By killing enemies, you gain blueprints which are used to unlock new items and abilities, which are not added to the item pool until you have unlocked them using the titular currency of 'cells'. However, it becomes plainly apparent as you start using the gear you unlock that not all equipment is created equal. Some weapons are powerful, or have many easily employed synergies, while others are simply a waste of an item slot. As the player controls what is unlocked out of the available blueprints, they are faced with the decision of unlocking many pieces of gear (and having a diverse itempool made primarily out of sub-par equipment), spending most of their run searching for good items or synergies; or simply only unlocking powerful gear, and as a result having very uniform and bland runs, if effective ones. Essentially, the player is punished for choosing to continue unlocking items, rather than upgrading a select few, and there is little draw to continue playing a game after reaching a point where any futher progress is detrimental. I think dead cells is a genuinely fun game with a lot of promise, and I understand that it is early-access and due to change. However, I cannot recommend a rouge-lite game that doesn't offer meaningful incentive to complete more than one run.

What makes this worse and, to me at least, implies that this was intentional is that upgrading gear deletes augment kits from the gear. A LOT of the PvP playerbase was f2p players who would come around a few times per week to play some games, and this group of players is now ~80% smaller because it is so inaccessible and such an unfun and unrewarding grind. What is so bizarre to me about this whole situation is that it would have only taken a few hours of playtesting to realise that augment bolster is necessary. They also removed ranked PvP from the game, which I think has overall damaged the quality of unranked games and removed incentive for a lot of the players who used to keep PvP alive. Gear has never mattered more in PvP than it does now, and gearing has never been more frustrating than it is now.Classes were nerfed in the most invasive and unfun ways. For the entirety of 6.X, hatred was pretty terrible in a lot of ways and never had a solid place in any meta. The only things that made this spec fun were its mobility options, DCDs that could be used offensively for fun and creative purposes, and a fluid DoT spread mechanic. Since 7.0, players have to choose between necessary DCDs (not really a choice because you literally need them) and movement options. SPOILERS BEWARE!Inscryption boasts a beautiful beginning with charming dialogue and wonderfully done atmosphere. Act 1 is a visual treat and, had it been the entirety of the game, would have honestly garnered more love from me. The rules are simple enough to learn quickly, with enough variation and ways to augment your cards that you can play all sorts of different ways. The boss fights in the cabin are lovely, too; the dark aesthetic marries perfectly with the haunting soundtrack, and the mechanics are all perfectly in theme with the boss, as well.Unfortunately, the game drops off quite hard after this. It may be a staple of Daniel Mullin's work, but the meta-fictional plot is unengaging and underwhelming. I'm far more interested in the world inside the game, and I could feel all of my immersion get forcibly torn away each time I was forced to sit through a segment involving 'the real world.' The game's plot and characters suffer for this, in my opinion, as so much time is diverted away from the Scrybes and into Lucas Carder. The fact Luke will occasionally quip in over your gameplay, just after enough time has passed for you to forget he existed, was nothing short of irritating.Act 3, at least for me, wasn't so terrible, though it certainly was /boring/ both to look at and read. The card game, however, was back to being reminiscent of the cabin, and I was pleased to go back to it with a fresh new set of mechanics. This does come with the caveat of the game playing much slower than before, though, so make what you will of it.The half-baked plot concludes with one final stand against each of the Scrybes, though all are cut short. I for one, actually quite enjoyed this! It looked amazing, and gave me a taste of the decks I hadn't really been able to enjoy in the slog of the second act. Unfortunately, as cool as the set piece is, the Scrybes are neutered for plot-reasons and you may only play a few turns with each one before moving on. This segment simply furthered my need for the game to throw away the focus on the metafictional: I would happily play a game going through the worlds of each Scrybe, as you had done with Leshy's cabin, and enjoyed it much more than the actual product.After this, the finale to the plot is... unsatisfying, at best, and honestly, comes off as downright laughable. Why should I care for Lucas Carder, or anything that happens to him? Why should I feel horror at PO-3's actions? What is the truth behind the mysterious card-turned-video-game? I've played other games that leave me turning questions such as these over in my head for weeks afterwards (shoutout to Signalis!), but with Inscryption, I felt no attachment to any of it. Honestly, I wanted the credits to roll faster, so I could get back to playing the cabin card game in Kaycee's Mod.I don't think that Inscryption is bad at a base level. It's a fun game bogged down by terrible writing, leaving a perfectly mediocre experience. But I don't want a mediocre game, I want a game that continues to channel the fun and wonder I had at the start.

2019 Let me preface this review: I don't get to game very much. When I do I enjoy a certain casual pace and a game that's not overwhelmingly detailed. (Basically, if I can't play for a couple months, I don't want to have to relearn how to play.) Don't confuse that for meaning I don't enjoy depth, because I do, but you can have simple mechanics with a lot of depth. I think Northgard succeeds here.So what is it? If you're expecting a "traditional" RTS, this isn't it. It's a pleasant mixture of something more like Civilization and WarCraft. Resourcing, research, trade, and building are very important parts to the game. This is bolstered very nicely by random map generation. I cannot emphasize what a great feature this is.Territorial expansion generally requires holding and expanding your own borders. While there are stealth aspects to attacking opponents, it's pretty much impossible to do something like a Zerg rush early on. That's just not how the game is designed.The main resource in the game is people. You have to expand. You can't buy new soldiers. You have to recruit existing villagers. This is another great dynamic. If you get to aggressive and get wiped out early, you can't just rebuild without cutting down on your production elsewhere.The changing seasons and "map hostility" are other great aspects. You might be ready to expand for some resource that you need or have an invasion planned only to get hit with a blizzard in the winter. It's another great mechanic that makes each game different and forces the player to adapt. Even early on there isn't a standard build order because the resources available on the map and the events that hit you often force reaction.Finally, I haven't played enough to be very objective about how balanced the clans are, but I have seen complaints that they aren't differentiated enough. I cannot disagree with that enough. The core mechanics are mostly the same, but each clan has very different paths to victory and expansion. As such, the pace is slower than something like StarCraft. If you're really into the warfare aspect of an RTS, this probably isn't ideal. Also, it's an RTS. It's not a hybrid RTS like Total War games and it's not Civilization. I think a lot of the negative reviews want this game to lean either more toward RTS warfare or depth of building. I think it strikes a very nice balance.For me, this game is a great balance of so many things and it's available on macOS, which is a big deal. I don't need to be a professional gamer to enjoy it. I don't have to sink tons of hours into it to enjoy it. I can hop online, grab a friend of two, and be done in a couple hours. If you're a working dad, like me, with a lot of obligations outside of your gaming rig, this is probably the most important feature a game can have!

2022 Give this game a chance. At first it totally looks AND feels like watered-down Endless Legend/Civ, but there's kind of an art to its simplicity. What they did cut out, they cut out completely; and what they left, they focused in on. Mechanically the game runs like a well-tuned machine. The combat system is WAY more involved than it let's on, but will feel a bit random until you take the time to figure out the method to the madness.Honestly, the games biggest flaw is that it doesn't explain its mechanics well-enough and what information they do explain is usually buried under different menu chains. Game picks up a lot once you do a good dive or two on the wiki, but play quite a few games with different factions before you do. The wiki is still missing a lot of good info, but the info it does have is makes the depth start to set in.Factions have TONS of flavor and I doubt they are balanced, but no idea. I play this kind of stuff to try each factions and get a few achievements for it. If you want to know about competitive depth, you'll need a different review. But if you want the kind of depth that makes each "run" interesting, this game is fantastic.Each faction also has a challenging storyline that doubles as the ONLY other victory condition to just murder. The storylines still involve a lot of murder however as they often spawn neutral hostile units. Depending on how these units spawn on top of all the random terrain features the possible problems can vary a lot.There's also wandering neutral armies that guard key resources locations and rare army-wide buffs, but ownership is king of the hill style and so only the last person to control the tile actually owns them. 2023 Ok, so, I have mixed feelings on this one. I played this exclusively with one other person, and I played as May.To be totally fair, I understand why this game is as popular as it is. It's got incredible mechanics, there are times where they throw the visual style and take it to gorgeous extremes. It also never gets dull, as the game is constantly throwing new mechanics at you and swapping out the old ones roughly around the time where they outstay their welcome. It does a little too much handholding on the controls for my tastes(yes, for the 100th time, I know F grapples objects), but given the amount of mechanics that this game throws at you, I can totally understand why they decided to tell the players what button does what every time any interaction comes up. The variety of the minigames is also really good and pretty well paced out to give you a break from the campaign nature of the game of going from point A to point B.Now, for the minor downsides. You need to make an EA account to play this, that does annoy me. But it's an EA game, so whatever, I got over it. I initially had some issues launching the game at all, but apparently something went wrong with the initial installation. Uninstalling and reinstalling the game got around that issues and the two of us had very few technical issues throughout the rest of the game. As for some of the sections. I don't understand what control scheme you are supposed to use for this. Both me and my friend used KBM, which I feel really served us well in the shooter portions of this, but some of the isometric and top down sections really did not suit themselves to the KBM control scheme. There were portions where I had to hold down W and tap D to really get the correct average direction to not fall of bridges, not to mention the dash had really weird angles to try and land on the correct platform. My partner also appeared to be having similar problems with the teleporting mechanic, but I can't comment too much on that because I didn't play Cody(and I'm not planning on going back to this to do so).All of that would be fine, and the upsides far outweigh what I've posted so far. The issue is the story. Oh boy the story is... how do I put this? You know that meme that was going around where people would constantly say "Better love story than Twilight"? Well, I can't make any comparisons to Twilight, never saw it you see. But you could take every one of those memes and put the text "Better love story than It Takes Two" and it would absolutely be correct.The story was kind of "meh" at the start. Ok, two people who are getting divorced get Isekai'd into dolls and basically a world created by their past mistakes. We have a weird "antagonist"(although not really? This game doesn't have a true antagonist, which is another problem in of itself) of a book that has them going through challenges to get them back together for love or whatever. They go through and try to figure out how to return to normal. For some reason Cody "figures out" that since Rose's(their daughter) tears caused them to go into this world, they must be the key to get them back, so they run off and try to get their daughter to cry on them so that they can go back to normal. It's a really weird leap of logic and the characters honestly have no reason to assume that this is true. Spoilers from this point on.Then they get to the castle level. Rose has a toy castle that they get to, and they decide the the best way to get Rose to cry is to kill the queen of the castle. Queen Cutie, Rose's toy elephant. They go up to the elephant, and brutally destroy her, limbs ripping off and Cutie begging for her life. This goes on for maybe... 2 minutes or more? All with both players needing to press buttons to continue the sequence. May and Cody are horrific people for doing this, and even if the rest of the story would have been tolerable, it is all soured by the fact that THIS is the first thing that they agreed they should do. They did comment that they felt like horrible people, but neither of them even remotely thought "Hey, maybe we shouldn't be doing this?" and that speaks volumes of their characters. Shocker, Rose's tears don't work, and they are stuck as dolls. They deserve it.And then they go to therapy. It's whatever, probably would be pretty decent if it wasn't completely overshadowed by the previous scene. It ultimately boils down to Cody and Rose need to find their passion or whatever. It's from this point that I will take a break from what is going on to our two "protagonists", and describe how Rose has been seeing all of this. Everything has basically been life as normal for Rose, she's more or less been left all on her own and trying to deal with the fact that her parents are getting divorced. Her age is never stated I don't think, but she's like 10 maybe? Her parents bodies are still in the house, but they are just kinda sleeping for Rose, she's got no idea any of this magic stuff is happening to her parents. She goes to her dad and he's just sitting upright at his desk, just sitting there with his eyes closed. She tells her dad about the book she's gotten and she thinks it would help the marriage. Her dad doesn't respond(for reasons obvious to the players) and Rose eventually leave, but what really stands out to me is that Rose never left the entrance of the room to go and actually see him. This all happened with Rose talking to her dad from the doorway. She eventually leaves the room, but she never approaches her dad. She also does the same thing with her mom as her mom is sleeping on the couch. Rose leaves her alone because her mom must "have that headache again". She does approach her mom to play her favorite song when she finds the vinyl recorder up in the attic, but Rose takes a look at what is going on(and has been going on since almost the start of the game) and makes the conclusion that she is the cause of the divorce and runs away from home. Like what? Ok, I can understand that she's not entirely thinking clearly because her parents told her that they are getting divorced, but shortly after that, both of your parents completely stop responding to the outside world, and she doesn't consider that they might be sick or injured? She has conversations with them were they(from her POV) are *completely* ignoring her and have gone catatonic, and she doesn't think that something is horribly wrong with them? The only way that I would believe that to be true would be if she has been neglected for a very, VERY long time. And that just makes me consider that it might be better if she were to run away to a friend's house or something. At least then she might be able to get some help. Just utterly heartbreaking how this implies what's been going on before the game even started.Returning to Rose and Cody(what? did you think my complaints about the story were done yet? Almost) they are going through therapy, slowly learning to get along again, but the real kicker for me is the final cutscene. It is revealed(or at least HEAVILY implied) that the only way that Cody and May could possibly get back to normal is to kiss. I will be honest, I was furious with the game after that scene. I know somebody who was in an abusive relationship. Like a real life threatening situation she was in. So what, somebody like that is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the situation that this game brings up? Honestly, if some people go through this scenario, the right call could EASILY be to stay that way, and run from your abuser never to return. Once you make it even a few houses over, you would never be found by your so called "partner", and the abuser would effectively be dead in the real world, never to prey on anyone else.It's a real shame. To have such fantastic visuals and mechanics linked to such an abysmally bad story. This game is the worst tragedy I have ever seen in every way.

review: 2021 It's decent..This comes from someone who's played all dark souls games multiple times and finds them them the most enjoyable. Both Sekiro and Souls games are made by FromSoftware. They are so similar, yet so different. While Souls games promote exploration and different play-styles, Sekiro forces you in a somewhat linear path and enforces a certain play-style (strong parry mechanics, with somewhat weak dodge mechanics). In Souls games, I often found myself feeling eager for more content, I always wanted to play more, to see more, to learn more; in Sekiro, I just wanted to get it over with. It doesn't mean Sekiro was a bed experience, it just means it wasn't as good as Souls games offered. While Souls games reward exploration and give a constant sense of progression, Sekiro makes you fight for every inch and punishes you for every mistake you make. Sounds just like our cup of tea, right? We all came for the hardcore experience, to fail a thousand times before finally climbing an obstacle after learning from a bunch of mistakes we made. Well, yes, but no, and this is the part that I strongly dislike about Sekiro.Sekiro punishes death too harshly. If you've played Dark Souls 2, you'll know deaths are not free. When you die in that game, you lose a % of your max health (lowering until ~50%). That health is only restored with Humanity items, a somewhat-rare and finite resource. Although tough, it forces you to always think and remain on your toes. In Sekiro, when you die, you lose half (50%) of your unspent experience points and money. That is not gone, completely irretrievable and lost in the void. While Souls games allow you to retrieve your souls, Sekiro does not. It, instead, uses a dice throw system that decides if you keep your stuff after death, or not, simply be luck. This, so called, "Unseen Aid" is 30%, at most. So, if you're super lucky, there's a 30% chance you don't lose half of your stuff on death, if not, well then, good luck collecting enough stuff to get stronger. On top of that, every time you die, somewhere, an NPC gets sicker, until, eventually, it gets completely sick and receives "Dragonrot". "Dragonrot" lowers your "Unseen Aid" % + locks out some of the dialogues/options in the game. So, now, instead of 30% chance of keeping your stuff, you're down to 8%, which, in my opinion, is beyond common sense. Humanity from Souls games has been replaced by a similar item, only here, instead of doing something beneficial to Sekiro, it heals all those afflicted with "Dragonrot", thus, reverting your "Unseen Aid"% back to 30%.In Sekiro, death basically boils down to you losing 50% of your stuff, thus hindering any sense of progression that the game could have had to offer.Sekiro is not all bad though. It's combat is amazing. The swordplay is the best I've ever seen, the animations are super fluid and the world looks beautiful. It also runs very smooth, just like everything FromSoftware puts out. Some of the boss-fights are the best I've ever experienced in any video game, ever. Most deaths feel like you're own fault and they all allow for a great learning experience.TL;DR: Sekiro is truly an amazing game, both from a visual and gameplay standpoint. Same as all FromSoftware titles, it's incredibly difficult, possibly even more so than Dark Souls on your first runs. Death is punished too harshly and brings nothing enjoyable to the table, it rather takes away a sense of progression and brings frustration. With all it's flaws, it's still a stellar gaming experience and I recommend it highly to all Souls fans out there.

2023 (The Positive part) The game gives you what you expect from a proper quality level-up of the game's previous version of PS2 quality to this day's quality expectations. The game offers much of what previous versions had to offer with more new content. Throughout my gameplay, there was almost nothing from bugs (Only a few) and one-time game crashes which is normal with all games. The game was scary and exciting with the details they gave to the zombies/Monsters as you can expect from Resident Evil. The remake of the game makes the story easier to understand than the original and they added more screen time for the other characters in the game. If you take your time to read the documents/papers around the map you will get a way better understanding of why and how everything ended up as it did there. In the original, most of the map wasn't so much to talk about, but in the remake, the mines have way more to tell, and make some other areas are more open to exploring. The nature part of the game gives great effects that set players up with a feeling of horror when the time goes by in the game.Some of the puzzle parts have been replaced with something less rage-inducing and some other harder for a great reward.You can now aim and move (AT THE SAME TIME) which you couldn't do until the Resident Evil 6 Game and it's great to see in Resident Evil 4 now. Mercenaries mode is not released yet but will come later on as a free post-launch DLC after what the news said. (The Negative part)In some places in the game (for example) when you look the outside of the map towards mountains quality is very similar to PS2 ( https://i.imgur.com/H5kArld.jpg ) A very big change in some of the characters when it comes to appearance, voice, and performance. (Funny part) don't look good if you hit the spacebar too many times too fast. The campaign called (Separate Way) is not in this game right now, if it will come later or not like a DLC, I'm not sure. You can't unlock the PRL 412 in this version of the game.In the original Ashley is in her early 20s, a personality that a teenager would have in such a situation which made her look scared and helpful when needed. In the Remake Ashley looks like she's in her early 30s, a personality that a woman would have in such a situation which looked like she won't go out without a fight.I personally don't like changes to characters that already exist that were already well made, I know it's a remake, but I was hoping this game would be more of a remaster instead. But some changes have to be made to allow the game to fit in with the current vision of the Resident Evil franchise, I guess.(Overall) Would I recommend this game to you? - YesIf you want a good horror story and fight what we don't hope will happen in real-life then this is a great game for you. I still enjoyed the game even if I didn't like some of the changes, but I also loved some of the changes as well (Luis in this game was great, well done!) The gameplay was amazing and I look forward to what else will come later on. If you don't like the remake, you can always go back to the original.

2019 Just finished the game! and o' my good lord!!!Former Fromsoft and souls hater here :) This game is something different and something unique even captivating about it. First of all Sekiro belongs to this world. Sengoku era Japan. That means seemingly endless conflict, ruthless competitions of Daimyos (Warlords), Samurai, Shinobis, clashing armies, disorder, ruin and devastation of a country. However, Fromsoft makes something great with blending the history with Japanese mythology and fantasy elements and forges incredibly rich lore and a solid story. Hats off to you Miyazaki sir!Combat i think the best of the best of the gameplay! When swords start to clash that sound is sing to your ears. It's just so addictive! When in combat exchanging blows, parries, pirouettes, counters, blocks all feel like you're in a real sword fight. By the time you become so focused and so synchronized with your enemy to finish him as a real Shinobi/Samurai. And this is all about. Combat in Sekiro is like dancing to the tune. When you develop your skills and learn new techniques game lets you improvise you in between. Slower, faster, aggressive... Those ways are all situational and they're all needed. And it's all about your playstyle but don't get me wrong. Attack and defence are just two phases to finish your enemy off and you gotta learn when to attack and when to defend to deliver the deathblow. The attack is the best defence and defence is the preparation of your next attack. Game is hard though. I mean really hard! If you lose focus, disrespect your enemy, become greedy and careless you'll die a lot! So, don't let your guard down and don't be overconfident! More techniques and tools just let you only to use more ways to defeat your enemies. They do not make you an invincible killing machine. Not at all. YOU are the weapon and you alone. Each and every boss in-game is well crafted and challenging in their way. They're the ultimate test of your skills. They're mean and cruel and even ruthless but after a great fight and delivering the killing blow is pure gold. The priceless feel of accomplishment i say. Sekiro is not a boss fight game. They all have their own role in the story and their own past and legacy. Sekiro has a fantastic story, its own plot twists, dilemmas, choices. From Samurais to mythical creatures variety and design of enemies are all good. World, varied locations, art direction, musics, environmentals are frankly fantastic. Sometimes so colorful and vivid and sometimes grim dark and creepy. World of Sekiro is simply breathtaking, captivating and haunting! Buy this masterpiece fellow gamers! Even if you're not souls fan (just like me) leave your prejudices aside if you have any. This game is unique and something new and fresh! It's cruel yes, its hard yes, real hard yes but not sadistic. I finished the game with zero cheese, zero cheat & tricks. Fair & square! Yea you do not have to be a Souls veteran to play this game. All you need is focus and patience. That'll be all.And if you love Japanese history and culture, Samurai movies and all boy o' boy!Draw your Katanas gentlemen!

2022 I'll be honest, the game itself is great. Well made, few errors I've ever encountered, a solid if short Solo Mode, honestly one of Konami's best, recent games.The "Gem Economy" is an absolute improvement over Konami's other F2P Yu-Gi-Oh! game. Each pack is double the price of "gems", but gems are far more abundant (at least, they are initially) and easy to obtain (again, initially) without spending anything, and if you're lacking cards, you can get them directly with these little "rarity tokens" you get by breaking down cards of a certain rarity. I will say that getting certain kinds of "tokens" are much harder to get than others, but eh, still an improvement.The primary reason I'm putting it down, and will rarely touch it again, is the same reason I've always put down other Yu-Gi-Oh! simulation games in the past: the people who play it.Don't bother playing a deck you actually LIKE. If you're not running a deck that stops your opponent from doing literally anything and everything, you may as well surrender, because you're sure as ♥♥♥♥ not gonna get a chance to play yourself. That's just not fun. I don't play Yu-Gi-Oh! to NOT play it, nor do I play it to deny other people the chance to play it, but there are way too many people who play the game who do. Because "single-player Duels" = easy wins/advancement, apparently. Who cares about dignity, am I right?If you're of a similar mindset to myself, by all means play the game, just don't touch the Ranked, then become quickly bored once you finish all the Solo Mode has to offer because there's nothing else to do in the game. At the time of writing, anyway. I've heard mention of Events in the future, which if true MAY be enough to draw me back, though I suspect it won't be enough to keep me invested in the long term.If you're okay with substituting Yu-Gi-Oh! for Solitare, hop right in, enjoy screwing over others like the con man you are, and know that I am judging you very harshly.It figures that the only real problem I have with this isn't even Konami's direct fault.EDIT: So Master Duel's first Event came out recently. Honestly, the entire thing is such an excellent summation of Master Duel overall it's not even funny. Excellent concept and well put together (aside from the abundance of connection errors from its first 24 hours, but that got cleared up quick), abundant initial rewards before quickly drying up and drip feeding the rest in the tiniest amounts, and almost entirely let down by the people who play the thing who favour expedient rewards over actually enjoying the damn thing. Though, hilariously, the problem there is the exact reverse of my previous point about the Ranked Mode. Rather than everyone building "don't let your opponent play" decks, people are actually playing decks designed to lose as quickly as possible. Which is honestly just a different form of "don't let your opponent play" in my eyes.If this is the standard we're setting for Master Duel Events going forward, my previous prediction was on the money.

Where there's many simulator-like games on Steam, Crime Scene Cleaner is one of the most polished (in my experience) simulator type games I've ever played. Not only does it present itself as a simulator game, but the developers also made a story to go with it as well. You play as Kovalsky, a janitor by day, mob-hired crime cleaner by night. Needing the extra money for his daughter's treatment, Kovalsky trying his best as a widowed father to ensure that he is able to pay the treatment on time. With the use of environmental storytelling and narration from the protagonist, Crime Scene Cleaner makes each mission far more interesting than every right it has to be. For example, the mission in the prologue/demo, is one of many stories of Kovalsky's journey in the underground crime world, a personal problem that a client created and the protagonist has to deal with. Picking up evidence can tell the players as to what happened prior to the scenes that went down. Personally, some of my favorite missions are the smaller to medium sized ones that told an intriguing story as to why everyone has died in that mission. Although I found at least 80% of the missions enjoyable and the rest of the missions to be alright, there is one mission that I did not particularly find enjoyable. It was the second to last mission in which performances do dip, everything was hard to see due to the no light, and on top of that the level was definitely overwhelming, even more overwhelming than the last mission, despite the last mission taking longer for some reason. It might have to do with always having to pace back and fourth while the last mission in the game basically used its environment to maneuver around its gameplay. Overall, this is the one and only mission that I did not find particularly enjoyable, everything else was excellent or just alright. As for the gameplay, what can I say? It's a simulator game that takes heavy inspiration from Viscera, only that from my own perspective, is far less tedious. This is a great thing for pretty much a wider audience and I like that, but the story bits and the progress that one makes is why I finished this game and is heavily invested into it. The skill tree for cleaning is there too to make cleaning much easier. This game also has a bunch of secrets and easter eggs for you to collect. Such collectables include cassette tapes, which can be played in the background with some decent tunes to it. All varying from lo-fi hip hop, classical music, and rock. The main game for me and 100% all of the levels took me around 14 hours to complete and clocking in around 15-16 hours to get all achievements. The fact there is this much quality, from game performance to story to QoL, gameplay, and audio for the price of $20 USD is flat out insane. I've played games far less interesting and cost more while also having little to no value for what it's worth. Great on the devs for this one. Overall I would say if you like simulator games or you like to relax, this game is a definite must buy! Devs have also confirmed we may be getting free levels in the future and eventually DLC, if they do come out with DLC, I would buy it as soon as I can. I would not recommend this to people who like action or have an urge to stimulate your brain like its on ADHD. But if you go in with an open mind or if you have already played Viscera, this game is a must buy. 9/10 - Worth It!
