Early Access Review The best medieval-ish city builder. I happen to be a historian specialising in the Middle Ages, and games that market themselves as “historically authentic” often leave a lot to be desired as such games often don’t even try to emulate the time period beyond basic aesthetics. Since a lot of the hype around Manor Lords comes from its commitment to historical accuracy, I'll be reviewing it from that perspective. This game, although there is room for improvement, is clearly an earnest attempt to enable players to recreate reasonably authentic medieval towns and villages and gets closer to that goal than any of its rivals. After spending about a dozen hours building a large town, it's very much unfinished but what's there is good. There is currently one map with some RNG elements, such as your starting location and the starting location of a rival lord who also wants this land and whom you will eventually have to fight. You will build houses which can, as was typical in the Middle Ages, have a productive plot of land to the rear for a vegetable garden or household animals like goats or a chicken coop, and the system for building them is intuitive, flexible, and a joy to use. You’ll have to manage trade with off-map settlements as well as maintain a militia to deal with bandits or the rival lord. On the whole, I really like it. There are some issues with the mechanics of the game:1. There is no way (that I can find) to limit the production of certain goods without micromanaging employment. It would be good to say “have a stockpile of 50” like you can in other settlement management games, and like you can with the trading system. I would like to not have to micromanage 14 houses just to regulate what planks are used for. 2. Combat is trivial assuming rough parity between the size of the armies. You have to try to lose a battle to lose a battle. 3. Bandit raids on your village happen off screen a lot of the time. Like, you can’t defend your settlement, you just get a notification that you’ve lost goods to bandits. Let us defend ourselves please, or let us have a bailiff to reign in the thieves. 4. Trade is overpowered, you can get to a point where the player can run the whole settlement through trade. Trade has no risks, so the game steers the player toward relying on trade rather than managing their villages. 5. The rival lord expands far too aggressively, even on its lowest settings. By the time you can claim a single neighboring parcel of land, you’ll be lucky not to have been boxed in completely. The AI takes one parcel a year, there are 8 provinces, and it starts with two while you start with one. This means that by year 5 the AI has the map locked down entirely while you’re still trying to get a decent harvest in. This sucks and is the game’s biggest problem right now. The game has a remarkable ability to enable the player to create authentic medieval town layouts, and you could probably recreate some medieval towns in the game pretty accurately. However, the game seems to be based on central Europe around 1400, so it does tend to lean toward villages and towns from that time and place. While you can emulate, for example, Norman town planning with its focus on commercial high/fore streets, you cannot build a medieval Italian town in this game because plazas are not a thing (yet), while building a village around a central green would be aesthetic rather than the functional heart of the village. This leads on to an area where the game and its commitment to historical accuracy will hopefully improve as development continues, which is forest and land management. In most medieval-ish town planning games (this one included) you put down a logging hut and they just cut down trees, then a forester plants new trees. This is not how medieval people generally managed their woodland, if only because it’s remarkably inefficient prior to mechanised forestry. Although the villages are historically authentic, the same effort has not been put into those villages’ relationship with the land (yet). Some suggestions:1. Coppicing. Coppicing was the practise of cutting a tree down to the stump to stimulate the growth of shoots around the stump, essentially tricking one tree into growing many trees. This would result in a large amount of harvestable wood within 7-10 years. However, the shoots were vulnerable to being eaten by deer.2. Pollarding. The same idea as coppicing, but it’s done about 2m up the tree trunk. You get less wood that’s harder to access, but deer won’t eat it. 3. Deeper deer management. Of course, if deer keep eating everything you could just kill all the deer. Deer culling was (and still is) an important part of forestry. Although the game does have deer management it is as simple as “don’t over-hunt”. It would be good to see this expanded to reflect the real world impacts of deer overpopulation or underpopulation.4. Wolf management. When creating new villages, they often encroached on the habitats of wolves. Wolves don't usually attack people, but if they get used to human contact and become habituated, they do. A mechanic for wolf packs similar to deer migration (except rather than going further away when bothered, they attack) might work well. It would be nice to fight something other than the tropey RNG bandit camp. It’s got a lot of promise, I’m sure I’ll enjoy sinking hundreds of hours into it over the years, but you might want to wait a year or so until it’s further along development.

A solid CRPG for genre veterans, probably not a good first CRPG however. Not without some major speedbumps though. My first playthrough took 90 hours.High quality writing for both characters and atmosphere. Does a great job of immersing you in the W40k world, and characters have a lot of personality.Combat has a basic cover system along with with the standard grid based, initiative order mechanisms. There is a LOT of fighting so you'll be doing a great deal of it. The fun in the combat system comes from pulling off insane gear/class combos int order to stack massive damage modifiers, giving yourself extra turns or building other game breaking combinations. There is a huge variety of class abilities, not to mention special gear, so there is a lot of room for build crafting. The combos you can pull off mean the only way the AI can catch up with you is massive HP pools. Even on normal, late game enemies have massive HP reserves compared to your party, and the fights still aren't hard because you can alpha strike way harder than the AI can. Between cover and some basic defensive abilities, the AI could rarely even hit my characters, though when it did, you don't have much of a HP pool to work with. It is hard to deny though that it's fun to build up combos and unleash massive burst attacks of all crits and watch those numbers pop.The number of talents available on most level ups and the interactions between all of your class abilities makes leveling up a very confusing affair. I was constantly left wondering if I was using my abilities/build to a relatively full extent because of how many different triggered abilities there are that interact with each other. Then take into account leveling up all of your companions and I sort of dreaded opening up the level up screen, which isn't great because you can get to over level 50 which means a LOT of time spent staring at the sea of talents and skills.The economic system gets rid of basic currency but then gives you an building minigame instead. The minigames give some additional story content on top of resource management, but it usually felt like a time suck more than anything else. Skipping it robs you of a lot of rewards, which may annoy you if you don't care for the resource management but don't want to be underpowered.Inventory system is a bit of a nightmare. Biggest QOL issue for me.Worth a play if you don't mind really putting your head into a game, and has plenty of replay value.

2023 Despite the concerns about the map being small, it actually is quite large despite covering a smaller geographic region. The lack of Mesopotamia is disappointing and I do hope that could be added in the future. The high density of settlements helps, and the outpost system adds more depth to the map. With outposts both facilitating movement of armies and able to provide additional garrisons to settlements among other bonuses they become higher priority targets when trying to conquer a region. This makes it so that instead of beelining settlement to settlement more careful planning is needed to take out the outposts (and outpost forts actually need to be laid siege to and captured) before capturing the settlement itself. It takes time for other systems to start opening up in the game as well, the deity, court and civil war, and legacy systems all open up over the first 20 or so turns, so some people may not have even played long enough to get to those. And after that is when more and more of the outside raiders arrive, Kaska are around from the start, but more come in, and so do Phrygians, Libu, various Sea Peoples, etc., which play into the need to build outposts to facilitate movement because the player needs to react to Sea Peoples suddenly plopping down an army on their shore. The multi-resource economy feels decently balanced, with until a larger area is controlled trade being needed to maintain enough resources to keep an army going while also developing settlements. Battles unfortunately do have some flaws of more recent TW with how quick they go down, and units sometimes being sticky. The new additions of higher quality units being able to make fighting withdrawals though is great and more tactics like this should be added in the future, just this opens up a lot more possibilities when previously to try to accomplish the same a unit would have to become fully disengaged and turned around. As for historical accuracy, CA does play a bit loose with timeline and relations. For Egypt at this time the succession was a mess and in chaos itself with rulers often in power for only a few years at a time, so CA does a reasonable job at trying to represent it in the style of a TW. For the Hittites though, Kurunta is a fair bit past his time (which I guess is why he is depicted as being so old in the game), Hartapu would make more sense ruling in Tarhuntassa (which as a side note is a lost city but CA does a decent job placing it based on the various locations academics have theorized it could be), as Hartapu is mentioned in an inscription by Suppiluliuma as having ruled Tarhuntassa.

2022 Product received for free OOOooohhhh Elden Ring Elden Ring is a game developed by the folks over at From Software, and directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, a man who started taking more pictures of himself rubbing his chin and looking thoughtfully into the distance after Dark Souls came out.And also Yui Tanimura, but the joke doesn't work if I mentioned them as well. You play as the Tarnished, someone who had lost grace with the Erdtree and banished from the Lands Between. But now everything has gone to the toilet so now you're being beckoned back to fix everything because of course you are. And so you embark on an adventure to become the Elden Lord, and put everyone who stands in your way into the dirt.Elden Ring, also known as Big Dark Souls, is an action RPG with combat and themes similar to previous Fromsoftware games from 2009 onward. Not Armored Core, though, you don't get a new one of those. I don't know how I can explain combat outside of you try to not die and smack things with a sword/axe/spear/club or light them on fire, or turn their bones to dust, or hit them with an arrow or crossbow bolt. You got a lot of options for murder via self defense in this game. Unlike previous games, Elden Ring is flat out an open world instead of a larger, connected one. You spend a lot of time hoofing it on foot or via mount to get to where you want to go. The main theme is exploration here, since the game doesn't tell you where you have to go.It just SHOWS you where you have to go. With large, noticeable landmarks and even a little arrow created by the Grace that says “This way, stupid.” There are no check markers or anything like that, but you can manually mark areas on your map so you don't lose your way. Area's are distinct and unique from one another, and the draw distance goes so far that you can see and keep track of landmarks from great distances.What I'm trying to say is you have to actively be trying to not know where to go. Bosses go anywhere from a total blast to a complete slog, though I'm pretty sure it changes depending on what build you're going for. There are bosses I had to cave and summon a friend for, but most of them you can probably just fight through if you're willing to adapt. But its always funny to just be minding your own business when some regular dude with a sword shows up specifically to start problems. Elden Ring is kind of the perfect Dirk simulator, as in you wander in random directions and pick fights with strangers. I liked -most- of the areas I had to go through, and finding catacombs was also fun for the time I was actively seeking them out. There are some things I don't like, though.For one, it feels like the enemies are pulling some fighting game crap and reading my buttons sometimes, although I don't know how true that actually is or if its just me being paranoid. There's also a gross reuse of certain bosses, forcing you to fight the same dude a couple of times. But sometimes their stronger! OR THERE ARE TWO! Either way, it can be disappointing. Also, this might just be a Dirk thing, but I was hoping all the underground stuff would be longer. Once I found the ant hill that led to a ruined city I was hooked. It does that thing where the deeper you go the more messed up everything gets, especially with the implications and other horrid ♥♥♥♥ you can find down there.Elden Ring, in a sense, was the Dark Souls game I wanted. Big world, lots of stuff to hit with a sword, and random dungeons I can just explore and rob. Its probably not my favorite game of 2022, but its up there. Oh my god, its 2022. There's nothing I can say about this game that hasn't been said before. I wish it wouldn't randomly stutter at times, and From really needs to work on its online exploits and balances. Its fun to explore, fight, and its fun to play with friends, so if those are all your check boxes, then hey, good to go!Elden Ring gets 9 Names that are too similar out of 10.Special, big boy hugs and kisses thanks to ViceVerscant for gifting me Elden Ring while I was picking through garbage to find Burger King Coupons. Early Access Review Review of Manor Lords: A Historian’s Perspective on Historical Accuracy and Gameplay As a historian specializing in the Middle Ages, I often scrutinize games that tout historical authenticity. Manor Lords, celebrated for its commitment to creating authentic medieval environments, presents a unique opportunity to examine its fidelity to the period. After a dozen hours spent constructing a large town, here are my detailed thoughts. Historical Authenticity Strengths: Manor Lords impressively approaches the recreation of medieval towns and villages. The intuitive building system allows for the construction of houses with rear productive plots—typical of the Middle Ages—for vegetable gardens and small livestock like goats and chickens. This feature not only enhances the game’s authenticity but also enriches the player’s engagement with medieval town planning. Limitations: Despite its strengths, the game's representation is predominantly centered around Central Europe circa 1400. This focus limits the ability to replicate town planning from other regions, such as Norman commercial streets or Italian town squares. Additionally, while the architectural elements are well-rendered, the relationship between villages and their surrounding landscapes could be improved. Current forestry management practices in the game do not accurately reflect historical methods like coppicing or pollarding, which were more sustainable and efficient. Gameplay Mechanics Building and Resource Management:The flexible building system is a highlight, yet the resource management aspect lacks depth. For instance, there is no simple way to limit production of certain goods without micromanaging each house, which detracts from the strategic aspects of village management. Combat and Threats: Combat mechanics are overly simplistic, and bandit raids often occur off-screen, which removes a layer of interaction and defense strategy. The game could benefit from allowing players to actively defend against these threats or manage them through appointed village officials like a bailiff. Economic Model: The trade system, while robust, is disproportionately powerful and risk-free, which skews gameplay towards trade dependency rather than balanced village management. This aspect could be recalibrated to offer a more realistic and challenging economic environment. AI Competitiveness: The AI for the rival lord is overly aggressive, even on lower settings, leading to frustrating gameplay where the player feels unfairly boxed in. This needs balancing to allow for more strategic growth and competition. Suggestions for Improvement Enhanced Land Management: Implement historically accurate forestry practices such as coppicing and pollarding, and introduce more nuanced wildlife management, including deer and wolf interactions that reflect historical realities.Combat and Security Enhancements: Enable on-screen defenses against bandit raids and more complex strategies for village protection.Balanced Economic Systems: Introduce risks and challenges to the trading system to prevent it from overshadowing other aspects of village management. Conclusion Manor Lords is a commendable endeavor in the medieval city builder genre, offering a more historically authentic experience than many of its contemporaries. While there are areas ripe for improvement, particularly in land management and economic balance, the game’s foundation is solid. It is likely to provide many engaging hours of gameplay, especially as it continues to develop. Potential players may want to wait for further updates that address current limitations, but the game already stands as a strong entry in the genre.Keep on doing your best!

2016 I've played all of the Souls games, including Demon's (although never finished it to the very end). Ever since I first played Dark Souls years ago, I fell in love with the franchise. It was the first Souls experience to me. That game showed me that games can still be very challenging, with amazingly well made fantasy worlds including all sorts of nightmarish creatures. Dark Souls 3 continues the epicness the earlier ones had. I love this game, even if some moments felt impossible or quite frustrating lol. It has much of the same old gameplay mechanics from previous games, but with new additions too and the combat is mostly fast-paced.I feel like it's a great mix of Dark Souls and Bloodborne, without the dash-dodge of BB. The world itself in Dark Souls 3 is amazing in my opinion, not as well made as the perfect design in Dark Souls with those upper and lower journeys, which is the best in the series. But it's still really cool and you can basically go visit every place you see in the distance eventually. That's one thing I love about these games, to feel like you actually are in this huge unkown mysterious world. As previous games, DS3 doesn't hold your hand. You have to figure out where to go, how to fight enemies and bosses, learn their weakness and patterns to win and death will teach you again.There were few areas or enemies which I didn't like so much because of reasons, but that is a part of these games. I do love how DS3 pays tribute to DS1 in few ways, but I won't go into more detail about that.The soundtrack is soooo fantastic and introduces many cool songs, which fit well in the intense boss fights to make them even greater :D.New monster design is mostly amazing, as I said it reminds me of Bloodborne with certain opponents. Also some of the monsters feels like, as if they were taken inspiration from Berserk manga again as the creator is a fan of it, which is of course really great. I have to say that the boss design and fights are some of the best I have ever encountered, there are many memorable ones and at least 3 were really tough to me. One of the bosses felt a bit disappointing because of the way to defeat it, but was still so cool. I think I did every boss fight as solo, except one. And when you do it alone, the feeling and adrenaline rush is so much greater. The last boss of DS3 could very well be the hardest fight I've ever fought in games and I loved that, even harder than Artorias of DS1. Part of it could be because having a different build than in previous games so it honestly felt impossible, I dunno. But oh boy...it was just insane and such a thrilling fight. Lots of suffering, but eventually when you survive alone these kind of encounters, that feeling of victory is so good. I don't think many other games give that satisfaction and this is one big reason I love the Souls games. Fighting alone in the dark places, against a gigantic or just ultra aggressive bosses is simply one incredible feeling.The multiplayer is similar to DS1. When you summon friends for co-op, they can help you on the road a long time or help kill a boss which is nice. Not badly done like in DS2 where you disappear after killing a couple enemies. I've read many being disappointed with the game, like having connection issues or getting banned for no reasons. Which sucks. But I personally barely had any issues as my Chloe in my 60h+ journey, there was perhaps only 5-6 times when I couldn't enter boss fog door to help a fellow player after he summoned me. Because of connection lag, but that's it.Well it seems I ended up writing more than I first planned :). I say Dark Souls 3 is definitely a worthy send-off to the franchise, as it is informed to be the last one. An epic dark journey and amongst my most favorite experiences ever. I recommend this to those who want to experience challenging and really cool gaming moments. For fans of Souls it's a must.10/10

review: 2021 I've put in hundreds of hours and nearly every save I start ends around turn 40 for the same reason: It's dull.TLDR: Interesting and meaningful choices are lacking and repetitive, arcadey gameplay robs the game of much of its potential.Regardless of character, faction, or map location the gameplay loop endlessly repeats. With recruitment tied to general type and level there is little sense of infrastructure within your territory. There's no need to recruit from specialized troop training regions, or march your armies to get outfitted at a master armorer in which you've been investing for many turns (unless you truly care about the very marginal percentage increases all but the highest-level improvements offer). The armies are all samey, with the limited engine turning battles into an uninteresting slog. Shogun 2 and Empire are other Total War games that feature similar unit rosters across factions, but the key difference between those games and 3K is that the basic units in the older games can utilize multiple different tactical skills (e.g. melee/bayonet for Empire line infantry and the yari wall for the spear Ashigaru in Shogun) besides the basic attack that offers tactical flexibility and interesting choices. 3K offers none of this. Ji infantry have one attack: right click and hope that they hold the line. The sword units and ax units theoretically offer variety but these are cut down by hero units, against which these units have no advantages. The only unpredictable aspect of combat is discovering exactly how the enemy cavalry will suicide-charge through your rear to get to your archers - usually well-ahead of the army and completely unsupported. A counter charge by one or two hero units usually ends this threat - the only threat - and allows the battle to proceed in identical fashion to the dozen others before. Hero units appear varied but only act so when using their special abilities, otherwise each is the same as the next apart from minor damage variances. Sun Ce plays exactly like Lu Bu, Liu Bei like Cao Cao, and Kong Rong like any other anonymous newgen strategist character. They're single entity versions of the general's bodyguard unit in any other historical TW game wearing a rock-paper-scissors themed costume. The abilities aren't even that interesting because most are shared within a hero's class and are only reached after spending upgrade points on perks shared across classes. Each character comes with a "unique" trait but most only manifest if said character is faction leader, heir, or prime minister (a late game court position) so these functionally never impact the game for recruited lords.Managing the economy is painfully simple and needlessly complex at the same time. Most of the buildings are worthless - a high level garrison, as an example, that debuffs enemy supplies is too expensive to build quickly enough to be of use in frontline cities and entirely unnecessary in your central core unless your campaign has already fallen apart at the seams - while others require city sizes larger than most territories need or can support, leading to spells where building new structures is vital but also impossible. At a certain point in most games money becomes trivial, especially after conquering AI territories with maxed-out settlements. The AI generally generates money faster than you but units are cheap - since units are tied to a general's level most AI generals don't have enough experience to recruit better, more expensive units - so the investment goes into their economy. Conquering a moderately-sized opponent's land can double your income, and by turn 80 you can expect a per turn income of several thousand at minimum. Decisions about what-to-build-where become irrelevant because you don't have to weigh consequences. Upgrades go from requiring careful timing to trivially consequential. Some factions, notably the bandit and Nanman, have buildings that supply special unit recruitment, but these influence the global recruitment pool rather than local. A Nanman general in newly-conquered Han territory could suddenly recruit literal tigers despite being in the plains of central China simply because a new building was built hundreds of kilometers away. I'm not griping about authenticity or hIsToRiCaL aCcUrAcy but rather the fact that the structure of the economy and the battle systems are such that you are thrust ceaselessly into a grind of "custom battle"-like encounters. No battles feel decisive because of the endless pool of newgen generals from which to recruit and the ability for whole units to respawn and re-muster if the general survives to retreat or flee back into the faction court. If I defeat a unit of Cao Cao's Leopard and Tiger cavalry in battle it should feel like an accomplishment, and I shouldn't see them return a few turns later at full health like Team Rocket. Losing elite units, and especially elite armies, should be devastating to a faction. This would highlight the strengths of factions that focus on large armies filled with cheap units (e.g. Liu Bei) and heighten the tensions for factions based around elite, tide-turning units (e.g. Ma Teng). Killing your way through a noble's court should leave them weakened, panicked, and desperate. Limiting the vassalage diplomacy option to only high-level lords removes an interesting gameplay option to resolve minor border disputes early game, and by late game your empire size provides enough of a debuff that most factions refuse without significant compensation - if they are willing to negotiate at all! You would think a game set in an age of intrigue and self-serving tyrants would allow the player and the AI to place self-preservation as a priority, but most lords prefer to suicide-war with you than negotiate. In older Total War games killing through the family had devastating effects on a faction's administration and survival. In 3K no amount of filial destruction results in greedy heirs tearing a realm apart, or rival factions usurping a ruling family's claim to secure power and survival. If the history of the Three Kingdoms period played out like the game depicts the Sima family would never have gained control! You can't tout your diplomacy and politics systems when Rome 2 and Attila have more consequential political systems.This game has all the hallmarks of a modern Total War title: a veneer of advanced mechanics and depth covering a repetitive, arcadey core that lacks interesting and meaningful choices. Many of the consequential faction dynamics of older historical titles is done away with in favor of court mechanics that have little impact beyond draining your treasury, and simplified battle and economic systems present dull, obvious choices to the point that attempts at deviations actively cripple your save. I wish I hadn't pumped so many hours into this game searching for something interesting.

2021 So I played the game for 100 hours so I could get an honest review of it instead of playing it for 5 and saying it is trash or not playing it enough for me to notice it's critique. I will compare this game to other RPG's or similar games. If you want a summary of this review I will write it at the bottom of this review along with the reviews of the DLC's but on to the start. INTRODUCTION: My Fallout Experience (the 1000 word essay) on how this game is greatWe have all heard of "Fallout New Vegas" and I, as many others have been taught or shown across the internet is that this is the definitive best fallout game. So after some time I decided to get the game with all it's DLC's and decided that I would check out the game and see if all the hype was concrete or was just fallout fans with rose tinted glasses.I start of with installing and starting the game and realizing that it is completely uncompatable with windows 10. This may be on Bethesda's part as I know fallout 3 has this exact issue as well. So my journey begins in the mod manager and .ini files to enable more memory usage. But after these fixes the game only crashed twice throughout my whole 100 hour playthrough. (The mods included in my mod list have no effect on the game but only made it crash less and fix memory usage)So I start of with an amazing introduction to the main factions and the story taking place in Fallout New Vegas from the get go by a aged but still good cinematic. Comparing it to the Fallout 4 cinematic I would say this one introduces alot more of the world to the player compared to the black and white war scene all about "war never changes". I start of the game with making my character. In comparison to other RPG's like Skyrim (or Fallout 4) this game truly gave you the tools to make your own character. Everything from the wacky dialogue options to actual things that could impact your gameplay is decided from what S.P.E.C.I.A.L points, skills and perks you picked. This really made it feel like your decisions mattered from the get go. So I get on my mary way out on to the Majave wasteland and instantly get hit with this massive world to explore but I follow a long the main story and talk to "Easy Pete" and get introduced to these amazing dialogue options. Comparing it to other Bethesda games they were truly fleshed out and you could totally make sense of the conversation when you could actually read a sentance that your character would say instead of a few words or "yes" and "no".At this point I also get introduced to the Karma system where bad and good actions could impact your late game stats. As I get hit with these intrequet systems that I would say are pretty overwhelming if you don't expect it or are not used to RPG's or other roleplaying games I also discover the grave sight and see a grave. You can dig a grave but only if you have a shovel, so I go to the little ponsy shop in Goodsprings right next to the grave sight and buy a shovel. With this I had made an impact on my gameplay through my choices and ended up with a laser rifle. A mid game weapon at level 2. When this happened I knew I was gonna have a good time with this game. I made my way and thought I would make my way to the big glowing tower that is the "Lucky 38" and boy did I get turned into shreds by those deathclaws. Facing the strongest enemy in the game and it not feeling like a cake walk like in a later released fallout game. It showed me where my place was which was killing powder gangers and thugs after I got my ass beat by every abomination I came across. It set a milestone for me to get through that valley and kill those radscorpions that plagued me when I left goodsprings. The game made me feel like I was in for a journey, a journey that was mine to make and my choices mattered. Here the characters, the voice acting, the effects. They were lasting and they did change the story for my character which made the game so much more enjoyable. After my introductions to the game as a whole I got to know the factions in the game a little more and if I were to summarize them I would describe them as such. The Legion are the "bad guys" who are misogynistic, dog ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, twink boy-toy slave owners that base themselves on the ideals of the roman enthusiast Ceasar. Then we have the NCR (New Californian Republic) the "good guys" who traveled into New Vegas to help the citizens and by "help" they mean help the areas with recources they need.SUMMARY: GAMEPLAY:The game held up to the expectations I was expecting which was shocking as I went into the game thinking "this game is the best RPG I have ever played". But it truly is the best RPG I have ever played and the best RPG on my game list. I love all the elements of this game and how your actions can impact the games surroundings and that your choices matter for the story and in general gameplay.COMBAT:The gun play is simple yes, yet satisfying and a lot of perks you learn compliment the experience. Melee is simple and don't involve more complex combat except block and swing but it is satisfying turning a ghoul's head into mash potatoe. STORY:The main story has a simple premise but has complex solutions as you can shape the ending of the game however you deem fit which is something truly rare in games these days. Even story telling games don't dwell into your choices mattering this much for the outcome of the story.SOUND/MUSIC:If you don't turn on the radio in this game you are truly missing out on some bangers I am telling ya, but seriously the sound design in this game is as everything else truly masterful. You will have to explore the vaults and everything else with it's matching soundtrack that either puts shivers down your spine, makes you enticipate what combat scenario is next or makes you jam in out in the lobby halls of the casinos.GRAPHICS:Now this game is 10 years old so I didn't wanna slack on it too hard but even some games that came out the following year looked a lot better than this. But the graphics are not too bad, they are still good especially by 2010 standards and give more of a Fallout feeling to it all. Something about the graphical design of New Vegas just give more of a rustic run down wasteland sort of feeling with its orange tones but that might just be me.DLC'S:I really enjoyed 3/4 DLC's which were. Old World Blues, Honest Hearts, Lonesome Road. If you are playing New Vegas these DLC's are a must play in my opinion as they are truly great DLC's. Dead Money on the other hand did not hit home for me as many others. But if you like dialogues with character building and clues of a mystery to solve and puzzles I can see how you would enjoy this DLC as well.ARCHITECHTURE:The buildings just look great, you know what they are supposed to be and in what conditions. You know what buildings stand out and which ones you can enter apart from some instances.THE BAD:Now there are alot of great things with this game that is for sure, like how great the RPG elements are and so on. But there is a few bad things, like how the game isn't functional from the get go and that you have to manually fix it. There is also the landscape which has some unique parts like red rock canyon and the area around the strip that look notorious and when you are there you know exactly where you are. 2020 Season of the PatheticTL;DR at bottomThere is a lot to unpack with this disappointment of a game. To start off, Destiny 2 used to be great, but it started to go downhill (so fast in fact that you'd think it actually fell off a cliff)since the Shadowkeep expansion. It used to have amazing gunplay and it felt great to use all kinds of weapons. Now however, Bungie is essentially a mad scientist that constantly nerfs everything that the player can use. Which has led to a point where now everything feels weak to use and no longer satisfying. Whenever they do buff something, they inevitably undo that buff because now everyone was using the only good weapon. I no longer care for grinding new weapons, nothing feels good to use anymore and it feels pointless to get new weapons or grind god rolls for older weapons if they're gonna be useless in the future.There is a lot of content in the game, but somehow, they've managed to make it boring with how the quest system is designed. Every quest you get will be repeating the same kind of activities. Kill X enemy 50 times, do X public event 10 times, do X matches 10 times, search X place again. There are some quests that mix things up a little bit, but those are far and few in-between and still follow the do X 20 times. And then there's the very unsatisfying end-game content.Content in this game is wasted. There's no point in doing older things, which is a good and bad thing at the same time. But whenever new content is added now, it gets removed 3 months later. Because of that, it adds pressure for me and others to complete it all ASAP. We want to do everything ASAP because we want to experience what is offered and experiment with what is available. If we don't do everything ASAP, there isn't enough time to earn what Bungie has temporarily unlocked in the final weeks and it'll be removed eventually. We'll never again get the chance to earn certain loot. It's not fun having that pressure. It's nothing but FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out). The end game is a joke and is a waste of time. Your weapon selection for end game PvE activities is heavily limited, you don't get a chance to use some of the only fun weapons you like. End-game PvP, Trials of Osiris is nothing but hackers, is unrewarding, constant connection issues (which is a problem with the whole game) and disconnected from a game equals a loss and temp ban. The PvP can be fun however, learning how to play using your abilities effectively and learning the weapons. Unfortunately, the competitive game modes are not fun because of what I mentioned before.End-game PvE content is a mixed bag. Raids and Dungeon are absolutely fun, I love the sense of teamwork and players helping other players learn how to do the raids and activities. I do like the idea of the endgame Nightfalls (except for how they've handled the new Grandmaster difficulty) and the new champion enemies added. Unfortunately, the new enemies are monotonous, being practically invincible to all weapons type except what bungie want you to use for that season. Weapons I find fun to use are worthless, making the gameplay loop crap because what I find fun to use isn’t allowed.Speaking of the gameplay loop of this game, all I can say is "o'god, give me a break". Bounties, bounty after bounty after bloody bounty. Do X amount of bounties to get a reward, do X number of kills with weapons you don't like, do X number of streaks in PvP. It's always the bloody SAME! Just over and over again. What was the definition of insanity? To get rewards that progress your character, you have to do mind-numbing activities and bounties constantly, which makes the game boring and repetitive. You do get lots of loot, and you can say that's good, but in reality, it's quantity over quality. The amount of crap that you get is stupid. Almost all weapons and armour that you pick up in the world is utterly useless and waste more of your time. You'll be constantly destroying what you pick up because it's worthless and doesn't progress you in any way.The good elements of this game are the world itself. The environments are great and you can always tell where you are, what planet you're on. Not much ever looks the same. The music is great, the game visually looks great and some exotic weapons may be fun. There is a lot of lore in this game that you can explore and inevitably get disappointed in because those stories will never be touch again by the devs. Character armour is a mixed bag, some things look badass and epic, while others look like an absolute joke and are vomit-inducing. But because how this game has to be played, it'll all become boring, repetitive and unrewarding, which is unfortunate because there are some things that are great.TL; DRThis game is pointless, pathetic, unsatisfying and ultimately a waste of time. Since Shadowkeep, it has been rapidly going downhill with bare bone content releases that add up to nothing. New content added will be removed in 3 months, never having any real impact to the game world. Meta is constantly changing every few months, so you never get a chance to truly master a build/playstyle. Anything remotely fun to use is nerfed, any buff added to weapons are inevitably reverted. 2023 I enjoyed this game, however there are a couple of things that make the experience SO much more balanced and fair that the game doesn't tell you. In fact, I think most people who quit did so because they didn't realize how the combat system is actually supposed to work.Basically, you can block AND deflect at the same time. That's the magic that makes the game playable, but the game NEVER will tell you this. It tells you that you can block, and that you can deflect. And if you are coming from basically any other game, you would intuitively think that you have to choose one or the other. That's often how it works, especially if you are coming from a Soulsborne game. But in this game, if you aren't blocking at all times, YOU WILL DIE. Once you learn that you can hold block at all times and still deflect, the game will click for you and feel much less punishing.The other important tip is to never use dodge, unless you're dodging forward to mikiri counter. The dodge distance is so small that you don't really get out of enemy attack range with it, and you have a laughably small amount of i-frames. So 90% if you dodge to evade an attack, you will just get slapped and lose half HP. It is possible to dodge through attacks with i-frames, but we are talking something small like 2 frames. It feels very tight, so it's really never worth trying.That being said, it's still very challenging. Any encounter with multiple enemies is basically death if you try to engage them at once. Not unlike a Soulsborne game, you will want to use stealth or kiting to eliminate groups. The posture system ensures that even by holding block at all times you can still get killed fairly easily if you aren't hitting your deflects.My main gripe with this game is the overworld. It's semi-open, but everything kind of just blurs together and there isn't as much of a reward for exploration because most of the loot is just random bobbles that you will never use. Such as buffs to finding spirit emblems (these are practically infinite items, WHY even let you buff this??), buffs to finding sen, etc. Because the game doesn't have weapons or armor as loot, you rarely find anything that sparks joy or excitement. The best thing you can find early-mid game are bags of sen, but even those are rare. All in all, it's a great experience and doesn't overstay its welcome. I think a sequel or spiritual successor could do very well.

2023 As an old gamer that played the Diablo series from the very first game, but mostly the second game, I am very much enjoying this bleak, desaturated, dreadful version of Sanctuary. Diablo 3 in contrast felt more cartoony to me, I cleared it and then not much else.I'll list what makes this game stand out to me, then mostly compared to Diablo 2, with me only having cleared the first act in this game.Convenience, incredible amounts of convenience. No potion belt, you have charges, no mana potions, you have skills that generate or consume your resource, all crafting material goes into a separate inventory, you see elites on the minimap, quest tracking with path finding, no stat points to distribute but just levels. This might be almost too much convenience, but at this point in my life, I'm happy.Quests, there is so much to do. I remember having at the most six quests per act in Diablo 2, and now only the first area has 38 side quests. There is a lot of things to do, which sure can be samey, go there kill that, but after all that is mostly what Diablo is about so I'm enjoying it. Supposedly there are six acts, and the amount of side quests increase, so this will keep me busy for quite some time.Gamepad support. As it were, I played Diablo 3 for many hours straight when it came out, and that gave me basically a persistent RSI in both hands. So I have a rocky relationship with the third installment even if I love the series. I got to try the PS3 version of Diablo 3 at DreamHack, and I loved how that played, and asked if we would get that on PC but was told no, thus I did not play more Diablo 3. To my delight, the gamepad experience in this game is stellar. The auto-targetting might feel a bit like cheating, but at this point I see it as an accessibility feature for someone like me who is physically uncomfortable playing with a mouse.Graphics. That said, I have been playing mostly scrappy indie titles for the last decade and more, due to feeling AAA was mostly samey rehashes and endless sequels, so I'm awfully out of date and not acclimatized to current AAA graphics. I am very happy looking at this game, and the gritty, grimy, earthy, feel of it.All in all, I'd say this feels like a mix between classic Diablo and World of Warcraft. The questing very much feels like WoW, although not as tedious, and some events will have other players randomly pop in, to my surprise and initial annoyance, but I've gotten used to it and now like seeing what other classes can do. Disabling and enabling my default device and then entering the audio options has been a fix so far.If I could wish for something, it would be stereo 3D output in some shape or form, so I can play this on a virtual desktop in VR with perfect separation. That is basically what I now dream about while playing this game, me having been a VR fanatic for more than a decade, getting depth and scale in almost everything I play that has 3D graphics. I'll still play this as is though, evidently.

Early Access Review Wonderful and upbeat game! Exactly what I needed for a farming game fix, down to the cozy vibes and the soft music. The 90's anime art style mixed with classic RPG graphics and fantasy story telling is so charming and something I don't see a lot of anymore, and the character designs are fantastic! There's so much variety in the NPCs and how they act, it reminds me of a anime I'd catch on a Saturday morning or a fondly remembered GBA game. And I mean that in all the best ways.Speaking of the NPCs, I've had an issue with farming/country life sims lacking in a lot of character interaction lately. A lot of farming games feel they don't put a great deal of writing into the NPCs and may story beats can feel bland, so this game has been a breath of fresh air! The NPCs are very well written with their own little character arcs each. I've played for a full in-game year and I've just now realized how little I run into looping dialogue, even from NPCs I talk to once a day. They have multiple things to say at different times of the day and love to comment on any new things that happen around the town. It does wonders to make the world feel that much more lived in! My main criticism is that at times, the farming feels a little secondary to all the other things you can do. And the monster encounters in the mines can feel pretty clunky to fight. Other than that, the only other issues mostly comes from the issues that come from it being so early access. There's a clear dev wall I've reached after about an in-game year of playtime, and sometimes I get a screen-tearing issue when my character moves around. But for a game that only entered early access a month ago, the amount to do and how well the game runs is fantastic. I can't recommend this enough if you like cozy farming games.

2023 I don't think I can praise this game highly enough. You don't even need to start playing to see the flavor and style that permeates every bit of the game. It's beautiful and silly and every bit of text and art keeps that feeling, whether you're reading one of the many text logs that build the world's lore, taming one of the many creatures present in the game's universe, or dealing with a disaster befalling your base.And disaster will fall, but it never feels random, unpredictable, or unfair. While some survival games start tough as nails but eventually allow the player to reach a point where they are invincible, even 300 in-game days into a save I've found myself facing a new dilemma, frequently of my own creation. Progressing well with your technology and have machines manufacturing everything your characters need? Now you're generating heat that can kill off nearby crops, leading to a food shortage. Find a vent that generates unlimited water? It might also be too hot or cold and damage your characters. Accidentally create a web of piping for your colony's multiple toilets, sinks, and showers that causes a backup of 'polluted water' and renders all that plumbing unusable? Your colonists will drown in their own filth and become ill. There are no random earthquakes, invasions, or other disasters that cause your colony to fall to the winds of chance. You are always the disaster, and overcoming each of the trials that befall your colony feels immensely rewarding and gratifying.ONI never holds your hand, but it gives you all the information and tools you need to solve the many dangers that can befall your colony. There's no one-size-fits-all solution to any problem. Need to generate oxygen so your characters don't suffocate? You can use algae to convert small amounts of carbon dioxide to oxygen or use electrolyzers to convert water to oxygen and hydrogen (which can be used to generate power). Need to deal with the carbon dioxide your characters are exhaling? You can use algae, find creatures that breathe it and produce oil, or pump it right out to space. Nearly every problem has multiple solutions and the signs of impending disasters are always there, giving the player ample time to come up with their own solution once they see it coming.This game is the gold standard of the survival colony sim genre. The actions of the characters are predictable and if they do something stupid, there was always something the player could have done to avoid it. There are many, many things that can go wrong, but none of them are ever random or unpredictable. The tech tree is massive and there are plenty of things for your characters to build and do. I feel like even after playing the game for nearly 300 hours I'm still making new discoveries and learning new things to do to make my colonies thrive (or bring them to ruin). It's a game that would easily be worth it at a AAA price point, but it's less than half the price and frequently on sale for under $10.

2015 Re-reviewing this game for 2021 for DLC: The Vanilla Endless legend is a tightly-balanced masterpiece. Asymmetrical factions, streamlined strategic layer with minimal micromanagement, terrific tactical combat, and a great story to boot. If you haven't played it, you definitely should. Many of the elements that Civ 6 added originated here (and still work better here).Unlike Civ 6, because the base game is so tightly designed, DLC is more of a mixed bag. I strongly recommend disabling ALL DLC for the first playthroughs if you pick up the bundle on sale. Good expansions to layer in are the first two:Guardians--Adds big guardian units, legendary deeds and wonders. A pretty good expansion to enable in all games.Forgotten--Adds stealth and espionage and a stealth faction. The stealth faction is an expert faction, I don't recommend it for intermediate players.The next two DLC is more situational:Shifters--Adds a very strong faction that dominates winters and new winter mechanics. These new winter mechanics can be overwhelming if you aren't playing as the Allayi, so you may want to leave it disabled.Tempest--Adds a very cool naval "it comes from the deep" faction as well as naval points of interest. Naval combat is unfortunately anemic compared to land combat, and may not be to everyone's tastes.The final two DLC were outsourced, and suffer from major bugs as well as uninteresting, game-breaking mechanics and un-intuitive UX changes. Inferno--Can be interesting, but very broken. Buggy, unintuitive UI for terraforming. Dust eclipses are just Shifters winters, and add nothing to the game. I leave this expansion uninstalled after playing through the faction once.Symbiosis--Total disappointment, broken, buggy faction that adds a terrible mechanic to the game in the form of Urkans. Not even worth playing once.I still wholeheartedly review the base game, and if you can get the DLC bundle at a discount, go for it. Just be aware that you will want to turn off even the good DLC at first.

2023 Title: Total War: PHARAOH - A Disappointing ExperienceRating: ★☆☆☆☆Total War: PHARAOH, the latest addition to the Total War series, left me thoroughly disappointed and dissatisfied. As an avid fan of the franchise, I had high expectations for this game, but unfortunately, it fell far short of delivering an enjoyable experience.From the very beginning, it became apparent that the game lacked meaningful progression. By turn 80, I had hoped to witness significant developments and face exciting challenges. However, I found myself constantly struggling with food shortages, which severely hindered my ability to build a formidable army or expand my empire. This perpetual struggle made the game feel tedious and frustrating.The inclusion of the "merchant" mechanic felt like a pointless addition. It lacked depth and failed to contribute anything substantial to the gameplay. Moreover, the striking similarities between Total War: PHARAOH and its predecessor, Troy Total War, were impossible to ignore. With only minor changes, it felt like I was playing a recycled version of the same game. Considering the hefty price tag of £49.99, this lack of innovation was unacceptable.The AI in Total War: PHARAOH was abysmal. Their actions and decision-making were illogical and predictable, resulting in lackluster and unchallenging battles. Diplomacy, a crucial aspect of the Total War series, felt utterly pointless in this game. The absence of meaningful interactions and consequences rendered it a wasted opportunity for strategic negotiations and alliances.In conclusion, Total War: PHARAOH failed to meet even the most basic expectations. The lack of progression, underdeveloped mechanics, high price point, and subpar AI make it impossible for me to recommend this game to fellow Total War enthusiasts. It is a disappointing addition to the series and a regrettable purchase.

Early Access Review What a cool, difficult, unintuitive, atmospheric, adorable little game. Once you figure out how to actually control this thing the road opens up before you and it actually becomes a bit more relaxing to play. Infuriatingly the controls cannot be remapped, the sensitivity of the controls cannot even be changed, and the controls can be very, very, VERY twitchy. For a game demanding such diabolically precise control this is a bit inexcusable but hey... Early Access I guess? I cannot imagine even playing this thing with a keyboard, much less doing well with one. Basically impossible. I'm not going to talk about the bugs because other reviews have covered the common ones and there is nothing game breaking or exceptionally bad for this stage of development.Once I did master the controls (I used an xbox 360 controller) I really started enjoying the maps. They're great, and the gameplay is basically Tony Hawk meets 1080 with an emphasis on clean cornering and route selection. The soundtrack is very good but needs more songs, and the game badly needs more maps, more goals per map, and QoL improvements relating to the controls but the bones are absolutely there. Will this develop into an incredible classic to rival the greats of the extreme sports genre? It could. I hope this is the beginning and not basically all we're going to get, as so sadly often happens with other similar Early Access releases.I will update this review as the game develops.

I can very highly recommend this game.GAMEPLAY:The handling feels great, especially after getting more used to the game, lots of fun.Majority of the game will be doing races (Of Course) During the day you will be racing for money in "Legal Races" and during the night you will race for reputation in "Illegal Races". This reputation will act as your level, and unlock more cars, parts, and new activities. All in all, a different but cool mechanicThe night portion functions very interestingly. You race for reputation, after each race you get the base amount of rep that the race rewards. However it is multiplied at the end of the night by your "Heat Level" which can go up to 5. Heat is earned by completing races, having run ins with cops, whether that be during races or in between them, and completing certain collectibles. You finish a night in one of two ways, heading to a garage to reap the rewards, or getting busted by the police, and losing a large portion of the rep you gained and a fair sum of money. This brings me to a topic that many people complain aboutCOPS: Cops during the day will not chase you for literally anything, unless you crash into one. However, at night, if you have any amount of heat, a cop will begin chasing you if you enter its line of sight (Displayed on the map). The part in which people often complain about is the difficulty of escaping the police. I will say that it can be very difficult and overwhelming at times, especially when starting out. However now that I'm further in, I've learned ways to get rid of them quickly and have faster cars to have a better chance. But in the beginning of the game with slower cars, if you don't escape the cops quickly, and allow reinforcements to come, you are in for a bad time. All in all, the cops really aren't TOO bad, you just need to get used to it and progress a little bit. Some tips: duck behind buildings and take lots of turns, go off road if they are a little behind you or about to lose you, and take any jump you see, they will often not follow you or crash if they do.CAMPAIGN: I've seen a few complaints in reviews about the story line being short... honestly, I think it's very well paced and took me a decent amount of time to complete. The main story has some cheesy moments but I genuinely enjoyed it, it came with a couple twists and turns while having decent characters. It isn't some masterpiece, but enjoyable for sure. Along with the main campaign there are multiple side campaigns with smaller characters, each focusing on different types of races. Off-Road, Street, and Drift, all with cars unlocked for completing them.CUSTOMIZATION: People often praise NFS: Underground II for having the best customization, and they're not wrong, it was amazing. However, this is the best we've had since. You can change every single part of your car. One of the best parts is the decal system, there are TONS of pre-generated decals to add, some to collect around the map, and even a huge selection of base shapes to make incredibly intricate designs. Along with this comes the community for these designs, you can upload and download designs from other players, which is a very cool feature. I've gone through and it's crazy how detailed some people can get. Along with the visual customization, there is an insane amount of tuning that can be done to your car. you can even engine swap. the fact that the game lets me put a V8 into a civic is great. **No visual customization effects performance, and no performance upgrades effect your visuals.**MULTIPLAYER:The multiplayer functions in a really simple, yet enjoyable way. It's essentially the same as playing solo but with other players roaming the map. You can do solo races, story missions and just about anything on your own, or invite friends to do the races and such with you. (You can also invite the whole lobby to races) I've experienced no griefing, just people who pull up to check out your car. or try to drag race for fun. (However I'm sure someone out there will just ram into cars a bunch because that's just in every game somewhere)CONCLUSION:All in all, NFS Heat is a great game, my biggest issue is probably the fact that the cars spit fire a little too much, and that's one of the smallest details about the game, so that should tell you something. If you like cars, you'll love this, and even if you don't you might enjoy it. A friend of mine who has never shown much interest in cars is now looking more into them and having a great time with the game too. It's a low stress game and a great way to relax, with a great amount of fun and even a huge amount of tiny details and easter eggs referencing the classic NFS games. TL:DRGreat game :) Buy it and have some fun

2019 Total War: Three Kingdoms embraces the story it's inspired by, Romance of the Three Kingdoms by Luo Guanzhong, rather than strict historical accuracy. Soldiers can run around the battlefield seemingly forever without getting tired. Their leaders are larger-than-life figures with complicated backstories and rivalries, who carry legendary spears and are able to defeat entire units single-handed. There's an option to turn some of these things off at the start of a campaign by engaging Records Mode, if you want stamina to play a more important role in unit repositioning or to get rid of the duels and get generals' bodyguards to do most of their fighting instead. The alternative, Romance Mode, feels like an honest embrace of what Total War has really been all along, though. It's a version of history that's closer to an epic movie, where the broad sweep is familiar but subtleties are ignored whenever they would be inconvenient to the action.Diplomacy is one of the most substantial and welcome areas to be changed. Where before there was so much guesswork involved that dealing with rival nations felt like passing notes in class and then waiting for an answer ("Do you want to form a defensive alliance with me, y/n"), in Three Kingdoms it's completely transparent. Depending on the state of my relationship with a rival, I can make various kinds of offers and deals to them. I can offer trade, marriages, and territory swaps. I can menace them for food and cash. Or I can charm or strong-arm them into joining me as an ally, vassal, or subject.Leaders die and are replaced by their offspring or their partners. Managing my empire’s nobles is similarly invigorating, tasking me with taking care to keep my extended family in a state of reciprocal contentment. (It strikes me that this skill, rather than martial prowess, is the true mark of great leaders of the past.) Three Kingdoms makes people management feel like it’s a game in itself, rather than the clumsy chore it’s so often been in past games.The real-time battles are more immediately exciting than the numbers game. Units with crossbows chunter out steady volley after volley of bolts, horseriders form up into wedges at the last minute and charge, infantry lock down their shields and absorb damage. An army can have three generals, each with a retinue of up to six units. This lends itself to balanced armies with one general for cavalry, one for infantry, and one for archers and catapults. Which is not to say you can't make unbalanced or hyper-specialised armies, it just feels wrong.Generals have personalities that suit their roles, expressed as they banter with each other during battles. They even gain traits and develop rivalries and friendships with each other the longer they spend together. You want to build them and arm them like party members in an RPG. While generals have attack animations right out of kung-fu movies, when ordinary soldiers collide there's a lot of milling around and swiping at the air going on.Verdict:Just buy it! - IGN, PC Gamer, The Kotaku review, TechSpot, GamePlanet, GameSpot, Metacritic, Polygon, Destructoid, Ranker, GamesRadar and Dr.New

Dragon's Dogma 2 is a fantastic game, but not for everyone, and you gonna have to decide for yourself, reading/watching reviews from multiple sources, if the game is for you or not.Note: I haven't finished the game yet, but I am almost at endgame, with 120 hours played so far: I took my time to explore and find as much as I could and to do as many quests as I could. So far I had an absolute blast, and I would restart the game from scratch tomorrow if I could (just to say I would do it all over again).Positives- For me it has one of the best exploration gameplay I experienced in a long time: there is a ton of stuff packed in the environments and exploration is always rewarded.- Combat is so much fun and being able to change among 10 different vocations at will keeps the combat always fresh and engaging. Climbing on monster is a lot of fun and every battle is a surprise (and usually a messy one).- Vocations variety: every vocation/class (there are 10) plays completely different from one another and they are all fun (although some more than other depending on your taste). Being able to have only 4 abilities equipped there is a lot of room to play each vocation as you like it. The augment system is also really cool, allowing you to use Augments from other vocations once unlocked. This provides a ton of customization on your character build.- Pawns: the Pawn system is absolutely unique and I would never thought I would have so much fun playing in a party of 3 AI controlled characters. The system works well enough (without being perfect of course), but what they achieved with Pawns behavior is pretty incredible. I really hope they will keep refine and improve the system because is one of the most unique feature of this game.- Equipment: the equipment system is simple, streamlined and easy to understand use. Upgrading items is effortless because you will drop 95% of the materials you need to upgrade your armor/weapons while playing, and the missing 5% it's easy enough to find without too much grind.- Quest intertwined with one another: although questing is not the best feature in the game, I loved the fact that many quests and NPCs are intertwined and connected: it gives a feeling that the world and the characters are believable.- Emerging gameplay/storytelling: the game creates a unique game experience for each player by generating random events while you are exploring, so two players rarely have the same experience. It's easy to get lost and sidetracked while exploring the world and I feel this is one of the most fun things in a game.Negatives- Enemies variety: the variety of enemies could be bigger (although for me it's ok and I still enjoy combat a lot) in particular in comparison do the original game.- Dungeons size and variety: unfortunately dungeons consists of mostly caves (although I never found 2 identical ones in the world) and usually they are not too big. There are a couple of really big caves (the biggest close the the start of the game) several mid size caves and many mid-small caves. Some caves are more packed with enemies than others so the experience may vary. The big/medium size ones are usually a lot of fun, while the small ones feels a little small/empty (basically a place to let you find some loot).- Difficulty: the game difficulty doesn't scale too well inn the long run, becoming easier and easier the longer you play: I wished the game remained harder and more challenging in the long run.- Camera behavior in narrow places: the game camera often gets bumped into walls/things (especially during combat) that could be frustrating: I hope Capcom will improve the camera behavior in the future to improve the experience (this is NOT a deal-breaker, the game is totally playable: this is just a personal pain point and I wanted to mention it.Controversial Topics- Performance: I played on a beefy PC ( AMD Ryzen 9 7900X, 32 GB of RAM, Geforce RTX 4070, Western Digital Black hard disks) and I had no performance issues whatsoever. Yes in the 2 big capital cities (Vermund and Battahl) the framrate drops a bit but for me was never unplayable and the framrate dips never really bothered me. Out of these 2 big cities performance were almost flawless for me. It may depend on your machine and on your settings: in my case to play it safe I turned ray trace off and I enable DLS on performance mode, and the game still looks great at 3840 x 2160 played on a big 65" TV. I also tried the game on my 27" pc monitors at 2560x1440 and the game was running great (and I am sure I could have enabled raytracing and disable DLS on without any issue).- Fast travel: I heard way too much drama about the lack of fast travel and I don't agree. Fast travel is limited at the beginning of the game for good reasons, because the developers wants you to take your time and explore the world without jumping all over the place (that break immersion and flow). From mid game onward you will have enough "Port Crystals" (the device to teleport to) and "Ferrystones" (the object that allow to teleport) that fast travel will not be a problem when necessary. Of course you have to choose WHEN is important to fast travel and when you can instead take an Oxcart or walk. It's part of the enjoyment of the game for me and I am 100% fine with it.- One save slot: even on this topic I don't agree with the people complaining about it. I feel that the fact of having one save is a good thing and encourage you to commit to the choices you make and to the errors you inevitably make. Also on PC is super easy to quit the game (ATL + F4) to prevent the game to save in a situation you don't like the outcome. Also in reality you have 2 save slots: the autosave/manual save and the Inn/House save slot: if you use these 2 in a smart way you will have no problems.- Micro-transaction: I heard so much nonsense about this ... yes micro-transactions are there BUT they are absolutely unnecessary and invisible to the player: the game NEVER mentions them and they are absolutely not providing you with anything that you can't also obtain for yourself playing the game. So just ignore the transactions and play the game as if they don't exist.Of course I would have preferred that micro-transactions were not there (I personally HATE them and I never wasted money on micro-transactions in my life) but this what big companies like Capcom do since a long time: just vote with your wallet and ignore them: they implement micros and you just ignore them.ConclusionAll in all Dragon's Dogma 2 is a fantastic game if you love action RPG with a big focus on world exploration and discovery this is the game for you.

This is a rather difficult game to review as a non-Warhammer fan. Because from my perspective it is a competent hack-and-slash-shooter devoid of personable characters or any intriguing plot-elements. But to a Warhammer fan it is grimdark-personified; each human a cog in the Emperor's ever-marching war machine which renders every man and women as barren of life as the land itself.Thus, this is less of a review of the story, and more so the game itself. Graphically, it looks rather stunning--with majestic vistas of the skull-regaled factories of the city worlds to the gruesome, steaming swamps of the backwater worlds. And while some people have reported issues of high-temps and crashes--issues that should be looked into and addressed--for the most part, and across a variety of systems, the game seems to run rather well. That shouldn't be a pro for any game, it should just be the standard. But it's 2024, so... bar's been pretty low for a while now.The overall gameplay loop consists of running down un-inspired corridors to face random-sized groups of enemies. And while the campaign is mercifully and justifiably short, devoid of any diversity of gameplay or objectives, what you're then left with is the Operations Mode. Best described as a Raid Mode of sorts. You're expected to run through these over and over to level up your character(s) and your equipment to then run these maps on a higher difficulty. And therein shines both the game's main strength and its main flaw. In the grim darkness of the far future, there is only war. And that motto does a lot to encapsulate the gameplay loop. There is only combat, and random objectives that rely on more combat. So it's a damn good thing then that the combat feels so damn good. Taking a chainsaw sword to a group of alien-baddies twice as short and thrice as frail as you will have you feeling like the Emperor's Chosen; pistols sound like a cannon and kick just as hard, and destroy just as much. Sniper Rifles are downright busted in the right hands. And I'll never, ever tire of grappling toward an enemy to deliver a skull-crushing dropkick. It speaks volumes that in a game with such limited enemy-variety and such non-existent diversity of gameplay I never got bored of the combat. It is fun, fluid and epic. It rewards aggression by granting you shields for each enemy killed through executions or perfect parries, and the ability to regen a bit of health lost to attacks if you're quick enough to retaliate. What isn't epic however is the un-inspired level-design, the lackluster repetition, and the horrid war of attrition that each mission eventually boils down to. Each mission has a fixed layout and main objective, they don't change from match to match; instead, what does change is the placement of enemies, the number of them, and the amount required of each objective. Sometimes you'll be forced to place two bombs, another time you'll be forced to place five. And while this doesn't do a whole lot to shake the tedium of repetition, what it does do--however--is change the difficulty rather drastically. You can run into a couple of tiny one-shot guys one run, and a horde of huge, melee-focused guys another. And that would be fine if it wasn't for the limitations of their combat system. Because while it is fun, it is also rather limited in your ability to utilize it for your own survival. Like I said above, you can regen a bit of health lost if you're quick enough with a melee attack, and you can regain shields through executions or a shot to the head through the use of a perfect parry. What this does is promote an aggressive playstyle that rewards parries of the smaller enemies, and the executions of the larger ones. However, larger, melee-based elites don't give shields for perfect parries. And so, with the random spawns of enemies, you could find yourself surrounded by ten melee-based enemies and be unable to regain shields--meaning you'll watch your health dwindle and be unable to do anything about it. Worse, if you're then at the same time getting pummelled at range, which completely removes the ability to act quick enough that you regain a bit of lost health. Well, you can get better perks, of course. But that doesn't change that fact that random spikes in difficulty that skill cannot compensate for aren't fun; difficulty doesn't mean tediousness. And with a failed run meaning the potential loss of gathered upgrade materials, it being up to chance rather than skill is frustrating at best, and infuriating at worst. I'm not max level yet, and so maybe there are more perks to counteract such things, but it doesn't make the grind to get to max level any less annoying.Class Progression is rather limited. You've no choice in what perk to begin with, meaning there's not really any build-variety. Weapon Progression offers a bit more variety, allowing you to choose whether you favour less speed and more damage, or vice versa. Multiplayer is fine. It's a nice little relic of the early 2000s obsession with tacked-on versus modes. Little unbalanced, perhaps. But all the more nostalgic for it. It has a rather limited customisation-system. Grapple-hook dudes can use a Knife and a Sword but cannot use a power-fist. Shield-Bros can use a power-fist but cannot use a hammer, etc, etc. Fans might blame that on lore--but if that's the case, I don't really see why you'd offer customization at all. Better then to do perks, rather than equipment. I do find it rather strange how unwelcoming the game is of newcomers. It doesn't go out of its way to ever explain any role, word or lore-based concept. And while one could argue that it is a game for fans, thinking that a Triple-A publisher would ever make a game of this size and not want to attract newcomers is downright naive. If you're not already a fan you'll either be real confused about a lot of what they're talking about, or you'll be spending half your playtime on the wiki. Overall it's a decent hack-and-slash-shooter that won't ever impress any non-Warhammer fan or person who enjoys a greater diversity of gameplay; it's all corridors and button-presses and horde-styled defence finales. But on the flip-side, it seems to be a delight for Warhammer fans; a crunchy, blood-soaked romp through a world of stainless steel and great, towering cathedrals, filled with horrid tech bonded with flesh, robot-skulls, and weapons galore, all of it in the Glorious name of the Emperor!
